NAMES.name: area_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Area enclosed by a nested equilibrium flux-surface contour in the poloidal cross-section, used as a radial geometry measure.
NAMES.long:
The flux-surface area is the poloidal cross-sectional area enclosed by a closed equilibrium flux surface. It is a geometric measure of the size of the region inside a given magnetic surface, distinct from the full three-dimensional [surface area of the flux surface](name:surface_area_of_flux_surface). The outermost value approaches the [area of the plasma boundary](name:area_of_plasma_boundary) when the selected surface is the last closed flux surface.

For a flux surface labeled by [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux), the enclosed area is

$$
A(\psi) = \int_{S(\psi)} dR\,dZ
$$

where $S(\psi)$ is the region enclosed by the flux-surface contour in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system, with $R$ the major radius, $\phi$ the toroidal angle, and $Z$ the vertical coordinate.

It is computed from equilibrium reconstruction by locating the closed flux contour and integrating the area inside that contour in the poloidal plane. Magnetic measurements, kinetic pressure constraints, and internal magnetic diagnostics can all affect the reconstructed contour geometry and therefore this area.

Typical values range from about 0.1-5 m^2 for small and medium tokamaks and can exceed 10 m^2 in large reactor-scale equilibria. The value increases monotonically from near zero at the magnetic axis to the boundary area for well-nested flux surfaces, while non-nested or open-field-line regions are outside its validity.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the oriented poloidal area element $dR\,dZ$ is taken with the contour orientation consistent with the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ basis.

NAMES.name: area_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Poloidal cross-sectional area enclosed by the last closed flux surface, measuring the size of the plasma column in a meridional plane.
NAMES.long:
The plasma-boundary area is the poloidal cross-sectional area enclosed by the last closed flux surface. It characterizes the geometric size of the confined plasma and is distinct from the full toroidal [surface area of the plasma boundary](name:surface_area_of_plasma_boundary). Together with the [poloidal length of the plasma boundary](name:poloidal_length_of_plasma_boundary), it provides a compact measure of boundary size and shape.

For a closed boundary contour in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the signed area can be written using Green's theorem:

$$
A_b = \frac{1}{2}\oint_{\partial\Omega_b} \left(R\,dZ - Z\,dR\right)
$$

where $A_b$ is the boundary area and $\partial\Omega_b$ is the last-closed-flux-surface contour enclosing the plasma domain $\Omega_b$.

The area is computed from equilibrium reconstruction by locating the separatrix or limiting boundary and evaluating the enclosed poloidal contour area by quadrature. It is also used to compare nested surfaces through [area of a flux surface](name:area_of_flux_surface) and to normalize shape metrics such as [outer triangularity](name:outer_triangularity). Typical values range from about 0.1-5 m^2 in compact or medium-size tokamaks and 5-25 m^2 in large tokamak plasmas, depending mainly on minor radius and elongation.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the plasma-boundary contour is traversed counter-clockwise in the poloidal $(R, Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: average_magnetic_flux_due_to_external_coil
NAMES.short: Area-weighted average over the plasma poloidal cross-section of the magnetic-flux contribution produced by currents in external coils. The vector components correspond to the relevant oriented flux components used in equilibrium force balance, excluding flux generated by plasma currents.
NAMES.long:
Average magnetic flux due to external coils is the cross-section-averaged contribution to magnetic flux from currents flowing in coils outside the plasma. It represents the vacuum-field part of the flux linkage seen by the plasma, separated into the relevant oriented flux components for equilibrium modeling and excluding the self-field contribution from plasma current.

For a plasma poloidal cross-section $A_p$ in the meridional $(R,Z)$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ system, the area-weighted average is

$$
\langle \boldsymbol{\Phi}_{\mathrm{ext}} \rangle = \frac{1}{A_p}\int_{A_p} \boldsymbol{\Phi}_{\mathrm{ext}}(R,Z)\, dA
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\Phi}_{\mathrm{ext}}(R,Z)$ is the vector of local external-coil flux contributions, $dA$ is the poloidal cross-section area element, and $A_p=\int_{A_p} dA$. The weighting is uniform in poloidal cross-section area unless a more specific flux-surface or volume average is defined by a related quantity.

In practice this quantity is computed from external-coil currents using vacuum magnetic-field Green functions, a coil-current circuit model, or an equilibrium reconstruction that separates coil-produced flux from plasma-produced flux. The averaging domain is normally the plasma cross-section bounded by the last closed flux surface or by the reconstructed plasma boundary used for the equilibrium.

Typical magnitudes range from 0.001-10 Wb in tokamak equilibria, depending on machine size, coil currents, plasma boundary location, and whether the component represents a poloidal or toroidal flux contribution.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetic field contribution from the external coils threads the oriented surface associated with the corresponding flux component in the direction of that surface's positive normal.

NAMES.name: beta
NAMES.short: The beta quantity is a two-component equilibrium vector collecting poloidal beta and toroidal beta. Its components compare volume-averaged plasma kinetic pressure with the magnetic pressure associated with the equilibrium poloidal field and the reference toroidal field.
NAMES.long:
Beta is a dimensionless equilibrium measure of how strongly plasma kinetic pressure competes with magnetic pressure. The paired quantity $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ collects the [poloidal_beta](name:poloidal_plasma_beta) and [toroidal_beta](name:toroidal_beta) components, with the first normalized to an equilibrium poloidal-field reference and the second to a toroidal-field reference.

The paired beta quantity is defined from the plasma-volume-averaged pressure as:

$$
\boldsymbol{\beta} = \left(\beta_\mathrm{p}, \beta_\mathrm{t}\right) = \left(\frac{2\mu_0\langle p\rangle}{B_{\mathrm{p,ref}}^2}, \frac{2\mu_0\langle p\rangle}{B_{\mathrm{t,ref}}^2}\right)
$$

where $\langle p\rangle$ is the volume average of the total kinetic pressure inside the last closed flux surface and $\mu_0$ is the permeability of free space. For the equilibrium beta components, $B_{\mathrm{p,ref}}$ is the magnitude of the boundary-averaged poloidal field inferred from the enclosed plasma current, commonly written $B_{\mathrm{p,ref}}=\mu_0 |I_p|/L_\mathrm{pol}$ with $L_\mathrm{pol}$ the poloidal perimeter of the last closed flux surface, and $B_{\mathrm{t,ref}}$ is the magnitude of the vacuum toroidal field at the reference major radius $R_0$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ system, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.

In practice, the components are computed from an equilibrium reconstruction using the reconstructed pressure distribution, plasma boundary, total plasma current, and reference toroidal field. The poloidal component is especially sensitive to plasma current and boundary shape, while the toroidal component is primarily a measure of pressure relative to the operating toroidal field strength.

Typical conventional tokamak values are $0.1-2$ for $\beta_\mathrm{p}$ and $0.005-0.05$ for $\beta_\mathrm{t}$, with higher toroidal beta values, about $0.05-0.4$, possible in spherical tokamak regimes. Both components are dimensionless and non-negative for physical pressure and magnetic-field magnitudes.

NAMES.name: elongation
NAMES.short: Ratio of plasma-boundary vertical half-height to horizontal minor radius in the cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, measuring vertical stretching.
NAMES.long:
Elongation, denoted $\kappa$, describes the vertical stretching of a closed flux surface or plasma boundary in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. For a boundary-like value it summarizes the overall shape of the last closed flux surface, while asymmetric shaping is resolved by [upper elongation](name:upper_elongation) and [lower elongation](name:lower_elongation_of_plasma_boundary).

A common geometric definition is

$$
\kappa = \frac{Z_{\max}-Z_{\min}}{2a}
$$

where $Z_{\max}$ and $Z_{\min}$ are the upper and lower vertical extrema of the flux-surface contour, and $a = (R_{\max}-R_{\min})/2$ is the horizontal minor radius from the outer and inner radial extrema $R_{\max}$ and $R_{\min}$.

Elongation is obtained from magnetic equilibrium reconstruction using magnetic probes, flux loops, pressure constraints, and shape measurements that determine the plasma-boundary contour. It is used with boundary position quantities such as [major radius of plasma boundary](name:major_radius_of_plasma_boundary) and shape parameters such as [outer triangularity](name:outer_triangularity) to characterize plasma shaping and vertical stability.

Representative tokamak boundary values are about 1.0 for a circular cross-section, 1.5-2.0 in many elongated H-mode plasmas, and up to about 2.5 in strongly shaped configurations before vertical-stability and control limits become restrictive.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $Z_{\max}$ lies above $Z_{\min}$ in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame and the horizontal minor radius $a$ is positive.

NAMES.name: inner_major_radius_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of the high-field-side midplane crossing of a nested magnetic flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The inner major radius identifies where a given nested magnetic flux surface intersects the outboard-inboard midplane on the high-field side of the magnetic axis. Together with the [outer major radius of the same flux surface](name:outer_major_radius_of_flux_surface), it defines the radial width and Shafranov-shifted placement of that surface relative to the [major radius of the magnetic axis](name:major_radius_of_magnetic_axis).

For a flux surface labeled by poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$, the inner major radius can be defined by the inboard midplane root:

$$
R_{\mathrm{in}}(\psi_s) = \min\{R : \psi(R, Z_{\mathrm{axis}}) = \psi_s\}
$$

where $R$ is major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $Z_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the vertical coordinate of the magnetic axis, and $\psi_s$ labels the selected flux surface.

This quantity is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by finding flux-contour intersections with the midplane defined by the magnetic-axis height. It is constrained mainly by magnetic measurements and pressure-current consistency, and it is often interpreted alongside the [major radius of the geometric axis](name:major_radius_of_geometric_axis) to separate geometric centering from magnetic-axis displacement.

Typical values span about 0.5-3 m in medium-size tokamaks and about 4-6 m in large devices, depending on plasma major radius, minor radius, elongation, and boundary position.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the flux-surface intersection lies at positive major radius $R$ measured outward from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: inner_triangularity
NAMES.short: Dimensionless boundary-shape parameter measuring the high-field-side D-shaping displacement of the plasma boundary relative to an untriangular elliptical cross-section.
NAMES.long:
Inner triangularity describes the triangular distortion of the high-field-side portion of the last closed flux surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. It refines the global [triangularity](name:triangularity) by isolating the inboard-side contribution, while [outer triangularity](name:outer_triangularity) describes the corresponding low-field-side shaping.

A local geometric definition can be written as the normalized radial offset of the inboard boundary from an elliptical reference contour:

$$
\delta_{\rm in} = \frac{R_{\rm ell,in}(Z_*) - R_{\rm b,in}(Z_*)}{a}
$$

where $R_{\rm b,in}(Z_*)$ is the inboard boundary major radius at the reference vertical location $Z_*$, $R_{\rm ell,in}(Z_*)$ is the matching untriangular elliptical-contour major radius, and $a$ is the plasma minor radius. This form makes the quantity dimensionless and separates triangular distortion from size measures such as [major radius of the plasma boundary](name:major_radius_of_plasma_boundary).

Inner triangularity is computed from reconstructed plasma-boundary contours constrained by magnetic probes, flux measurements, and internal profile or polarimetric information when available. Representative values in shaped tokamak equilibria are 0.1-0.5, with weakly shaped or nearly elliptical plasmas near 0 and strongly D-shaped configurations approaching about 0.6. It is interpreted together with [upper triangularity](name:upper_triangularity), [lower triangularity](name:lower_triangularity), and [minor triangularity](name:triangularity) to characterize asymmetry of the full boundary shape.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the high-field-side triangular distortion displaces the relevant plasma-boundary point toward smaller major radius $R$ relative to the corresponding untriangular elliptical reference contour.

NAMES.name: internal_inductance
NAMES.short: Dimensionless measure of plasma current-density peaking derived from the volume-integrated poloidal magnetic-field energy.
NAMES.long:
Internal inductance measures how strongly the plasma current density is peaked through its contribution to the poloidal magnetic-field energy inside the plasma. Larger values indicate more magnetic energy stored at smaller minor radius and are closely related to the effective [plasma inductance](name:plasma_inductance) that enters the global current balance.

A common equilibrium definition is

$$
l_i = \frac{2}{R_0 \mu_0^2 I_p^2}\int_V B_p^2\,dV
$$

where $R_0$ is the reference major radius, often associated with the [major radius of the magnetic axis](name:major_radius_of_magnetic_axis), $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability, $I_p$ is the total toroidal plasma current, $B_p$ is the poloidal magnetic-field magnitude, and the integral is over the plasma volume. The poloidal field is constrained by the boundary magnetic-flux geometry, including the [poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary).

Internal inductance is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction using magnetic probes, flux loops, plasma boundary constraints, and, when available, internal current-profile diagnostics such as motional-Stark-effect polarimetry. Representative tokamak values are about 0.5-1.5 for broad to moderately peaked current profiles, with values above 1.5 indicating strongly peaked current density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the poloidal magnetic-field energy inside the plasma is nonzero.

NAMES.name: lower_elongation_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Ratio of the plasma-boundary vertical extent below the geometric axis to the horizontal minor radius in the cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Lower elongation describes the vertical stretching of the lower half of the last closed plasma boundary relative to its horizontal size. It separates up-down asymmetric shaping from the whole-boundary [elongation](name:elongation) and complements [upper elongation](name:upper_elongation), which measures the corresponding upper half.

A common geometric definition is

$$
\kappa_\mathrm{lower} = \frac{Z_\mathrm{geo} - Z_\mathrm{min}}{a}
$$

where $Z_\mathrm{geo}$ is the vertical coordinate of the geometric axis, $Z_\mathrm{min}$ is the lowest vertical coordinate of the plasma boundary, and $a = (R_\mathrm{max}-R_\mathrm{min})/2$ is the horizontal minor radius formed from the outermost and innermost boundary major radii in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

It is obtained from magnetic-equilibrium reconstruction constrained by external magnetic measurements and, when available, profile or polarimetric constraints that improve the boundary shape. Boundary-shape families often use lower elongation together with [lower triangularity](name:lower_triangularity), [lower inner squareness](name:lower_inner_squareness), and [lower outer squareness](name:lower_outer_squareness) to describe the lower divertor-facing contour.

Typical values are near 1 for nearly circular plasmas, 1.4-2.0 for shaped tokamak H-mode equilibria, and can exceed 2 in strongly elongated lower single-null configurations before vertical-stability limits become restrictive.

NAMES.name: lower_inner_squareness
NAMES.short: Dimensionless boundary-shape parameter measuring how the lower inboard quadrant departs from an elliptical plasma cross-section toward a squarer or boxier contour.
NAMES.long:
Lower inner squareness describes fourth-order shaping of the plasma boundary in the lower inboard quadrant of a poloidal cross-section. It separates corner-like boxiness from elongation and triangularity, complementing [upper inner squareness](name:upper_inner_squareness), [lower outer squareness](name:lower_outer_squareness), and [upper outer squareness](name:upper_outer_squareness) for the other three boundary quadrants.

A common geometric definition compares the reconstructed boundary point with a matched elliptical reference in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame:

$$
\zeta_{\mathrm{li}} = \frac{\left(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{b,li}} - \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ell,li}}\right) \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{li}}}{a}
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{b,li}}$ is the lower-inboard boundary point, $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{ell,li}}$ is the corresponding point on the matched ellipse, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_{\mathrm{li}}$ points toward decreasing $R$ and decreasing $Z$, and $a$ is the minor radius. [Inner triangularity](name:inner_triangularity) describes an inboard left-right displacement of the boundary, whereas squareness measures the residual corner shape after the lower and inner extrema are fixed.

The parameter is computed from equilibrium reconstruction by fitting the last closed flux contour or separatrix and evaluating the lower-inboard quadrant relative to an elliptical reference shape. Magnetic diagnostics, plasma boundary imaging, and flux-surface reconstruction constrain the boundary points used in the fit.

Common values are near 0 for an approximately elliptical boundary, about -0.2 to 0.2 for moderate shaping, and can approach absolute values of 0.3-0.4 in strongly shaped scenarios.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the lower inboard boundary in the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame lies farther toward the lower-inner corner than the elliptical reference shape used in the squareness definition.

NAMES.name: lower_outer_squareness
NAMES.short: Dimensionless lower-outboard plasma-boundary shape parameter measuring how the lower outer quadrant departs from an ellipse toward a squarer or rounder contour.
NAMES.long:
Lower outer squareness describes the fourth-order shape of the plasma boundary in the lower outboard quadrant. It complements triangularity and elongation by resolving whether the lower outer corner of the last closed flux surface is more rectangular or more rounded than an ellipse with the same main size and triangularity. The other quadrants are described by [upper outer squareness](name:upper_outer_squareness), [lower inner squareness](name:lower_inner_squareness), and [upper inner squareness](name:upper_inner_squareness).

A practical geometric definition compares the actual boundary position with a reference ellipse in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height:

$$
\zeta_{lo} = \frac{R_{lo} - R_{\mathrm{ell},lo}}{a}
$$

where $\zeta_{lo}$ is lower outer squareness, $R_{lo}$ is the boundary major radius at the lower outer shaping point, $R_{\mathrm{ell},lo}$ is the corresponding reference-ellipse major radius, and $a$ is the plasma minor radius; the three length variables are expressed consistently.

It is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction or boundary fitting using magnetic measurements, flux-surface constraints, and plasma shape control targets. Representative values in tokamak equilibria are about -0.2 to 0.2 for modest shaping and can approach -0.4 to 0.4 in strongly shaped scenarios. It is often interpreted together with [outer triangularity](name:outer_triangularity), which controls the outboard midplane indentation rather than the quadrant squareness.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the lower outer boundary point lies at larger major radius than the corresponding reference ellipse.

NAMES.name: lower_triangularity
NAMES.short: Dimensionless measure of the inward or outward horizontal displacement of the lower plasma-boundary apex relative to the reference axis and minor radius.
NAMES.long:
Lower triangularity describes the geometric shaping of the lower half of a tokamak plasma cross-section. It complements [upper triangularity](name:upper_triangularity) and contributes to the overall boundary distortion summarized by [triangularity](name:triangularity), with stronger positive values corresponding to a more D-shaped lower boundary.

A common definition uses the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height:

$$
\delta_l = \frac{R_{\rm ref} - R_l}{a}
$$

where $R_{\rm ref}$ is the reference-axis major radius, $R_l$ is the major radius of the lower boundary apex, and $a$ is the minor radius used for the same flux surface or boundary. Alternative equilibrium conventions may choose the magnetic axis or geometric axis for $R_{\rm ref}$, but the quantity remains a dimensionless lower-boundary shaping parameter.

Lower triangularity is computed from reconstructed magnetic equilibria by fitting or tracing the plasma boundary contour constrained by magnetic measurements, pressure information, and internal magnetic diagnostics when available. It is used with [inner triangularity](name:inner_triangularity) and [outer triangularity](name:outer_triangularity) to distinguish localized shaping from a single global boundary descriptor.

Representative values in diverted tokamaks range from about -0.2 to 0.6, with advanced-shape plasmas often operating near 0.2-0.5 in the lower half. Near-zero values correspond to an approximately elliptical lower boundary, while negative values indicate outward displacement of the lower apex.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the lower extremum of the plasma boundary lies at smaller major radius $R$ than the reference axis used in the triangularity definition.

NAMES.name: magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Equilibrium magnetic-field vector in the plasma, whose direction and strength set field-line geometry, charged-particle gyromotion, and magnetohydrodynamic force balance.
NAMES.long:
The magnetic field is the equilibrium vector field that confines charged particles, defines magnetic flux surfaces, and supplies the Lorentz force in magnetohydrodynamic balance. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height; its projections correspond to the radial, toroidal, and vertical magnetic-field components.

The field decomposition is

$$
\mathbf{B} = B_R \hat{R} + B_\phi \hat{\phi} + B_Z \hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, $B_R$ is the radial component, $B_\phi$ is the toroidal component, $B_Z$ is the vertical component, and $(\hat{R}, \hat{\phi}, \hat{Z})$ are the cylindrical basis vectors. In equilibrium modeling, this field is constrained together with [magnetic_flux](name:magnetic_flux), [magnetic_shear](name:magnetic_shear), [internal_inductance](name:internal_inductance), and [beta](name:beta) through force balance between pressure gradients and electromagnetic forces.

The magnetic field is inferred from external magnetic probes, flux loops, polarimetry, motional-Stark-effect measurements, and equilibrium reconstruction. Representative tokamak values are 1-6 T for the dominant toroidal field, 0.1-1 T for the poloidal field in high-current plasmas, and smaller radial components in nearly axisymmetric equilibria.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a component of $\mathbf{B}$ points along the corresponding positive direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ basis: outward in $+R$, increasing toroidal angle in $+\phi$, or upward in $+Z$.

NAMES.name: magnetic_flux
NAMES.short: Magnetic flux in equilibrium flux-surface space, with poloidal and toroidal contributions that label nested surfaces and set field-line helicity.
NAMES.long:
Magnetic flux measures the amount of magnetic field threading an oriented surface in an equilibrium configuration. In magnetically confined plasmas, the poloidal and toroidal flux components define nested magnetic surfaces, connect directly to the safety-factor family through field-line helicity, and provide the flux geometry underlying quantities such as [magnetic shear](name:magnetic_shear) and [internal inductance](name:internal_inductance).

For a surface $S$ with oriented area element $d\mathbf{S}$, the magnetic flux $\Phi$ is defined from the [magnetic field](name:magnetic_field) $\mathbf{B}$ by

$$
\Phi = \int_S \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{S}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector and $d\mathbf{S}$ is the outward or conventionally oriented surface element. The component [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux) labels equilibrium flux surfaces, while [toroidal magnetic flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux) measures the field threading a poloidal cross-section; their radial variation determines the local field-line pitch.

Magnetic flux is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction constrained by magnetic probes, flux loops, pressure information, and internal field-angle measurements such as polarimetry or motional-Stark-effect diagnostics. It is also checked against global electromagnetic quantities, including stored magnetic energy and pressure balance metrics related to [beta](name:beta).

Typical absolute flux magnitudes span about 0.1-5 Wb in medium-size tokamaks and can exceed 10 Wb in large high-current devices, depending on plasma current, toroidal field, and plasma size.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetic field component normal to the chosen oriented surface points along the surface normal defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame; for horizontal poloidal-flux disks this corresponds to $B_Z$ in the $+Z$ direction, and for toroidal flux through a poloidal cross-section the normal follows increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: magnetic_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short: Magnetic-flux perturbation produced by pressure-driven diamagnetic drift currents, used to constrain plasma stored energy and magnetization in equilibrium analysis.
NAMES.long:
Diamagnetic magnetic flux is the flux linked by the magnetic-field perturbation generated when plasma pressure gradients drive diamagnetic drift currents. It provides an integral measure of the plasma magnetization and is closely related to the pressure contribution that also affects [flux-surface-averaged magnetic field] and equilibrium quantities such as [safety factor](name:safety_factor).

A useful definition is the linked perturbation flux through a chosen surface $S$:

$$
\Phi_{\rm dia} = \int_S \delta \mathbf{B}_{\rm dia}\cdot d\mathbf{S}
$$

where $\Phi_{\rm dia}$ is the diamagnetic flux, $\delta \mathbf{B}_{\rm dia}$ is the magnetic-field perturbation produced by the diamagnetic drift current, and $d\mathbf{S}$ is the oriented surface element. The associated current is driven by pressure gradients, with the leading magnetized-plasma scaling $\mathbf{j}_{\rm dia} \sim \mathbf{B}\times\nabla p / B^2$, where $p$ is plasma pressure and $B$ is magnetic-field magnitude.

It is measured with diamagnetic flux loops or compensated magnetic-loop systems and is also inferred in equilibrium reconstruction together with magnetic and kinetic constraints. The directional component [poloidal magnetic flux due to diamagnetic drift](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift) resolves the same physical contribution into the poloidal-flux channel, while [toroidal magnetic flux due to poloidal current](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_due_to_poloidal_current) describes a different current-driven flux contribution. Representative magnitudes range from 10^-3-10^-1 Wb in medium-size tokamaks and can approach order 1 Wb in large, high-pressure plasmas.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the diamagnetic-flux contribution is linked with magnetic-field perturbation in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: magnetic_flux_due_to_poloidal_current
NAMES.short: Toroidal-field magnetic-flux contribution generated by poloidal current in an equilibrium current decomposition. It denotes the flux of that current-driven magnetic field through specified oriented surfaces; in axisymmetric equilibria the canonical component is the toroidal magnetic flux through a poloidal cross-section.
NAMES.long:
Magnetic flux due to poloidal current is the surface integral of the magnetic-field contribution produced by electric currents flowing in poloidal directions. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, poloidal current flows in planes spanned by $R$ and $Z$ and generates primarily the toroidal magnetic-field component $B_\phi$; therefore the principal flux contribution is toroidal through a poloidal cross-section. In non-axisymmetric equilibria the same concept applies to the full three-dimensional field contribution from poloidal current sources and its flux through the specified oriented surface.

For an oriented surface $S$, the flux contribution is defined by

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{pc}}(S) = \int_S \mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{pc}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}} \, dA
$$

where $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{pc}}$ is the magnetic-field contribution generated by poloidal current (obtained from the equilibrium current distribution via Ampère's law), $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the unit normal defining the positive orientation of $S$, and $dA$ is the surface-area element. The component [toroidal magnetic flux due to poloidal current](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_due_to_poloidal_current) corresponds to this flux through a poloidal cross-section whose normal points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

In practice this quantity is computed from an equilibrium magnetic-field decomposition using the reconstructed current distribution from a Grad-Shafranov-based axisymmetric model or a three-dimensional field calculation, then integrating over the chosen oriented surface. Measurements constraining it come indirectly from magnetic probes, flux loops, polarimetry, and global equilibrium constraints rather than from a direct flux diagnostic.

Typical absolute magnitudes are about 0.1-5 Wb in small tokamaks, 1-20 Wb in medium-size devices, and 10-100 Wb or more in large high-field or reactor-scale equilibria. The value scales with the toroidal magnetic field generated by poloidal current and with the area of the surface being threaded.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetic field $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{pc}}$ generated by poloidal current points in the same direction as the oriented surface normal; for a positively oriented poloidal cross-section this is the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: magnetic_shear
NAMES.short: Dimensionless logarithmic radial derivative of the safety factor, measuring how rapidly neighboring magnetic field lines change helicity between flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
Magnetic shear expresses the radial variation of field-line pitch on nested magnetic flux surfaces. It controls how quickly neighboring field lines separate in poloidal angle after toroidal transits, making it central to ideal MHD stability, tearing-mode behavior, and drift-wave turbulence. It is defined from the same field-line helicity described by the [safety factor](name:safety_factor), with special values often interpreted together with [safety factor at the magnetic axis](name:safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis) and [minimum safety factor](name:minimum_safety_factor).

For a toroidal-flux radius coordinate $\rho_{\rm tor}$ and safety factor $q(\rho_{\rm tor})$, the local magnetic shear $s$ is

$$
s = \frac{\rho_{\rm tor}}{q}\frac{d q}{d \rho_{\rm tor}}
$$

where $\rho_{\rm tor}$ labels flux surfaces and $q$ is the number of toroidal turns per poloidal circuit. The definition is a logarithmic radial derivative, so large magnitude indicates rapid change of magnetic pitch across adjacent flux surfaces.

Magnetic shear is computed from an equilibrium reconstruction after obtaining the $q$ distribution from external magnetic measurements and, when available, internal constraints such as motional-Stark-effect polarimetry or Faraday polarimetry. Because it involves differentiating $q$, smoothing and uncertainty propagation are important near extrema such as the location associated with [poloidal magnetic flux at minimum safety factor].

Representative values are near zero at a broad or flat $q$ minimum, about 0.5-2 in many tokamak cores, negative in reversed-shear regions, and several units in steep edge pedestal or scrape-off-layer gradients.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the safety factor increases outward with increasing toroidal-flux radius coordinate.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_closest_wall_point
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of the first-wall location geometrically nearest to the plasma boundary, used to identify the radial location of the limiting gap.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the major-radius coordinate of the wall point that minimizes the distance to the plasma boundary in a poloidal cross-section. It locates the radial position of the nearest material surface relative to the boundary and complements the [vertical coordinate of the closest wall point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point). Together with the [plasma-boundary gap distance], it identifies where the limiting wall clearance occurs.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system, with $R$ measured from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ the vertical coordinate, the coordinate is

$$
R_{\mathrm{cw}} = R\left(\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{cw}}\right), \qquad \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{cw}} = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\mathbf{x}\in W} d\left(\mathbf{x}, B_p\right)
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{cw}}$ is the closest wall point, $W$ is the wall surface or contour, $B_p$ is the plasma-boundary contour, and $d$ is the shortest geometric distance in the poloidal plane.

The value is computed from an equilibrium boundary and a geometric description of the surrounding wall or limiter. It is used in boundary-clearance analysis alongside the [major radius of the plasma boundary](name:major_radius_of_plasma_boundary) and the [major radius of the plasma-boundary gap reference point](name:major_radius_of_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point).

Typical values range from about 0.5-4 m in present medium-size tokamaks and about 4-9 m in reactor-scale devices, depending on wall geometry and plasma position.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the closest wall point has positive major radius measured outward from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_current_center
NAMES.short: Current-weighted major-radius coordinate of the centroid of the toroidal plasma current distribution in a poloidal cross-section.
NAMES.long:
The current-center major radius locates the radial centroid of the toroidal plasma current distribution in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system, where $R$ is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is vertical height. It complements the [vertical coordinate of the current center](name:vertical_coordinate_of_current_center) and can differ from both the [magnetic-axis major radius](name:major_radius_of_magnetic_axis) and the [geometric-axis major radius](name:major_radius_of_geometric_axis) when the current profile is asymmetric or vertically displaced.

For an axisymmetric equilibrium, the current-weighted centroid is defined over the plasma poloidal cross-section $S$ by

$$
R_J = \frac{1}{I_p}\int_S R\, j_\phi(R,Z)\, dS
$$

where $R_J$ is the current-center major radius, $j_\phi$ is the [toroidal plasma current density](name:toroidal_plasma_current_density), $dS$ is an element of poloidal cross-sectional area, and $I_p = \int_S j_\phi\,dS$ is the [plasma current].

This quantity is computed from equilibrium reconstruction by integrating the reconstructed toroidal current density over the plasma cross-section, with constraints from magnetic probes, flux loops, polarimetry, motional-Stark-effect measurements, and kinetic pressure information when available.

Representative values are close to the device major radius: about 1-3 m in medium-size tokamaks and 6-7 m in reactor-scale devices. Differences between the current center and magnetic or geometric axes are often a few centimeters to several tens of centimeters, depending on shaping, pressure, current-profile peaking, and vertical position control.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured outward from the toroidal symmetry axis in the $+R$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_geometric_axis
NAMES.short: Horizontal center position of the plasma cross-section, expressed as the major-radius coordinate in the tokamak geometry.
NAMES.long:
The major radius of the geometric axis is the $R$ coordinate of the geometric center of a closed plasma cross-section in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It describes the horizontal placement of the plasma shape independently of the magnetic-axis location, which is captured by [major radius of magnetic axis](name:major_radius_of_magnetic_axis). Together with the [vertical coordinate of geometric axis](name:vertical_coordinate_of_geometric_axis), it specifies the geometric center used in equilibrium shape characterization.

For an axisymmetric closed contour, the geometric-axis major radius is commonly defined from the inner and outer radial extrema:

$$
R_{\mathrm{geo}} = \frac{R_{\mathrm{out}} + R_{\mathrm{in}}}{2}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{out}}$ and $R_{\mathrm{in}}$ are the outermost and innermost major-radius coordinates of the contour. The related quantities [outer major radius of flux surface](name:outer_major_radius_of_flux_surface) and [inner major radius of flux surface](name:inner_major_radius_of_flux_surface) provide these extrema for individual flux surfaces.

This quantity is computed from equilibrium reconstruction by locating the radial extrema of the reconstructed boundary or flux-surface contour; magnetic probes, flux loops, and internal constraints improve the inferred plasma position. Typical values range from about 0.5-1.5 m in compact tokamaks, 1.5-3.5 m in medium-size devices, and near 6 m in large reactor-scale configurations.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the geometric axis lies at positive major radius $R$ measured outward from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate locating the innermost closed magnetic-flux surface, which defines the plasma magnetic axis in a toroidal equilibrium.
NAMES.long:
The major radius of the magnetic axis is the $R$ coordinate of the innermost nested magnetic-flux surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis and $Z$ is vertical height. It locates the magnetic center of the equilibrium and is distinct from the shape-based [major radius of the geometric axis](name:major_radius_of_geometric_axis) and the current-weighted [major radius of the current center](name:major_radius_of_current_center).

The magnetic axis is identified as the stationary point of the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$ in the poloidal cross-section:

$$
\nabla \psi(R_{\rm axis}, Z_{\rm axis}) = \mathbf{0}
$$

where $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux, $R_{\rm axis}$ is the major-radius coordinate of the magnetic axis, and $Z_{\rm axis}$ is its vertical coordinate. The flux value at this point is the reference for [poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis).

This quantity is computed from magnetic equilibrium reconstruction using external magnetic measurements, flux loops, and internal constraints such as polarimetry or motional-Stark-effect measurements when available. It is also used as a reference position for interpreting flux-surface geometry and plasma radial displacement relative to the vessel and coil system.

Representative values are about 1-3 m in medium-size tokamaks and about 5-7 m in reactor-scale devices, depending on machine size and plasma position. During controlled displacements, shifts of several centimeters to tens of centimeters from the nominal geometric axis can occur.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetic axis lies at positive major radius $R$ measured outward from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate locating points on the plasma boundary relative to the toroidal symmetry axis in the poloidal cross-section.
NAMES.long:
The major radius of the plasma boundary is the $R$ coordinate of a point on the outermost closed flux surface or separatrix in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Together with the vertical coordinate of the boundary contour, it defines the poloidal shape used to derive geometric measures such as [minor radius of the plasma boundary](name:minor_radius_of_plasma_boundary), [area of the plasma boundary](name:area_of_plasma_boundary), and [poloidal length of the plasma boundary](name:poloidal_length_of_plasma_boundary).

In a Cartesian frame $(x, y, z)$ with $z=Z$, the cylindrical major radius is defined by

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are horizontal Cartesian coordinates measured from the toroidal symmetry axis. The plasma-boundary major-radius values can also be summarized relative to the [major radius of the geometric axis](name:major_radius_of_geometric_axis) when defining elongation, triangularity, and radial gaps.

This quantity is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by locating the last closed magnetic flux surface using magnetic measurements, plasma pressure constraints, and, when available, internal magnetic-field diagnostics. It is also compared with the [major radius of the closest wall point](name:major_radius_of_closest_wall_point) and the [major radius of the plasma-boundary gap reference point](name:major_radius_of_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point) when assessing plasma-wall clearance.

Representative boundary major-radius values span about 1-4 m in medium-size tokamaks and about 4-8 m in reactor-scale devices, with the range over the boundary reflecting the plasma minor radius and shaping.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R$ is measured outward from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate, measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, of the boundary reference point used to define plasma-wall gap distance.
NAMES.long:
The plasma boundary gap reference point is the point on the plasma boundary or separatrix used to evaluate the clearance to nearby wall structures. Its major radius locates that point in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. Together with the [vertical coordinate of the plasma boundary gap reference point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point), it defines the poloidal-plane location used to form the [distance of the plasma boundary gap].

For a reference point with Cartesian position $(x_\mathrm{ref}, y_\mathrm{ref}, z_\mathrm{ref})$ in a right-handed $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$, the major-radius coordinate is

$$
R_\mathrm{ref} = \sqrt{x_\mathrm{ref}^2 + y_\mathrm{ref}^2}
$$

where $R_\mathrm{ref}$ is the major radius of the gap reference point and $x_\mathrm{ref}$ and $y_\mathrm{ref}$ are its horizontal Cartesian coordinates relative to the toroidal symmetry axis.

This coordinate is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction or shape-control geometry by locating the relevant point on the reconstructed boundary, often in relation to the [major radius of the plasma boundary](name:major_radius_of_plasma_boundary) and the [major radius of the closest wall point](name:major_radius_of_closest_wall_point). Representative values span about 0.5-10 m across present and reactor-scale tokamaks, depending on device size and which boundary sector defines the active gap.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the reference point lies in the $+R$ direction from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_secondary_strike_point
NAMES.short: Radial location, measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, where the secondary separatrix intersects a divertor target.
NAMES.long:
The secondary strike-point major radius is the $R$ coordinate of the intersection between the secondary separatrix and a divertor target in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is the radial companion to the [secondary strike-point vertical coordinate](name:vertical_coordinate_of_secondary_strike_point) and distinguishes the secondary separatrix contact from the primary [strike-point major radius](name:major_radius_of_strike_point).

For a point expressed in a right-handed Cartesian $(x, y, z)$ frame whose $z$ axis is the vertical $Z$ axis and whose origin lies on the toroidal symmetry axis, the major radius is

$$
R_{\mathrm{sp,sec}} = \sqrt{x_{\mathrm{sp,sec}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{sp,sec}}^2}
$$

where $x_{\mathrm{sp,sec}}$ and $y_{\mathrm{sp,sec}}$ are the horizontal coordinates of the secondary strike point.

This quantity is computed from equilibrium reconstruction by finding where the secondary separatrix intersects the modeled plasma-facing target surface. Its inferred position can be checked against divertor heat-flux patterns from infrared thermography, visible emission, or embedded target probes, while its relation to [vertical_coordinate_of_strike_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_strike_point) specifies the full poloidal location of the contact point.

Typical values are device-size dependent: about 1-2 m in compact tokamaks, 2-4 m in medium-size tokamaks, and 5-8 m in large reactor-scale configurations. Changes of a few centimeters can be operationally important for divertor heat-load sharing and strike-point sweeping.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the secondary strike point lies in the $+R$ direction away from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_secondary_x_point
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate locating the secondary magnetic null where the secondary separatrix intersects itself in the divertor geometry.
NAMES.long:
The secondary X-point is a magnetic null associated with a secondary separatrix, often present in diverted equilibria with double-null or near-double-null topology. Its major radius $R_{\mathrm{X2}}$ gives the radial location of that null in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. Together with the [vertical coordinate of the secondary X-point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_secondary_x_point), it fixes the secondary null position and complements the primary [major radius of the X-point](name:major_radius_of_x_point).

For an axisymmetric equilibrium, the major-radius coordinate can be written from horizontal Cartesian coordinates as:

$$
R_{\mathrm{X2}} = \sqrt{x_{\mathrm{X2}}^2 + y_{\mathrm{X2}}^2}
$$

where $x_{\mathrm{X2}}$ and $y_{\mathrm{X2}}$ are the horizontal coordinates of the secondary magnetic null in a right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$. The point itself is identified by the local vanishing of the poloidal magnetic field on the secondary separatrix.

This coordinate is computed from magnetic-equilibrium reconstruction constrained by external magnetic sensors, flux measurements, and, where available, internal magnetic diagnostics. It is used to distinguish secondary-null geometry from strike-point geometry, such as the [major radius of the secondary strike point](name:major_radius_of_secondary_strike_point), and from global geometric references such as the [major radius of the geometric axis](name:major_radius_of_geometric_axis).

Representative values span about 0.5-3 m in compact and medium-size tokamaks and can reach 5-8 m in large devices, depending on divertor configuration and plasma shaping.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the secondary X-point lies in the $+R$ direction away from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_strike_point
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of an unspecified divertor strike point where the reconstructed separatrix intersects a material target.
NAMES.long:
The strike-point major radius locates the divertor contact point of the last closed flux surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is distance from the machine symmetry axis. Together with [vertical coordinate of strike point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_strike_point), it specifies the poloidal-plane position that governs divertor heat-load placement. If primary and secondary strike points are distinguished, compare this quantity with [major radius of secondary strike point](name:major_radius_of_secondary_strike_point).

For a strike-point position expressed in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$, the major radius is

$$
R_{\rm sp} = \sqrt{(x_{\rm sp}-x_0)^2 + (y_{\rm sp}-y_0)^2}
$$

where $x_{\rm sp}$ and $y_{\rm sp}$ are the horizontal Cartesian coordinates of the strike point, and $x_0,y_0$ define the toroidal symmetry axis.

It is computed by intersecting the reconstructed separatrix or plasma boundary with the divertor target geometry. Magnetic equilibrium reconstruction constrained by external magnetics, internal profile constraints, and divertor imaging provides the most common determination; planned trajectories may also be derived from position-control models. Related geometric references include [outer major radius of flux surface](name:outer_major_radius_of_flux_surface) and [inner major radius of flux surface](name:inner_major_radius_of_flux_surface), which describe midplane intersections rather than target intersections.

Typical values range from about 0.5-3 m in compact and medium-size tokamaks and can exceed 5 m in large devices, depending on divertor geometry and plasma shape.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R_{\rm sp}$ is measured outward from the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_x_point
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of the primary separatrix X-point where the poloidal magnetic field vanishes and separatrix branches intersect.
NAMES.long:
The X-point is a saddle point of the poloidal magnetic flux on the plasma separatrix, marking where separatrix branches meet and defining the divertor topology. This quantity is the $R$ coordinate of that primary null in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It complements the corresponding secondary-null coordinate [major radius of the secondary X-point](name:major_radius_of_secondary_x_point) and the divertor target geometry described by [major radius of the strike point](name:major_radius_of_strike_point).

At an X-point, the poloidal gradient of the equilibrium flux vanishes and the critical point has saddle topology:

$$
\nabla_p \psi(R_X, Z_X) = 0
$$

where $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux, $\nabla_p$ is the gradient in the poloidal $(R,Z)$ plane, and $(R_X,Z_X)$ are the X-point coordinates. The reported quantity is $R_X$.

The coordinate is computed from magnetic equilibrium reconstruction by locating the separatrix saddle point consistent with external magnetic measurements and, when available, internal constraints such as polarimetry or motional-Stark-effect measurements. In diverted tokamaks, representative values are about 1-3 m in medium-size devices and 5-7 m in reactor-scale configurations, depending on plasma size, elongation, triangularity, and divertor geometry. Changes in this coordinate alter the connection length and strike-point placement, linking it geometrically to [major radius of the strike point](name:major_radius_of_strike_point) and [vertical coordinate of the strike point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_strike_point).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the X-point lies in the $+R$ direction from the machine symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: maximum_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Absolute strength of the equilibrium magnetic-field vector, independent of field direction and used to assess gyromotion, magnetic pressure, and coil or plasma operating limits.
NAMES.long:
Magnetic-field magnitude is the norm of the equilibrium magnetic-field vector and measures the local field strength independent of direction. It sets charged-particle Larmor radii, gyrofrequencies, magnetic pressure, and the field-strength extrema used in operating limits such as [maximum magnetic field magnitude](name:maximum_magnetic_field_magnitude). It is the scalar counterpart of the vector [magnetic field](name:magnetic_field).

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius, $\phi$ the toroidal angle, and $Z$ the vertical height, the magnitude is

$$
|\mathbf{B}| = \sqrt{B_R^2 + B_\phi^2 + B_Z^2}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the equilibrium magnetic-field vector and $B_R$, $B_\phi$, and $B_Z$ are its radial, toroidal, and vertical components in T.

The magnitude is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction constrained by magnetic probes, flux loops, polarimetry, and motional-Stark-effect measurements; in coil regions it is computed from conductor currents and geometry. Representative values are 1-6 T on axis in present tokamaks, below 1 T near some edge or scrape-off-layer regions, and up to about 10-13 T on high-field superconducting coil conductors. Flux-surface summaries such as [flux-surface mean magnetic-field magnitude] and extrema such as [minimum magnetic-field magnitude](name:minimum_magnetic_field_magnitude) describe how this local field strength varies over equilibrium geometry.

NAMES.name: maximum_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short: Peak absolute magnetic-field strength attained on a poloidal-field coil conductor surface, used to assess electromagnetic and superconducting operating limits.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the extremum of the magnetic-field modulus on the conductor surface of a poloidal-field coil. It is the surface peak relevant to insulation stress, Lorentz loading, and superconducting critical-current margins, and it specializes the broader [maximum magnetic field] to the conductor-surface field rather than a field value at a plasma diagnostic location such as [poloidal magnetic field at measurement position](name:poloidal_magnetic_field_at_measurement_position).

For a conductor surface $S_c$ and magnetic-field vector $\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})$, the defining operation is

$$
B_{\max} = \max_{\mathbf{x} \in S_c} \left|\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})\right|
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is position on the conductor surface and $|\mathbf{B}|$ is the Euclidean magnitude of the local magnetic-field vector.

The value is computed from magnetostatic field models using coil currents, conductor geometry, and mutual fields from neighboring coils and plasma current. The surface over which the maximum is taken is determined from the coil geometry, for example using the [radial outline of poloidal field coil](name:radial_outline_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [major radius of poloidal field coil](name:major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) to define the conductor location in the machine cross-section.

Typical peak conductor fields are a few T for resistive shaping coils, about 4-7 T for NbTi superconducting poloidal-field coils, and can approach 10-13 T for high-field superconducting designs. Because this is a magnitude and a maximum, it is always non-negative.

NAMES.name: minimum_magnetic_field_magnitude
NAMES.short: Lowest magnetic-field strength found anywhere on a closed equilibrium flux surface, often near the outboard low-field side.
NAMES.long:
The minimum magnetic-field magnitude is the smallest field strength reached along a closed equilibrium flux surface. It identifies the low-field part of the surface that helps set magnetic-mirror trapping boundaries, neoclassical orbit widths, and magnetic-well structure. It is the magnitude-resolved counterpart of [minimum magnetic field](name:minimum_magnetic_field_magnitude) and complements the high-field-side extremum [maximum magnetic field magnitude](name:maximum_magnetic_field_magnitude).

For a flux surface labeled by poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$, the defining relation is

$$
B_{\min}(\psi) = \min_{\mathbf{x}\in S(\psi)} \left|\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x})\right|
$$

where $S(\psi)$ is the closed flux surface, $\mathbf{x}$ is position on that surface, and $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector.

This quantity is computed from an equilibrium magnetic-field solution after reconstructing the nested flux surfaces from external magnetics, internal magnetic pitch constraints, polarimetry, or motional-Stark-effect measurements. It is often used together with [flux-surface mean magnetic-field magnitude] to characterize field variation around a surface.

Typical values range from about 0.2-1 T in spherical tokamaks, 1-4 T in medium-size tokamaks, and 4-8 T in high-field or reactor-scale scenarios. Because it is a magnitude and an extremum over a surface, it is always non-negative.

NAMES.name: minimum_safety_factor
NAMES.short: Smallest safety-factor value attained on closed magnetic flux surfaces, identifying the lowest-helicity region most relevant to MHD stability.
NAMES.long:
The minimum safety factor is the lowest value of the magnetic-field-line winding number over the set of closed magnetic flux surfaces in an equilibrium. It summarizes the deepest low-q region of the plasma and complements local values such as the axis value [safety factor at the magnetic axis](name:safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis) and edge-relevant values such as [safety factor at normalized poloidal flux].

A common definition is

$$
q_{\min} = \min_{\psi \in \Omega_{\rm closed}} q(\psi)
$$

where $q_{\min}$ is the minimum safety factor, $q(\psi)$ is the safety factor on the flux surface labeled by poloidal magnetic flux $\psi$, and $\Omega_{\rm closed}$ is the closed-flux-surface region. The location of this minimum can be identified by the [poloidal magnetic flux at minimum safety factor], while the radial variation that produces the minimum is characterized by [magnetic shear](name:magnetic_shear).

The value is computed from magnetic equilibrium reconstruction using external magnetic measurements, pressure and current constraints, and internal pitch-angle information when available from polarimetry or motional-Stark-effect diagnostics. Representative values are near 0.7-1.2 in sawtoothing inductive tokamak plasmas, above 1 in sawtooth-free operation, and about 1.5-3 in reversed-shear or advanced scenarios.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a magnetic field line advances in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame during a positive poloidal circuit around the magnetic axis.

NAMES.name: minor_radius_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Half the radial width of the last closed flux surface, obtained from the outermost and innermost major-radius intersections of the boundary.
NAMES.long:
The plasma-boundary minor radius is the effective horizontal half-width of the last closed flux surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It complements the [major radius of the plasma boundary](name:major_radius_of_plasma_boundary) in setting the boundary aspect ratio and is a basic size parameter for interpreting [area of the plasma boundary](name:area_of_plasma_boundary), [poloidal length of the plasma boundary](name:poloidal_length_of_plasma_boundary), and shape parameters such as [elongation](name:elongation).

For an axisymmetric boundary contour, the minor radius $a_b$ is defined from the radial extrema of that contour:

$$
a_b = \frac{R_{\max} - R_{\min}}{2}
$$

where $R_{\max}$ and $R_{\min}$ are the largest and smallest major-radius coordinates reached by the plasma boundary.

This quantity is computed from an equilibrium reconstruction after identifying the outermost closed flux contour or separatrix. The reconstruction is constrained by magnetic probes, flux loops, plasma current measurements, and, where available, internal magnetic diagnostics such as motional-Stark-effect polarimetry.

Representative values are 0.2-0.8 m in compact tokamaks, 0.8-1.2 m in medium-size devices, and about 2 m in ITER-scale equilibria. The related [toroidal-flux radius of the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_flux_radius_of_plasma_boundary) gives a flux-surface-equivalent radial scale rather than the geometric radial half-width.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the outer radial intersection of the plasma boundary has larger major radius than the inner radial intersection in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Dimensionless label of the flux surface selected as the plasma boundary, formed by scaling poloidal magnetic flux between the magnetic axis and boundary.
NAMES.long:
The normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the plasma boundary identifies which equilibrium flux surface is being used as the boundary or last-closed-flux-surface reference. It is the boundary counterpart of the absolute [poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary) and is closely related to geometric boundary measures such as the [toroidal-flux radius of the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_flux_radius_of_plasma_boundary).

A common definition is

$$
\psi_N = \frac{\psi - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}{\psi_{\mathrm{b}} - \psi_{\mathrm{axis}}}
$$

where $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux at the selected surface, $\psi_{\mathrm{axis}}$ is the magnetic-axis flux, and $\psi_{\mathrm{b}}$ is the boundary flux; these flux variables are in Wb. For a boundary-referenced equilibrium, this coordinate is expected to be close to 1 at the selected plasma boundary.

The value is computed during magnetic equilibrium reconstruction from magnetic measurements, pressure and current constraints, and the inferred closed-flux-surface topology. Representative values are 1 for the adopted boundary surface, with small deviations used to document alternative fixed-boundary, limiter, or separatrix definitions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the selected boundary flux lies farther from the magnetic-axis flux in the outward flux-surface ordering.

NAMES.name: normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate
NAMES.short: Dimensionless radial label for nested equilibrium flux surfaces, formed from the square root of enclosed toroidal magnetic flux relative to its boundary value.
NAMES.long:
The normalized toroidal flux coordinate is a flux-surface label that increases from the magnetic axis to the plasma boundary. It provides a geometry-based radial coordinate for comparing thermodynamic, current, and transport quantities on nested magnetic surfaces, and is closely related to the enclosed [toroidal magnetic flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux). Unlike [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux), it is normalized to a boundary reference so that different equilibria can be compared on a common radial scale.

A common definition is

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor,n}} = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,b}} - \Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}}}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor,n}}$ is the normalized toroidal flux coordinate, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by the flux surface in Wb, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,axis}}$ is its magnetic-axis value in Wb, and $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor,b}}$ is the boundary reference value in Wb.

It is computed from magnetic equilibrium reconstruction using magnetic measurements and, when available, internal constraints such as motional-Stark-effect or polarimetry data. Experimental measurement locations are mapped to this coordinate by finding the equilibrium flux surface passing through the measurement point or the minimum value along a line of sight.

Representative values are 0 at the magnetic axis and about 1 at the last closed flux surface or chosen fixed-boundary reference. The coordinate is often used together with the [toroidal flux radius](name:toroidal_flux_radius), while [normalized poloidal flux coordinate of plasma boundary](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary) provides the analogous boundary normalization based on poloidal flux.
NAMES.sign: Positive when enclosed toroidal magnetic flux increases from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: outer_major_radius_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate where a magnetic flux surface intersects the outboard midplane, measuring its farthest radial extent from the symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
The outer major radius of a flux surface is the outboard midplane intersection of a nested magnetic surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It complements the [inner major radius of a flux surface](name:inner_major_radius_of_flux_surface) and, together with the [major radius of the magnetic axis](name:major_radius_of_magnetic_axis), determines the local horizontal half-width of that surface.

For a flux surface labeled by poloidal magnetic flux value $\psi_s$, the outboard midplane radius is commonly defined by

$$
R_{\rm out}(\psi_s)=\max\{R:\psi(R,Z_{\rm axis})=\psi_s\}
$$

where $\psi(R,Z)$ is the equilibrium poloidal flux function and $Z_{\rm axis}$ is the vertical coordinate of the magnetic axis.

This quantity is computed from equilibrium reconstruction by locating the contour of constant flux and finding its outer intersection with the magnetic-axis midplane. Magnetic diagnostics, pressure constraints, and kinetic profile information can all constrain the reconstructed surface geometry. Typical values range from about 1-3 m in medium-size tokamaks and about 6-9 m in reactor-scale devices, depending on plasma size and elongation; the related [major radius of the geometric axis](name:major_radius_of_geometric_axis) gives the midpoint reference for boundary shape.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R$ is measured outward from the toroidal symmetry axis in the $+R$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: outer_triangularity
NAMES.short: Dimensionless measure of the outboard-side indentation of the plasma boundary relative to an elliptical cross-section.
NAMES.long:
Outer triangularity describes the shaping of the plasma boundary on the outboard, large-major-radius side in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is one member of the quadrant-resolved triangularity family, complementing [inner triangularity](name:inner_triangularity), [upper triangularity](name:upper_triangularity), and [lower triangularity](name:lower_triangularity), and reduces to the global [triangularity](name:triangularity) only when the boundary shape is represented by a single triangularity parameter.

A common geometric estimate compares the outboard boundary to an elliptical reference with the same geometric center and minor radius:

$$
\delta_{\rm out} = \frac{R_{\rm ell}(Z_{\rm out}) - R_{\rm b,out}(Z_{\rm out})}{a}
$$

where $\delta_{\rm out}$ is the outer triangularity, $R_{\rm b,out}$ is the major radius of the outboard boundary at the chosen outboard-side shaping point, $R_{\rm ell}$ is the corresponding major radius of the reference ellipse, $Z_{\rm out}$ is the vertical coordinate of that point, and $a$ is the boundary minor radius.

It is obtained from an equilibrium boundary reconstruction by fitting the last closed flux-surface contour or separatrix in the poloidal plane. Representative tokamak boundary values are about -0.1-0.6; positive D-shaped plasmas often have outer triangularity in the 0.2-0.5 range, while nearly circular plasmas are close to zero. The related [minor triangularity](name:triangularity) is useful when the shape model separates quadrant-resolved triangularities from a minor-radius-based triangularity measure.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the outboard boundary is indented toward smaller $R$ relative to the corresponding elliptical reference in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: parallel_plasma_current_density
NAMES.short: Field-aligned projection of the plasma current density, distinguishing current flowing along magnetic-field lines from geometric toroidal or poloidal components.
NAMES.long:
The parallel plasma current density is the component of the plasma current-density vector along the local magnetic-field direction. It separates field-aligned conduction from geometric projections and is the local density underlying the integrated [parallel plasma current], while [plasma current density] denotes the full vector quantity.

For a flux-surface-averaged equilibrium representation, the field-aligned current density can be written as

$$
j_\parallel = \frac{\langle \mathbf{J} \cdot \mathbf{B} \rangle}{B_0}
$$

where $\mathbf{J}$ is the plasma current-density vector in A m$^{-2}$, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector in T, $\langle\cdot\rangle$ denotes a flux-surface average, and $B_0$ is the reference toroidal magnetic-field magnitude in T. Locally, the same physics is expressed by the projection $\mathbf{J}\cdot\hat{b}$, where $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the magnetic field.

This quantity is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction constrained by magnetic measurements, motional-Stark-effect or polarimetry information, and current-drive or pressure-profile modeling. It is closely related to [parallel plasma electrical conductivity](name:parallel_plasma_electrical_conductivity), because Ohmic and inductive current drive depend on the field-aligned electric field through the parallel conductivity.

Core tokamak values span about 0.1-5 MA m$^{-2}$ in many present devices, with larger central values in high-current or strongly driven scenarios and much smaller values near the plasma edge. The radial structure reflects Ohmic drive, bootstrap current, externally driven current, and the safety-factor and magnetic-shear constraints of the reconstructed equilibrium.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the projection of the plasma current-density vector onto the local magnetic-field direction is positive.

NAMES.name: plasma_current_density
NAMES.short: Electric charge flow per unit area carried by the plasma, including field-aligned and toroidal projections in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
Plasma current density is the local flow of electric charge carried by electrons and ions in a magnetized plasma. In axisymmetric equilibrium it is dominated by toroidal and field-aligned components, and it is the source of the poloidal part of the equilibrium [magnetic_field](name:magnetic_field) and associated [magnetic_flux](name:magnetic_flux).

The defining magnetostatic relation is Ampere's law with displacement current neglected:

$$
\nabla \times \mathbf{B} = \mu_0 \mathbf{j}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic field in T, $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability in N A$^{-2}$, and $\mathbf{j}$ is the plasma current density in A m$^{-2}$. In resistive regions the current density is also related to the [electric_field](name:electric_field) through the [plasma_electrical_conductivity](name:plasma_electrical_conductivity), with kinetic corrections from bootstrap and driven-current mechanisms.

It is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction using magnetic probes, flux loops, polarimetry, motional-Stark-effect constraints, and current-drive or conductivity models rather than measured directly at every point. Representative core values in tokamak plasmas are $10^5$-$10^7$ A m$^{-2}$, with sharper edge gradients during high-confinement or transient events.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the projected current density is aligned with the positive basis direction of its component, including increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame for toroidal projections and the local magnetic-field direction for parallel projections.

NAMES.name: plasma_inductance
NAMES.short: Effective self-inductance of the toroidal plasma current channel inferred from its magnetic-field energy and total plasma current.
NAMES.long:
Plasma inductance is the effective self-inductance associated with magnetic energy linked to the toroidal plasma current channel. It differs from the dimensionless [internal inductance](name:internal_inductance), which normalizes poloidal magnetic energy to describe current-profile peaking rather than giving an electrical inductance.

A common energy definition is

$$
L_p = \frac{2 E_{\mathrm{mag}}}{I_p^2}, \qquad E_{\mathrm{mag}} = \frac{1}{2}\int_S \psi\, j_{\mathrm{tor}}\, dS
$$

where $L_p$ is the plasma inductance in H, $E_{\mathrm{mag}}$ is magnetic energy in J, $I_p$ is total plasma current in A, $\psi$ is poloidal magnetic flux in Wb, $j_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is toroidal current density in A m$^{-2}$, and $S$ is the plasma poloidal cross-section.

It is computed from equilibrium reconstruction using magnetic diagnostics and current constraints; the same reconstruction also supplies related quantities such as [magnetic flux] and the current-profile information summarized by [internal inductance](name:internal_inductance). In circuit models, plasma inductance combines with [plasma resistance](name:plasma_resistance) to determine the inductive and resistive voltage response of the plasma current channel.

Typical values range from about 0.1-5 microhenry in medium-size tokamaks and can reach several to tens of microhenry in larger, high-current devices, depending on plasma size, shape, and current distribution.

NAMES.name: plasma_resistance
NAMES.short: Effective resistance of the toroidal plasma current channel inferred from total Joule dissipation divided by the square of the plasma current.
NAMES.long:
Plasma resistance is the global effective electrical resistance of the current-carrying plasma column. It compresses spatially varying resistivity, current-density structure, and electric-field alignment into a single dissipative circuit parameter, complementary to the stored-field response described by [plasma inductance](name:plasma_inductance).

The defining relation is the ratio of total Ohmic power to the square of the total plasma current:

$$
R_p = \frac{\int_V \mathbf{E}\cdot\mathbf{J}\,dV}{I_p^2}
$$

where $R_p$ is the plasma resistance in ohm, $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric field in V m$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{J}$ is the current density in A m$^{-2}$, $dV$ is a volume element in m$^3$, and $I_p$ is the total plasma current in A.

It is computed from equilibrium or transport analysis using reconstructed current density, electric field, and plasma current, or inferred from circuit voltage balance after separating inductive and externally driven voltage contributions. Its local physics is governed by collisional transport along magnetic-field lines, so [parallel plasma electrical conductivity](name:parallel_plasma_electrical_conductivity) and [parallel plasma current density](name:parallel_plasma_current_density) determine how strongly current concentrates in hot, well-conducting regions.

Typical hot tokamak core values are about 10$^{-9}$-10$^{-6}$ ohm, while colder startup or edge-dominated phases can reach 10$^{-5}$-10$^{-3}$ ohm. Lower resistance corresponds to higher electron temperature and reduced Ohmic dissipation for a given plasma current.

NAMES.name: plasma_stored_energy
NAMES.short: Total confined plasma energy obtained from three-halves of the plasma-volume integral of total equilibrium kinetic pressure.
NAMES.long:
Plasma stored energy is the global thermal and fast-particle energy content implied by the equilibrium pressure distribution. In this usage it corresponds to the equilibrium pressure-integral quantity, closely aligned with [stored plasma energy](name:plasma_stored_energy) and [MHD plasma stored energy](name:plasma_stored_energy), rather than the perpendicular-pressure interpretation used for [diamagnetic plasma stored energy](name:plasma_stored_energy).

For an isotropic equilibrium pressure model, the defining relation is

$$
W = \frac{3}{2}\int_{V_p} p\,dV
$$

where $W$ is the stored plasma energy, $V_p$ is the plasma volume, $p$ is the total kinetic pressure including thermal and fast-particle contributions, and $dV$ is the volume element.

The quantity is computed from equilibrium reconstruction constrained by magnetic measurements and, when available, kinetic-pressure information from diagnostics such as Thomson scattering, charge-exchange spectroscopy, and motional-Stark-effect measurements. It is a central confinement metric and is related to beta through the comparison of pressure energy with magnetic-field energy; [beta], [total plasma kinetic pressure of flux surface], and [internal inductance](name:internal_inductance) provide complementary equilibrium constraints.

Representative values range from about 1e4-1e6 J in small or medium tokamak plasmas, 1e6-2e7 J in large present-day high-performance discharges, and above 1e8 J in reactor-scale scenarios.

NAMES.name: poloidal_angle
NAMES.short: Angular coordinate specifying position around a toroidal plasma cross-section in the poloidal plane.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal angle $\theta$ labels position around a magnetic surface or plasma cross-section in the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.
