It complements radial flux labels such as the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the plasma boundary](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary) when describing equilibrium geometry and field components on nested surfaces.

For a geometric angle referenced to a center $(R_0,Z_0)$ in the poloidal plane, one common defining convention is

$$
\theta = \operatorname{atan2}\!\left[-(Z-Z_0),\, R-R_0\right]
$$

where $(R,Z)$ is the point being labeled and $(R_0,Z_0)$ is the chosen magnetic or geometric center. This definition sets the zero direction on the outboard midplane and fixes the positive direction by the sign convention below.

Poloidal angle is computed from equilibrium reconstruction grids, magnetic-surface contour geometry, or probe-orientation surveys in the poloidal plane. It is used to map local quantities such as [poloidal electric field](name:poloidal_electric_field) around a surface and to parameterize boundary geometry associated with the [area of the plasma boundary](name:area_of_plasma_boundary) and the [poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary).

Typical values span one full turn, either $0$-$2\pi$ rad or an equivalent wrapped interval such as $-\pi$-$\pi$ rad.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the angle increases clockwise in the $(R,Z)$ poloidal plane when viewed at fixed toroidal angle $\phi$, starting from the outboard midplane direction of increasing $R$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_length_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Arc length of the closed plasma boundary contour in the poloidal cross-section of an equilibrium flux surface.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal length of the plasma boundary is the perimeter of the last closed magnetic surface projected into the poloidal cross-section. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, it measures the closed contour length in the $(R,Z)$ plane. Together with the enclosed [area of the plasma boundary](name:area_of_plasma_boundary), it characterizes boundary size and shaping.

For a boundary contour parameterized by poloidal label $\theta$, the defining line integral is

$$
L_{\mathrm{pol}} = \oint_{\partial\Omega_p} ds = \oint_{\partial\Omega_p} \sqrt{\left(\frac{dR}{d\theta}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dZ}{d\theta}\right)^2}\, d\theta
$$

where $\partial\Omega_p$ is the closed plasma-boundary curve, $ds$ is the differential arc length, and $R(\theta)$ and $Z(\theta)$ describe the contour in the poloidal plane.

This quantity is computed from equilibrium reconstruction by tracing the outermost closed flux contour, often constrained by magnetic measurements and kinetic pressure information. The same boundary contour sets the [poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary) and the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the plasma boundary](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary); comparisons with wall geometry use the [distance of the plasma boundary gap].

Representative values are 5-8 m for medium-size tokamaks, 12-15 m for large present devices, and about 20-25 m for reactor-scale equilibria, increasing with major radius, elongation, and triangular shaping such as [upper elongation of the plasma boundary](name:upper_elongation_of_plasma_boundary).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the boundary contour is traversed in the positive poloidal orientation used to evaluate the closed line integral.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Signed projection of the magnetic-field vector onto a specified local poloidal unit direction in the R-Z plane of the right-handed IMAS cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame. It depends on the chosen poloidal angle and is distinct from the non-negative poloidal-field magnitude.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic field is the signed component of the magnetic-field vector along a chosen local poloidal unit direction in the plane spanned by $\hat{R}$ and $\hat{Z}$ of the right-handed IMAS cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. Unlike the radial component $B_R$ and vertical component $B_Z$, this scalar is not unique until the flux coordinate or poloidal angle that defines $\hat{\theta}$ is specified.

For an axisymmetric equilibrium, the projection can be related to the cylindrical poloidal-plane components and to the gradient of poloidal magnetic flux:

$$
B_\theta = \mathbf{B}\cdot\hat{\theta} = B_R\,(\hat{R}\cdot\hat{\theta}) + B_Z\,(\hat{Z}\cdot\hat{\theta}), \qquad B_R = -\frac{1}{2\pi R}\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial Z}, \quad B_Z = \frac{1}{2\pi R}\frac{\partial\psi}{\partial R}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, $\hat{\theta}$ is the selected positive poloidal unit direction, $B_R$ and $B_Z$ are the radial and vertical components in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux.

In equilibrium reconstruction, $B_\theta$ is computed by first determining $B_R$ and $B_Z$ from the reconstructed field or flux gradient, then projecting those components onto the chosen local poloidal direction. Magnetic pickup coils and poloidal-field probes measure the component of $\mathbf{B}$ along their own sensitivity direction; they constrain $B_\theta$ only after the probe direction and the local definition of $\hat{\theta}$ are accounted for.

Typical signed values in tokamak equilibria are about -1-1 T, with edge and wall-probe values often in the range -0.5-0.5 T. The magnitude generally increases with plasma current and decreases with increasing major radius, while the sign can change with the selected poloidal direction or with local field reversal.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetic-field vector has a component in the chosen $+\hat{\theta}$ poloidal direction in the flux coordinate $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$ within the poloidal plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_field_at_measurement_position
NAMES.short: Local projection of the magnetic-field vector onto the poloidal direction at a specified magnetic measurement point, used to constrain equilibrium fields.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the local component of the magnetic-field vector in the poloidal plane at the measurement position. The poloidal plane is the meridional $R$-$Z$ plane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is the point-sampled counterpart of the broader [poloidal magnetic field](name:poloidal_magnetic_field) and complements the [radial magnetic field](name:radial_magnetic_field) component.

The measured projection is defined by the local dot product:

$$
B_{\mathrm{pol}}(\mathbf{x}_m) = \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x}_m) \cdot \hat{e}_{\mathrm{pol}}(\mathbf{x}_m)
$$

where $\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{x}_m)$ is the magnetic-field vector at measurement position $\mathbf{x}_m$, and $\hat{e}_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is the local unit vector in the selected positive poloidal direction.

It is measured with calibrated magnetic pickup coils, Hall probes, or other local magnetic sensors, and it is computed in equilibrium reconstruction by evaluating the reconstructed magnetic field at the sensor location and applying the same projection. Its interpretation is tied to the local flux geometry governed by poloidal flux quantities such as [poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis).

Values near the plasma boundary commonly range from a few mT to several tenths of a tesla, with larger excursions during rapid current redistribution, vertical motion, or strong shaping-control transients.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetic-field projection is along the positive local poloidal unit vector $\hat{e}_{\mathrm{pol}}$ at the measurement position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short: Flux of the poloidal magnetic-field component through an oriented toroidal surface, used as a radial label for nested equilibrium surfaces.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux is the [magnetic flux] associated with the poloidal component of the equilibrium magnetic field. In an axisymmetric confinement device it labels nested flux surfaces, while differences in this quantity between surfaces carry the physical content independent of any arbitrary offset. The complementary [toroidal magnetic flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux) measures toroidal-field flux through a poloidal cross-section, and their radial variation determines field-line helicity and magnetic shear.

A common definition is the flux of the poloidal magnetic field through an oriented toroidal surface spanning from the magnetic axis to the flux surface of interest:

$$
\psi = \int_{S_\mathrm{tor}} \mathbf{B}_\mathrm{pol} \cdot d\mathbf{S}_\mathrm{tor}
$$

where $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux, $\mathbf{B}_\mathrm{pol}$ is the poloidal magnetic-field component, and $d\mathbf{S}_\mathrm{tor}$ is the oriented area element of the toroidal integration surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

It is inferred from magnetic-equilibrium reconstruction constrained by external magnetic probes, flux loops, polarimetry, motional-Stark-effect measurements, and kinetic pressure information. The value at the magnetic axis, [poloidal magnetic flux at magnetic axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis), provides a common inner reference for flux-surface coordinates.

Representative axis-to-boundary flux differences are about 0.1-5 Wb in small and medium tokamaks and 10-100 Wb in reactor-scale equilibria, depending mainly on plasma current, size, and shaping.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the poloidal magnetic field threads the toroidal integration surface in the positive surface-normal direction defined by outward motion in the poloidal cross-section followed by increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Reference value of the equilibrium poloidal flux at the innermost closed flux surface where the poloidal flux gradient vanishes.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis is the value of the equilibrium flux function on the innermost closed magnetic surface. It provides the inner reference for the flux-surface label [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux), while [poloidal magnetic flux at plasma boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary) provides the corresponding outer reference.

For an axisymmetric equilibrium in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the flux at the magnetic-axis location $(R_\mathrm{ax}, Z_\mathrm{ax})$ may be written as

$$
\psi_\mathrm{ax} = \psi(R_\mathrm{ax}, Z_\mathrm{ax}) = \int_0^{R_\mathrm{ax}} B_Z(R', Z_\mathrm{ax})\,2\pi R'\,dR'
$$

where $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux function, $R_\mathrm{ax}$ is the major radius of the magnetic axis, $Z_\mathrm{ax}$ is its vertical coordinate, and $B_Z$ is the [vertical magnetic field](name:vertical_magnetic_field). The magnetic axis is identified by $\nabla\psi = 0$, so this value is an extremum of the flux function in a nested-surface equilibrium.

The value is obtained from magnetic-equilibrium reconstruction constrained by magnetic probes, flux loops, polarimetry, and motional-Stark-effect measurements. In present tokamaks, the boundary-to-axis flux difference commonly spans 1-20 Wb; the absolute axis value depends on the chosen flux gage and the sign of the equilibrium field configuration. Its radial variation is tied to the [poloidal magnetic field](name:poloidal_magnetic_field), since flux-surface spacing determines the local poloidal field strength.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertical magnetic field integrated over the horizontal disk bounded by the circular contour through the magnetic axis points in the $+Z$ direction.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Equilibrium poloidal magnetic flux on the last closed flux surface, setting the outer flux reference for plasma-boundary geometry.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary is the value of the equilibrium flux function on the last closed flux surface or selected separatrix. It provides the outer reference paired with [poloidal magnetic flux at the magnetic axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis) for labeling nested flux surfaces and defining the boundary value used by the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the plasma boundary](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary).

In an axisymmetric equilibrium, the boundary value can be represented in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame by integrating the vertical magnetic field over a horizontal disk whose rim intersects the selected boundary point:

$$
\psi_b = \int_0^{R_b} B_Z(R', Z_b)\,2\pi R'\,dR'
$$

where $\psi_b$ is the boundary poloidal magnetic flux, $R_b$ and $Z_b$ locate the boundary point, and $B_Z$ is the vertical magnetic-field component. The same boundary surface is geometrically related to quantities such as [area of plasma boundary](name:area_of_plasma_boundary), while [toroidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary) gives the complementary flux through the poloidal cross-section.

This quantity is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction constrained by external magnetic probes, flux loops, plasma current, pressure constraints, and internal magnetic measurements when available. Representative absolute magnitudes are about 1-20 Wb in medium-size and large tokamaks, with larger values for higher plasma current and larger machine size; the difference between axis and boundary values is often more physically relevant than the absolute offset.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the vertical magnetic field $B_Z$ threading the integration disk points in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: poloidal_magnetic_flux_due_to_diamagnetic_drift
NAMES.short: Poloidal magnetic-flux contribution generated by currents associated with plasma diamagnetic drift, isolating the equilibrium flux linked to pressure-gradient drift motion.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the poloidal part of the magnetic-flux contribution associated with diamagnetic drift currents in a magnetized plasma. It refines [magnetic flux due to diamagnetic drift] by selecting the poloidal magnetic-flux component rather than the total flux contribution. It is closely related to the reference equilibrium flux [poloidal magnetic flux at plasma boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary), but represents only the diamagnetic-drift contribution.

A useful axisymmetric definition is the contribution to the poloidal flux obtained by integrating the vertical diamagnetic magnetic-field component over a horizontal disk in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame:

$$
\psi_{\rm dia}(R,Z) = \int_0^R B_{Z,{\rm dia}}(R',Z)\,2\pi R'\,dR'
$$

where $\psi_{\rm dia}$ is the diamagnetic-drift contribution to poloidal magnetic flux, $B_{Z,{\rm dia}}$ is the vertical magnetic field produced by diamagnetic drift currents, and $R$ and $Z$ are major radius and vertical height. The associated diamagnetic current is driven by pressure gradients, so this flux contribution is sensitive to plasma pressure and magnetic geometry.

It is inferred from compensated diamagnetic flux-loop measurements or computed from equilibrium reconstructions that include pressure-gradient current effects. Representative magnitudes range from about $10^{-3}$-$10^{-1}$ Wb in present tokamaks, increasing with plasma pressure, volume, and magnetic-field strength. The analogous mechanism-specific decomposition for toroidal flux is illustrated by [toroidal magnetic flux due to poloidal current](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_due_to_poloidal_current).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the diamagnetic-drift contribution to $B_Z$ on the horizontal integration disk points in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: poloidal_plasma_beta
NAMES.short: Dimensionless equilibrium parameter comparing volume-integrated plasma pressure with the magnetic energy scale of the poloidal field generated by the plasma current.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal plasma beta measures how strongly plasma pressure contributes to equilibrium force balance relative to the magnetic pressure associated with the poloidal field produced by the plasma current. It is the explicitly plasma-qualified form of [poloidal beta](name:poloidal_plasma_beta) and is often interpreted together with [internal inductance](name:internal_inductance), which measures current-density peaking.

A common global definition is

$$
\beta_p = \frac{4 \int p\,dV}{R_0 \mu_0 I_p^2}
$$

where $p$ is the equilibrium plasma pressure in Pa, $dV$ is the volume element in m$^3$, $R_0$ is the reference major radius in m, $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability, and $I_p$ is the total toroidal plasma current in A. The pressure integral may include the pressure components used in the equilibrium force-balance model, so comparisons should use a consistent pressure convention.

It is inferred from magnetic-equilibrium reconstruction constrained by external magnetics, pressure diagnostics such as Thomson scattering and charge-exchange spectroscopy, and stored-energy constraints from diamagnetic measurements. Representative values are 0.2-2 in conventional tokamak H-mode plasmas and can exceed 3 in spherical tokamak regimes. It complements [normalized toroidal plasma beta], while [magnetic field] and [poloidal magnetic flux at plasma boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary) provide related equilibrium magnetic constraints.

NAMES.name: radial_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Projection of the magnetic-field vector along increasing major radius in the cylindrical R, phi, Z frame, capturing the radial part of the poloidal field.
NAMES.long:
The radial magnetic field is the component of the full [magnetic field] directed along the major-radius coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is distance from the toroidal symmetry axis, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. Together with the [vertical magnetic field](name:vertical_magnetic_field), it forms the poloidal-plane field whose magnitude is represented by the [poloidal magnetic field](name:poloidal_magnetic_field), while the [toroidal magnetic field](name:toroidal_magnetic_field) is the orthogonal toroidal component.

The defining projection is

$$
B_R = \mathbf{B} \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector and $\hat{R}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing major radius. In axisymmetric equilibrium calculations, $B_R$ is also obtained from gradients of the poloidal magnetic flux, so it is sensitive to vertical variation of flux surfaces.

This component is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction constrained by external magnetic probes, flux loops, motional-Stark-effect measurements, and polarimetry. Representative absolute values in tokamak equilibria range from near zero at symmetry locations to 0.01-0.5 T in shaped plasmas, generally smaller than the toroidal field but essential for determining flux-surface geometry and magnetic shear.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetic-field vector points toward increasing major radius $R$, away from the toroidal symmetry axis.

NAMES.name: safety_factor
NAMES.short: Field-line helicity on nested magnetic flux surfaces, giving the toroidal winding per poloidal circuit and controlling resonant MHD behavior.
NAMES.long:
The safety factor $q$ measures the helicity of magnetic field lines on nested equilibrium flux surfaces. It is the toroidal winding number per single poloidal circuit and identifies rational surfaces where $q=m/n$ can resonate with tearing, kink, or Alfvénic perturbations. Its extrema are often analyzed together with [poloidal magnetic flux at minimum safety factor].

A common flux definition is

$$
q = \frac{d\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}}{d\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is toroidal magnetic flux and $\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is poloidal magnetic flux linked to the same family of flux surfaces. Equivalently, $q$ is obtained from the field-line pitch determined by the equilibrium [magnetic field] and the geometry of each flux surface.

Safety factor values are reconstructed from magnetic equilibrium analysis constrained by external magnetic sensors, polarimetry, motional-Stark-effect measurements, and pressure information. In tokamak cores, $q$ near the magnetic axis is often 0.7-2, while edge values used for stability assessment are commonly 3-7; reversed-shear scenarios may have an off-axis minimum.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a magnetic field line advances in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame during one circuit in the positive poloidal direction around the magnetic axis.

NAMES.name: safety_factor_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Field-line winding number in the infinitesimal flux-surface limit at the magnetic axis, governing central magnetic helicity and kink stability.
NAMES.long:
The safety factor at the magnetic axis is the limiting value of the field-line winding number on nested equilibrium flux surfaces as the surface shrinks to the magnetic axis. It is the central value of the broader [safety factor](name:safety_factor) distribution and strongly influences sawtooth behavior, internal kink stability, and the relation to [minimum safety factor](name:minimum_safety_factor).

For nested flux surfaces, the safety factor is defined by the signed flux derivative

$$
q = \frac{d\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}}{d\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is toroidal magnetic flux and $\Phi_{\mathrm{pol}}$ is poloidal magnetic flux; the magnetic-axis value is the limit of this expression as the enclosed flux surface area tends to zero.

It is computed from magnetohydrodynamic equilibrium reconstruction constrained by external magnetic measurements and, when available, internal pitch-angle information from polarimetry or motional-Stark-effect diagnostics. Its radial variation connects directly to [magnetic shear](name:magnetic_shear), while edge stability studies often compare the axis value with [safety factor at normalized poloidal flux].

Typical central values range from 0.7-1.2 in sawtoothing tokamak plasmas and from 1.2-3 in reversed-shear or advanced scenarios.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the field-line helicity advances in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame for a positive poloidal circuit around the magnetic axis.

NAMES.name: safety_factor_at_normalized_poloidal_magnetic_flux_equal_to_0_95
NAMES.group: normalized poloidal magnetic flux equal to 0 95
NAMES.short: Field-line helicity evaluated on the near-edge closed flux surface whose normalized poloidal magnetic flux is 0.95.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the edge-near value of the [safety factor](name:safety_factor), evaluated on the closed flux surface where the normalized poloidal magnetic flux coordinate has value 0.95. It is commonly denoted $q_{95}$ and summarizes magnetic-field-line winding close to the last closed flux surface, where it strongly affects kink, peeling-ballooning, and edge-localized-mode stability. The equivalent surface is referenced by [safety factor of the ninety-five percent normalized poloidal magnetic flux surface].

The defining evaluation is

$$
q_{95} = q(\psi_N = 0.95) = \left.\frac{d\Phi_{\rm tor}}{d\Phi_{\rm pol}}\right|_{\psi_N=0.95}
$$

where $q$ is the field-line safety factor, $\psi_N$ is normalized poloidal magnetic flux with axis value 0 and boundary value 1, and $\Phi_{\rm tor}$ and $\Phi_{\rm pol}$ are toroidal and poloidal magnetic fluxes.

In practice, $q_{95}$ is obtained from magnetic-equilibrium reconstruction constrained by external magnetic probes and, when available, internal constraints such as motional Stark effect polarimetry or Faraday rotation. Its radial variation is linked to [magnetic shear](name:magnetic_shear), while flux-surface locations such as [poloidal magnetic flux at minimum safety factor] help identify the broader $q$ structure.

Representative values are 3-6 in conventional H-mode tokamak operation and 4-8 in higher-edge-safety-factor advanced scenarios; values near or below 2 at the edge are associated with stronger global MHD constraints.

NAMES.name: surface_area_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Surface area of a closed magnetic flux surface in an equilibrium plasma, equal to the geometric area swept out by that nested surface. It is non-negative and independent of the coordinates used to parameterize the surface.
NAMES.long:
Surface area of a flux surface is the total geometric area of a closed nested magnetic surface in an equilibrium plasma. It is an invariant property of the surface itself: different choices of flux label, poloidal angle, toroidal angle, or mesh parameterization describe the same area when they trace the same physical surface.

For a surface $\\Sigma$ parameterized by coordinates $u$ and $v$ with position vector $\\mathbf{x}(u,v)$, the area is

$$
A = \\int_\\Sigma dA = \\int \\left| \\frac{\\partial \\mathbf{x}}{\\partial u} \\times \\frac{\\partial \\mathbf{x}}{\\partial v} \\right| \, du \, dv
$$

where $dA$ is the physical surface element and the absolute value makes the result independent of the orientation of the parameterization. In an axisymmetric equilibrium described in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \\phi, Z)$ system, where $R$ is major radius, $\\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, this can be evaluated by rotating the poloidal contour about the symmetry axis, equivalently using the local element $2\\pi R\,dl$ along the contour. In a fully three-dimensional equilibrium, the same definition is evaluated from the metric of the closed surface in explicitly chosen flux coordinates such as $(\\rho, \\theta, \\phi)$ or from a triangulated geometric representation.

The area is computed from equilibrium reconstructions or magnetic-surface geometry by integrating the surface metric on each flux surface. It is commonly used with enclosed volume and flux-surface averages to characterize radial geometry, transport normalization, and the mapping between flux coordinates and physical space.

Typical values range from about 1-50 m^2 for compact tokamak plasmas, 50-500 m^2 for medium and large tokamaks, and can exceed 1000 m^2 for very large or highly shaped configurations.

NAMES.name: surface_area_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Total area of the toroidal last-closed flux surface that separates confined plasma from the surrounding open-field-line region.
NAMES.long:
The plasma-boundary surface area is the geometric area of the closed toroidal surface that encloses the confined plasma. It differs from the [poloidal cross-sectional area](name:area_of_plasma_boundary), which measures the area inside the boundary contour in a poloidal plane, and it is closely related to the enclosed [plasma volume](name:volume_of_plasma_boundary).

For an axisymmetric boundary described by a closed poloidal contour in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the surface area is

$$
A_{\mathrm{surf}} = 2\pi \oint_{\partial\Omega} R\, dl
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{surf}}$ is the boundary surface area in m$^2$, $\partial\Omega$ is the plasma-boundary contour, and $dl$ is the poloidal arc-length element in meters.

The quantity is computed from equilibrium reconstruction by identifying the outermost closed flux surface and integrating its reconstructed contour. Magnetic measurements, pressure constraints, and internal magnetic diagnostics constrain the boundary shape; shape parameters such as [inner triangularity](name:inner_triangularity), [outer triangularity](name:outer_triangularity), and [elongation](name:elongation) influence the resulting area.

Typical values range from about 20-80 m$^2$ in medium-size tokamaks and can exceed 600 m$^2$ in reactor-scale devices, depending mainly on major radius, minor radius, elongation, and triangularity.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the boundary surface element is counted with the outward normal enclosing the confined plasma.

NAMES.name: toroidal_beta
NAMES.short: Ratio of volume-averaged perpendicular plasma pressure to the magnetic pressure of the reference toroidal field.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal beta measures how strongly the plasma pressure loads the equilibrium compared with the magnetic pressure associated with the reference toroidal field. It is the toroidal-field-referenced component of [beta], distinct from [normalized beta], which rescales beta by plasma current and size for stability comparisons.

A common equilibrium definition uses the volume average of the total perpendicular pressure over the confined plasma volume:

$$
\beta_{\mathrm{tor}} = \frac{2\mu_0}{B_0^2 V}\int_V p_\perp\,dV
$$

where $p_\perp$ is the total perpendicular plasma pressure in Pa, $V$ is the confined plasma volume in m$^3$, $B_0$ is the reference toroidal magnetic field in T, and $\mu_0$ is the vacuum permeability. The reference field is associated with the toroidal direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height.

Toroidal beta is computed from pressure profiles combined with an equilibrium reconstruction that supplies the plasma volume and reference magnetic field. The pressure input is constrained by kinetic diagnostics such as Thomson scattering, charge-exchange spectroscopy, interferometry, and bremsstrahlung or soft-X-ray measurements, while the equilibrium geometry is constrained by magnetic measurements.

Representative tokamak values are about 0.005-0.05 in many L-mode and H-mode plasmas, with high-performance scenarios reaching 0.05-0.10. Larger values indicate stronger pressure loading relative to the toroidal magnetic pressure and are closely tied to global MHD stability limits.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the volume-averaged perpendicular plasma pressure is positive relative to the positive magnetic-pressure reference $B_0^2/(2\mu_0)$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_radius
NAMES.short: Minor-radius-like coordinate that labels nested equilibrium flux surfaces by the square root of enclosed toroidal magnetic flux.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal flux radius is a radial flux-surface label proportional to the square root of the [toroidal magnetic flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux) enclosed by a nested equilibrium surface. It behaves like a minor radius for nearly circular tokamak plasmas and is the dimensional counterpart of the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate).

A common definition is

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{tor}} = \sqrt{\frac{\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}}{\pi B_{0}}}
$$

where $\rho_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal flux radius, $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the enclosed toroidal magnetic flux in Wb, and $B_{0}$ is the reference vacuum toroidal magnetic field in T used for the conversion to a length scale.

The quantity is computed from magnetic-equilibrium reconstruction by integrating the toroidal magnetic field over the poloidal cross-section bounded by each flux surface. At the outer plasma edge it corresponds to the [toroidal flux radius of the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_flux_radius_of_plasma_boundary); core values range from near 0 at the magnetic axis to about 0.5-2 m at the boundary in present tokamaks.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the coordinate increases outward from the magnetic axis as the enclosed toroidal magnetic flux has the same sign as the reference toroidal magnetic field.

NAMES.name: toroidal_flux_radius_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Minor-radius-like flux coordinate locating the selected plasma boundary by the square root of enclosed toroidal magnetic flux.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal flux radius at the plasma boundary is the radial-like coordinate assigned to the last closed flux surface from the toroidal magnetic flux enclosed by that surface. It is a flux-surface label rather than a direct geometric half-width, so it complements the shape-based [minor radius of the plasma boundary](name:minor_radius_of_plasma_boundary).

A common definition relates the boundary value $\rho_{\rm tor,b}$ to the enclosed toroidal flux $\Phi_{\rm tor,b}$:

$$
\rho_{\rm tor,b} = \sqrt{\frac{|\Phi_{\rm tor,b}|}{\pi B_{\rm ref}}}
$$

where $\Phi_{\rm tor,b}$ is the [toroidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary), and $B_{\rm ref}$ is a reference toroidal magnetic-field magnitude used to convert flux to a length scale. The same boundary surface can also be labeled by [poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary) or by the [normalized poloidal flux coordinate of the plasma boundary](name:normalized_poloidal_flux_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary).

It is computed from magnetic equilibrium reconstruction after identifying the selected plasma boundary, using magnetic measurements and, when available, internal constraints such as polarimetry or motional-Stark-effect data. Representative boundary values range from about 0.2-1.0 m in compact or spherical tokamaks to 1-3 m in large tokamak plasmas.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal flux radius increases outward from the magnetic axis to the selected plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Projection of the magnetic-field vector onto the toroidal direction encircling the machine symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal magnetic field is the component of the [magnetic field] parallel to the toroidal basis direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. In axisymmetric tokamaks it is usually the dominant magnetic-field component and sets the main gyrofrequency scale, while [radial magnetic field](name:radial_magnetic_field) represents a perpendicular component relevant to field errors and equilibrium force balance.

The component is defined by projection of the vector field onto the toroidal unit vector:

$$
B_\phi = \mathbf{B} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $B_\phi$ is the toroidal magnetic-field component, $\mathbf{B}$ is the full magnetic-field vector, and $\hat{\phi}$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle.

It is computed from equilibrium reconstruction, magnetic-field models, toroidal-field coil currents, and magnetic diagnostics such as pickup coils, flux loops, polarimetry, and motional-Stark-effect constraints. The value at a special location is distinguished by [toroidal magnetic field at magnetic axis](name:toroidal_magnetic_field_at_magnetic_axis), while flux-surface quantities such as [toroidal magnetic flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux) integrate magnetic field over an area rather than projecting the local vector field.

Representative values are 1-6 T in present tokamaks and may approach higher fields in compact high-field devices; away from strong plasma-current corrections the vacuum contribution scales approximately as $1/R$ with major radius.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $B_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_field_at_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Toroidal component of the equilibrium magnetic field at the magnetic axis, setting the signed on-axis field direction and strength for nested flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the value of the toroidal magnetic-field component on the magnetic axis, the innermost point of the nested equilibrium flux surfaces. It is the on-axis evaluation of the broader [toroidal magnetic field](name:toroidal_magnetic_field) and is tied geometrically to the axis location described by [major radius of magnetic axis](name:major_radius_of_magnetic_axis).

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ major radius, $\phi$ toroidal angle, and $Z$ vertical height, the defining projection is

$$
B_{\phi,\mathrm{axis}} = \mathbf{B}(R_{\mathrm{axis}}, Z_{\mathrm{axis}}) \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle.

It is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction constrained by magnetic probes, flux loops, polarimetry, motional-Stark-effect measurements, and the imposed toroidal-field-coil current. It helps set the normalization and helicity of flux-surface quantities such as [poloidal magnetic flux at magnetic axis](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_magnetic_axis) and [toroidal magnetic flux](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux).

Representative on-axis tokamak values are 1-6 T in present devices and about 5 T in reactor-scale scenarios, with reversed-field operation carrying the opposite sign.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the toroidal magnetic field points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_flux
NAMES.short: Magnetic flux of the toroidal field through the poloidal cross-section enclosed by an equilibrium flux surface.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal magnetic flux is the part of the [magnetic-flux vector] associated with magnetic field crossing a poloidal cross-section of a nested equilibrium flux surface. It is an integrated quantity, unlike the local [toroidal magnetic field](name:toroidal_magnetic_field), and it provides the dimensional basis for the [normalized toroidal flux coordinate](name:normalized_toroidal_flux_coordinate).

For an axisymmetric equilibrium in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ basis, it can be written as

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}(\psi)=\int_{S_p(\psi)} \mathbf{B}\cdot\hat{\phi}\,dA
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}$ is the toroidal magnetic flux in Wb, $S_p(\psi)$ is the poloidal cross-section bounded by the flux surface labeled by poloidal flux $\psi$, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle, and $dA$ is an area element in the poloidal plane. Its radial variation is closely related to field-line pitch and therefore to the [safety factor](name:safety_factor).

The quantity is computed from equilibrium reconstructions by integrating the reconstructed toroidal field over the flux-surface cross-section, using magnetic diagnostics and internal constraints such as polarimetry or motional-Stark-effect measurements when available. Representative absolute values are about 1-20 Wb in medium-size tokamaks and can exceed 100 Wb in reactor-scale devices, depending mainly on toroidal field strength and [area of the flux surface](name:area_of_flux_surface). A separated contribution, when needed, is described by [toroidal magnetic flux due to poloidal current](name:toroidal_magnetic_flux_due_to_poloidal_current).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetic field crossing a constant-toroidal-angle poloidal cross-section points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ basis.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Flux of the toroidal magnetic field through the poloidal cross-section enclosed by the plasma boundary.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary is the total flux associated with the toroidal magnetic field through the poloidal cross-section enclosed by the boundary surface. In equilibrium analysis this boundary is commonly interpreted as the last closed flux surface or separatrix, and the value provides the outer reference for the [toroidal flux radius of the plasma boundary](name:toroidal_flux_radius_of_plasma_boundary).

For an axisymmetric plasma in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, the boundary value may be written as an area integral over a poloidal cross-section $S_b$ enclosed by the boundary:

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{tor},b} = \int_{S_b} \mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{S}_{\phi}
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor},b}$ is the boundary toroidal magnetic flux, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, and $d\mathbf{S}_{\phi}$ is the directed surface element normal to the toroidal direction. It is complementary to the [poloidal magnetic flux at the plasma boundary](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux_at_plasma_boundary), which labels nested magnetic surfaces and is often used for radial equilibrium coordinates.

The value is obtained from magnetic-equilibrium reconstruction constrained by external magnetic probes, flux loops, plasma current measurements, and internal constraints when available. Typical magnitudes range from a few Wb in compact devices to several hundred Wb in large, high-field tokamaks, scaling approximately with toroidal field strength and the cross-sectional area enclosed by the plasma boundary.

NAMES.name: toroidal_magnetic_flux_due_to_poloidal_current
NAMES.short: Toroidal flux threading the plasma-boundary poloidal cross-section from the magnetic field generated by plasma poloidal current.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the toroidal component of the magnetic flux contribution produced by plasma poloidal current. It isolates the part of the flux budget associated with the poloidal-current source, in contrast to total boundary fluxes or flux contributions from external conductors. It is the toroidal projection of [magnetic_flux_due_to_poloidal_current] and is closely related to the field component described by [toroidal_magnetic_field](name:toroidal_magnetic_field).

For a poloidal cross-section $S_p$ bounded by the selected plasma boundary, the toroidal flux contribution may be written as

$$
\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}^{(J_p)} = \int_{S_p} B_{\phi}^{(J_p)} \, dS_p
$$

where $\Phi_{\mathrm{tor}}^{(J_p)}$ is the toroidal flux contribution, $B_{\phi}^{(J_p)}$ is the toroidal magnetic-field component generated by plasma poloidal current, and $dS_p$ is the oriented poloidal-area element whose normal is $+\hat{\phi}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

It is computed in equilibrium reconstruction from the inferred current distribution and magnetic boundary geometry, constrained by magnetic probes, flux loops, polarimetry, and pressure-profile information. Boundary shape quantities such as [area_of_plasma_boundary](name:area_of_plasma_boundary) affect the integration surface, while magnetic structure quantities such as [magnetic_shear](name:magnetic_shear) and [internal_inductance](name:internal_inductance) constrain the current and field distribution that generate the flux.

Typical absolute magnitudes range from fractions of a Wb in small tokamaks to several tens of Wb in large, high-current devices, depending on plasma current, pressure, shaping, and the selected boundary surface.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the poloidal-current-generated magnetic field threads the oriented poloidal cross-section in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_plasma_current
NAMES.short: Net electric current carried by charged particles around the torus, obtained by integrating the toroidal current density over the plasma cross-section.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal plasma current is the net charge flow circulating in the toroidal direction of a magnetically confined plasma. It is the integrated counterpart of [toroidal plasma current density](name:toroidal_plasma_current_density) and is closely related to [plasma current], which is often used for the same global equilibrium current.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius, $\phi$ the toroidal angle, and $Z$ the vertical coordinate, it is defined by integrating the toroidal component of the current density over the poloidal plasma cross-section:

$$
I_\phi = \int_{S_p} \mathbf{j}(R,Z) \cdot \hat{\phi}\, dR\,dZ
$$

where $I_\phi$ is the toroidal plasma current, $\mathbf{j}$ is the electric-current-density vector, $\hat{\phi}$ is the toroidal unit vector, and $S_p$ is the plasma cross-section bounded by the last closed flux surface or separatrix.

It is measured directly by Rogowski coils and constrained in equilibrium reconstruction by magnetic probes, flux loops, polarimetry, and motional-Stark-effect measurements. The radial distribution of the current affects [internal inductance](name:internal_inductance), and its centroid is summarized by [major radius of current center](name:major_radius_of_current_center).

Representative values range from 0.1-2 MA in medium-size tokamaks, several MA in large present devices, and about 10-15 MA in reactor-scale scenarios.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the plasma current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: toroidal_plasma_current_density
NAMES.short: Projection of the plasma charge-flow density onto the toroidal direction, separating the current that circulates around the device from poloidal or field-aligned flow.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal plasma current density is the $\\hat{\\phi}$ projection of the local current-density vector carried by charged particles in the plasma. It is the component of [plasma current density] that drives the equilibrium poloidal magnetic field and controls current-profile effects such as [internal inductance](name:internal_inductance) and the [major radius of the current center](name:major_radius_of_current_center).

The local projection in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \\phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, is

$$
j_\\phi = \\mathbf{J} \\cdot \\hat{\\phi}
$$

where $\\mathbf{J}$ is the plasma current-density vector and $\\hat{\\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle. For flux-surface quantities, this component is often represented by an appropriate flux-surface average of the toroidal projection.

It is inferred from equilibrium reconstruction constrained by magnetic probes, flux loops, motional-Stark-effect polarimetry, and kinetic pressure information; consistency with [magnetic field] follows from Ampere's law. Ohmic current drive relates it to the [toroidal electric field](name:toroidal_electric_field) through the plasma conductivity, while bootstrap and auxiliary current drive modify its radial distribution.

Typical core values are about $10^5$-$10^7$ A m$^{-2}$ in present tokamaks, with higher values in compact high-field plasmas and lower values near the plasma edge.
NAMES.sign: Positive when positive charge current density points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \\phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: total_plasma_thermal_pressure
NAMES.short: Thermodynamic pressure entering equilibrium force balance, obtained by summing the thermal pressure contributions of all plasma particle species.
NAMES.long:
Total plasma thermal pressure is the isotropic kinetic pressure carried by the thermal particle populations that enters magnetohydrodynamic force balance. It represents the species-summed nonmagnetic pressure term in the equilibrium relation $\nabla p = \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B}$, and corresponds closely to [total thermal plasma pressure] and its flux-surface form [total thermal plasma pressure of a flux surface].

A common kinetic definition is

$$
p_{\mathrm{th}} = \sum_s p_s = \sum_s n_s k_B T_s
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{th}}$ is the total thermal pressure in Pa, $s$ labels thermal plasma species, $n_s$ is the species number density in m$^{-3}$, $T_s$ is the species temperature in K, and $k_B$ is Boltzmann's constant. If temperatures are expressed as energy per particle, the factor $k_B T_s$ is replaced by that energy.

It is inferred by combining kinetic measurements such as Thomson scattering, charge-exchange spectroscopy, interferometry, and ion-temperature diagnostics with equilibrium reconstruction constrained by magnetic measurements. The volume integral of this pressure contributes to [plasma stored energy](name:plasma_stored_energy), while its ratio to magnetic pressure is represented by [beta].

Representative core values are about $10^3$-$10^5$ Pa in present medium-size tokamaks and can approach $10^6$ Pa in high-performance reactor-scale scenarios; edge and scrape-off-layer pressures are much smaller.

NAMES.name: triangularity
NAMES.short: Dimensionless D-shaping parameter measuring the horizontal displacement of the plasma-boundary apex relative to an untriangular elliptical cross-section.
NAMES.long:
Triangularity describes how far a plasma boundary departs from an up-down symmetric ellipse toward a D-shaped cross-section. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, it measures the horizontal displacement of a boundary apex relative to the geometric center and minor radius, complementing vertical stretching described by [elongation](name:elongation). More specific variants such as [upper triangularity](name:upper_triangularity), [lower triangularity](name:lower_triangularity), [inner triangularity](name:inner_triangularity), and [outer triangularity](name:outer_triangularity) resolve which part of the boundary is being characterized.

A common local definition is

$$
\delta = \frac{R_{\rm geo} - R_{\rm apex}}{a}
$$

where $R_{\rm geo}$ is the midplane geometric-center major radius, $R_{\rm apex}$ is the major radius of the selected upper or lower boundary apex, and $a$ is the midplane minor radius. Positive triangularity corresponds to the familiar inboard-shifted D shape used to improve MHD stability and confinement access.

Triangularity is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction of the last closed flux surface or separatrix, using magnetic measurements and, when available, kinetic or internal magnetic constraints. Shape-control systems use it together with boundary size measures such as [area of plasma boundary](name:area_of_plasma_boundary) to regulate plasma-wall clearance and divertor geometry.

Representative tokamak values range from about -0.2 to 0.6, with conventional positive-triangularity H-mode plasmas often near 0.2-0.5 and negative-triangularity scenarios below zero.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the selected plasma-boundary apex is displaced toward smaller major radius $R$ relative to the untriangular elliptical reference.

NAMES.name: upper_elongation
NAMES.short: Dimensionless upper-half vertical shaping parameter comparing the plasma-boundary height above the geometric axis with the horizontal minor radius.
NAMES.long:
Upper elongation describes the vertical stretching of the upper half of the plasma boundary relative to its horizontal size. It isolates up-down asymmetric shaping by measuring only the portion of the boundary above the geometric axis, complementing [lower elongation](name:lower_elongation_of_plasma_boundary) and the full-boundary [elongation](name:elongation).

A common geometric definition in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame is

$$
\kappa_u = \frac{Z_{\max} - Z_{\mathrm{geo}}}{a}
$$

where $\kappa_u$ is the upper elongation, $Z_{\max}$ is the highest vertical coordinate of the plasma boundary, $Z_{\mathrm{geo}}$ is the vertical coordinate of the geometric axis, and $a$ is the horizontal minor radius of the boundary. The explicit boundary-qualified quantity [upper elongation of plasma boundary](name:upper_elongation_of_plasma_boundary) carries the same physical interpretation when the boundary object is named explicitly.

Upper elongation is computed from reconstructed plasma-boundary contours inferred from magnetic measurements, flux-surface fitting, and, when available, kinetic or imaging constraints on the last closed flux surface. It is used with shape parameters such as [outer triangularity](name:outer_triangularity) to characterize diverted and elongated equilibria.

Representative tokamak values are about 1.0 for nearly circular plasmas, 1.5-2.0 for elongated H-mode shapes, and above 2 only in strongly shaped configurations limited by vertical stability and wall clearance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the highest point of the plasma boundary lies in the +$Z$ direction relative to the geometric axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: upper_elongation_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Ratio of the upper vertical half-height of the last closed plasma boundary to its horizontal minor radius, describing up-down shape asymmetry.
NAMES.long:
Upper boundary elongation describes the vertical stretching of the upper half of the last closed plasma boundary relative to its horizontal minor radius. It separates the top-side shaping from the bottom-side shaping represented by [lower elongation of the plasma boundary](name:lower_elongation_of_plasma_boundary), while the full-boundary measure is summarized by [elongation](name:elongation).

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, a common geometric definition is:

$$
\kappa_\mathrm{upper} = \frac{Z_\mathrm{top} - Z_\mathrm{geo}}{a}
$$

where $\kappa_\mathrm{upper}$ is the upper elongation, $Z_\mathrm{top}$ is the highest point of the plasma boundary, $Z_\mathrm{geo}$ is the vertical coordinate of the geometric axis, and $a=(R_\mathrm{out}-R_\mathrm{in})/2$ is the horizontal minor radius from the outer and inner midplane boundary intersections.

The quantity is computed from an equilibrium boundary contour inferred from magnetic measurements, pressure constraints, and shape-control diagnostics. It is closely coupled to other boundary-shape parameters such as [outer triangularity](name:outer_triangularity), because elongation and triangularity together determine the D-shaped cross-section used for vertical stability and confinement optimization.

Typical values are about 1.0 for nearly circular plasmas, 1.5-2.0 in elongated diverted tokamak plasmas, and up to about 2.2 or higher in strongly shaped scenarios limited by vertical stability and wall clearance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the upper boundary extremum lies at larger $Z$ than the plasma geometric axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: upper_inner_squareness
NAMES.short: Dimensionless boundary-shape parameter measuring the quadratic deviation of the upper inboard plasma contour from an elliptical cross-section.
NAMES.long:
Upper inner squareness describes the higher-order shaping of the plasma boundary in the upper inboard quadrant. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height, it separates corner-like distortion from the lower-order elongation and triangularity captured by [upper triangularity](name:upper_triangularity). The corresponding quadrant parameters [lower inner squareness](name:lower_inner_squareness), [upper outer squareness](name:upper_outer_squareness), and [lower outer squareness](name:lower_outer_squareness) describe the other boundary corners.

A local geometric representation uses the signed displacement of the boundary from a reference ellipse fitted to the same lower-order shape:

$$
\zeta_{ui} = \frac{\left[\mathbf{x}_b(\theta_{ui}) - \mathbf{x}_{ell}(\theta_{ui})\right] \cdot \hat{\mathbf{c}}_{ui}}{a}
$$

where $\zeta_{ui}$ is the upper inner squareness, $\mathbf{x}_b=(R_b,Z_b)$ is the boundary point in the poloidal cross-section, $\mathbf{x}_{ell}$ is the corresponding reference-ellipse point, $\theta_{ui}$ labels the upper inboard quadrant, $\hat{\mathbf{c}}_{ui}$ points toward the upper inboard corner, and $a$ is the minor radius.

It is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction by fitting the last closed flux surface or separatrix contour with a boundary-shape parameterization. Magnetic probes, flux loops, polarimetry, and pressure-profile constraints can all influence the reconstructed contour from which the squareness is inferred.

Representative values are near 0 for an elliptical boundary and commonly fall in the range -0.2-0.3 for shaped tokamak plasmas; larger absolute values indicate stronger corner-like distortion and can affect vertical stability, divertor geometry, and plasma-wall clearance.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the upper inboard boundary is displaced from the reference elliptical contour toward the upper inboard rectangular corner of the cross-section.

NAMES.name: upper_outer_squareness
NAMES.short: Dimensionless boundary-shape parameter measuring departure of the upper outboard plasma corner from an elliptical cross-section.
NAMES.long:
Upper outer squareness describes the higher-order shaping of the plasma boundary in the upper outboard quadrant. It complements elongation and triangularity by measuring how full or flattened that corner is relative to an ellipse with the same midplane radii and vertical extent, and is naturally paired with [upper inner squareness](name:upper_inner_squareness) and [lower outer squareness](name:lower_outer_squareness).

A practical definition uses the signed radial displacement of the boundary from a reference ellipse at the upper outer diagonal location:

$$
\zeta_{uo} = \frac{R_b(Z_{uo}) - R_{\mathrm{ell}}(Z_{uo})}{a}
$$

where $\zeta_{uo}$ is the upper outer squareness, $R_b(Z_{uo})$ is the boundary major radius at the chosen upper outboard height, $R_{\mathrm{ell}}(Z_{uo})$ is the corresponding reference-ellipse major radius, and $a$ is the plasma minor radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

It is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction of the last-closed flux surface using magnetic measurements, and may be constrained further by boundary-sensitive diagnostics. Near-elliptical plasmas have values close to 0; shaped tokamak boundaries commonly fall in the range -0.3 to 0.3, with stronger corner shaping approaching about 0.5. Related asymmetries are captured by [lower inner squareness](name:lower_inner_squareness), while [outer triangularity](name:outer_triangularity) and [upper triangularity](name:upper_triangularity) describe lower-order radial shifts of the boundary.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the upper outboard boundary lies at larger major radius than the reference ellipse at the upper outer diagonal location.

NAMES.name: upper_triangularity
NAMES.short: Dimensionless measure of the inward or outward horizontal displacement of the upper plasma-boundary apex relative to the magnetic-axis reference and minor radius.
NAMES.long:
Upper triangularity describes the shaping of the upper part of a tokamak plasma boundary by measuring the horizontal indentation of the upper boundary apex relative to a reference major radius. It refines the overall [triangularity](name:triangularity) by separating the upper half of the cross-section from the lower half, which is represented by [lower triangularity](name:lower_triangularity). This separation is important for asymmetric diverted equilibria and for comparing upper and lower plasma shaping.

A common geometric definition is

$$
\delta_u = \frac{R_0 - R_u}{a}
$$

where $\delta_u$ is the upper triangularity, $R_0$ is the reference major radius of the magnetic axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R_u$ is the major radius of the upper boundary apex, and $a$ is the minor radius reference used for the same boundary. Related one-sided measures include [inner triangularity](name:inner_triangularity), [outer triangularity](name:outer_triangularity), and [minor triangularity](name:triangularity), which describe complementary aspects of boundary indentation.

Upper triangularity is obtained from magnetic-equilibrium reconstruction of the last closed flux surface or separatrix using magnetic probes, flux loops, pressure constraints, and internal magnetic measurements when available. Representative values in diverted tokamak plasmas range from about -0.3 to 0.6, with positive values associated with conventional positive-triangularity shaping and negative values associated with negative-triangularity scenarios.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the upper boundary apex lies at smaller major radius $R$ than the reference magnetic-axis major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point
NAMES.short: Height of the wall location nearest the plasma boundary, expressed as the Z coordinate in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) geometry.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the closest wall point identifies the height of the first wall location with minimum separation from the plasma boundary or separatrix in the poloidal cross-section. Together with [major radius of the closest wall point](name:major_radius_of_closest_wall_point), it specifies the wall-side endpoint of the shortest boundary-to-wall gap used in equilibrium geometry and plasma-wall clearance analysis.

A compact definition is obtained by minimizing the distance between the wall contour and the plasma boundary contour:

$$
Z_{\mathrm{cw}} = Z\!\left(\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\mathbf{x}_w \in W,\,\mathbf{x}_b \in B} \left|\mathbf{x}_w - \mathbf{x}_b\right|\right)
$$

where $W$ is the wall contour, $B$ is the plasma boundary or separatrix contour, $\mathbf{x}_w$ and $\mathbf{x}_b$ are points in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $Z_{\mathrm{cw}}$ is the vertical coordinate of the minimizing wall point.

This quantity is computed from an equilibrium boundary reconstruction and a device wall contour by geometric nearest-point search. It complements the [vertical coordinate of the plasma boundary](name:vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary) and the [distance of the plasma boundary gap], which describe the plasma-side location and the separation length. Representative values span about -5-5 m in large tokamaks, with smaller devices often within -2-2 m.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the closest wall point lies in the +Z direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_current_center
NAMES.short: Height of the toroidal-current centroid relative to the device midplane, obtained by weighting vertical position by toroidal plasma current density.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the current center locates the centroid of the toroidal plasma current distribution in the poloidal cross-section. It is the current-weighted companion to the horizontal centroid [major radius of current center](name:major_radius_of_current_center) and summarizes how the current channel is vertically displaced relative to the magnetic geometry.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $Z$ the vertical coordinate, the centroid is defined by

$$
Z_I = \frac{1}{I_p}\int_S j_\phi(R,Z)\,Z\,dS
$$

where $Z_I$ and $Z$ are in meters, $S$ is the plasma poloidal cross-section, $dS$ is its area element, $j_\phi$ is the [toroidal plasma current density](name:toroidal_plasma_current_density), and $I_p = \int_S j_\phi dS$ is the [plasma current].

This quantity is computed from equilibrium reconstruction using magnetic measurements and, when available, internal constraints such as polarimetry or motional-Stark-effect data that help determine the current-density distribution. In well centered tokamak plasmas it is often within a few centimeters of the geometric midplane; during vertical displacement or strong shaping it can differ by 0.1-0.5 m depending on device size and control state.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the current-weighted centroid is displaced in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_geometric_axis
NAMES.short: Height of the equilibrium cross-section’s shape-derived center used to track the vertical position of the plasma.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the geometric axis locates the shape-derived center of the plasma cross-section in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is a geometric reference for plasma position and shape control, complementary to the flux-defined [vertical coordinate of the magnetic axis](name:vertical_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis). Together with the [major radius of the geometric axis](name:major_radius_of_geometric_axis), it specifies the geometric-axis point in the poloidal plane, while [vertical coordinate of the plasma boundary](name:vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary) describes points on the boundary contour.

The coordinate is the projection of the geometric-axis position vector onto the vertical basis direction:

$$
Z_{\mathrm{geom}} = \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{geom}} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $Z_{\mathrm{geom}}$ is the vertical coordinate, $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{geom}}$ is the position vector of the geometric axis, and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector of the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

It is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction constrained by magnetic measurements, and may also be computed from fitted plasma-boundary or flux-surface geometry. In position-control applications it is compared with requested vertical plasma position and with boundary-derived references such as the [vertical coordinate of a plasma boundary gap reference point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point).

Typical values are near 0 m when the device midplane is the vertical origin and the discharge is vertically centered. Controlled offsets of a few centimeters are common, while large vertical excursions during loss-of-control events can reach 0.1-0.5 m in medium and large tokamaks.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the geometric axis lies in the +Z direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame relative to the coordinate origin.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis
NAMES.short: Height of the magnetic-axis point where nested poloidal flux surfaces contract to their innermost closed contour.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the magnetic axis is the $Z_\mathrm{axis}$ position of the innermost closed magnetic flux surface in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. Together with [major radius of magnetic axis](name:major_radius_of_magnetic_axis), it locates the center of the equilibrium flux-surface topology rather than the purely geometric center described by [vertical coordinate of geometric axis](name:vertical_coordinate_of_geometric_axis).

The magnetic axis is identified as a stationary point of the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi(R,Z)$:

$$
\nabla_{R,Z}\psi(R_\mathrm{axis}, Z_\mathrm{axis}) = 0
$$

where $\psi$ is the poloidal magnetic flux, and $R_\mathrm{axis}$ and $Z_\mathrm{axis}$ are the major-radius and vertical coordinates of that stationary point.

It is computed from magnetic-equilibrium reconstruction constrained by external magnetic probes, flux loops, plasma-boundary information, and internal pitch-angle measurements when available. In controlled tokamak plasmas, values often remain within about -0.2-0.2 m of the device midplane, while deliberately vertically shifted equilibria or transient control excursions can reach several tenths of a meter. Its position is also relevant when comparing axis-local quantities such as [toroidal magnetic field at magnetic axis](name:toroidal_magnetic_field_at_magnetic_axis) and vertical reference points such as the [vertical coordinate of an X-point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_x_point).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetic axis lies in the +Z direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Vertical position of points on the plasma-boundary contour in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, defining boundary height in the poloidal cross-section.
NAMES.long:
This quantity gives the height coordinate of a point on the plasma boundary, the outer closed contour separating confined plasma from the surrounding scrape-off or vacuum region. Because a boundary is a contour rather than a single point, an individual value is defined together with a contour parameter or ordered boundary point; global shape measures such as [elongation](name:elongation) and [area of the plasma boundary](name:area_of_plasma_boundary) summarize the same contour.

A boundary point can be written in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame as

$$
\mathbf{x}_b(s) = R_b(s)\,\hat{R} + Z_b(s)\,\hat{Z}
$$

where $s$ labels position along the poloidal boundary contour, $R_b(s)$ is the major-radius coordinate, and $Z_b(s)$ is the vertical coordinate. The related [vertical coordinate of the geometric axis](name:vertical_coordinate_of_geometric_axis) provides a central reference for interpreting the upper and lower boundary heights.

The boundary height is computed from equilibrium reconstruction using magnetic measurements, pressure and current constraints, and, when available, internal magnetic-field diagnostics. Representative values span about -3 to 3 m in medium-size tokamaks and a wider range in reactor-scale devices; gap-control applications compare this coordinate with the [vertical coordinate of the closest wall point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point) or a [plasma boundary gap reference point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the boundary point lies in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point
NAMES.short: Vertical height of the reference point used to define a plasma-boundary clearance, expressed in the right-handed cylindrical R-phi-Z frame.
NAMES.long:
The plasma-boundary gap reference point is the geometric point from which a clearance between the reconstructed plasma boundary and surrounding structures is evaluated. Its vertical coordinate locates that point along the $Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, complementing the radial location given by [major radius of plasma boundary gap reference point](name:major_radius_of_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point).

For a reference-point position vector $\mathbf{x}_{\rm ref}$, the vertical coordinate is the projection onto the vertical basis direction:

$$
Z_{\rm ref} = \mathbf{x}_{\rm ref} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $Z_{\rm ref}$ is the vertical coordinate and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector of the cylindrical frame.

This coordinate is computed from an equilibrium boundary reconstruction together with the chosen gap geometry; magnetic diagnostics and boundary-shape constraints determine the [vertical coordinate of the plasma boundary](name:vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary), while wall or limiter geometry determines nearby reference locations such as the [vertical coordinate of the closest wall point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_closest_wall_point).

Representative values range from about -3-3 m in medium-size tokamaks and can extend beyond this range in larger devices, depending on machine height and whether the selected gap is upper, lower, or outboard.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the reference point lies in the $+Z$ direction relative to the machine midplane of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_secondary_strike_point
NAMES.short: Height of the secondary divertor strike point relative to the device midplane, locating where the secondary separatrix intersects a divertor target.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the secondary strike point gives the height of the intersection between the secondary separatrix and a divertor target. Together with [major radius of secondary strike point](name:major_radius_of_secondary_strike_point), it specifies the strike-point position in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. The non-secondary counterpart [vertical coordinate of strike point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_strike_point) describes the corresponding strike point on the primary separatrix.

For a strike-point position vector $\mathbf{x}_{\rm sp,2}$, the coordinate is the projection onto the vertical basis direction:

$$
Z_{\rm sp,2} = \mathbf{x}_{\rm sp,2} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $Z_{\rm sp,2}$ is the secondary strike-point height and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector of the cylindrical frame.

The value is computed from magnetic-equilibrium reconstruction by tracing the secondary separatrix until it intersects the divertor target contour. External magnetic measurements, flux loops, and plasma-boundary constraints determine the reconstructed separatrix geometry; [vertical coordinate of secondary plasma boundary] provides the related boundary-height information.

Representative values range from about -4 to 4 m in large tokamaks, with lower-divertor strike points commonly below the midplane and upper-divertor strike points above it.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the strike-point position lies in the +Z direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_secondary_x_point
NAMES.short: Vertical height of the secondary magnetic separatrix null point relative to the device midplane in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) geometry.
NAMES.long:
The secondary X-point is the magnetic null associated with a secondary separatrix, where the poloidal magnetic field vanishes and the boundary topology changes. Its vertical coordinate locates that null in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It complements the radial location given by [major radius of secondary X-point](name:major_radius_of_secondary_x_point) and can be compared with the primary [vertical coordinate of X-point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_x_point).

For the secondary X-point position vector $\mathbf{r}_{X2}$, the coordinate is the projection onto the vertical basis direction:

$$
Z_{X2} = \mathbf{r}_{X2} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $Z_{X2}$ is the secondary X-point vertical coordinate, $\mathbf{r}_{X2}$ is measured from the device coordinate origin, and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector.

The value is computed in equilibrium reconstruction by finding the saddle point of the poloidal magnetic flux, equivalently the point where the local poloidal field components vanish. Magnetic probe and flux-loop constraints, supplemented by divertor imaging or strike-point observations, help determine the separatrix geometry including the linked [vertical coordinate of the secondary strike point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_secondary_strike_point) and [vertical coordinate of the secondary plasma boundary]. Typical values span about -2 to 2 m in present tokamaks, with lower-null configurations negative and upper-null configurations positive relative to the midplane.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the secondary X-point lies in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame relative to the device midplane.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_strike_point
NAMES.short: Height of the divertor contact point where the separatrix intersects a material target, measured along the device vertical axis.
NAMES.long:
The strike-point vertical coordinate gives the height of the point where a separatrix field line intersects a divertor target or other plasma-facing surface. Together with the horizontal location given by [major_radius_of_strike_point](name:major_radius_of_strike_point), it fixes the strike-point position in the poloidal cross-section and is used to assess divertor heat-load placement and plasma-shape control.

In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius, $\phi$ the toroidal angle, and $Z$ the vertical height, the coordinate is the projection of the strike-point position vector onto the vertical basis direction:

$$
Z_{\mathrm{sp}} = \mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{sp}} \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{sp}}$ is the position vector of the strike point and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector.

The value is obtained from magnetic-equilibrium reconstruction by locating the separatrix and finding its intersection with the modeled divertor target surface; it may also be constrained by magnetic diagnostics, divertor imaging, and heat-flux measurements. If multiple separatrix intersections exist, this name denotes the generic strike point, while [vertical_coordinate_of_secondary_strike_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_secondary_strike_point) distinguishes a secondary one.

Typical values span about -2 to 2 m in medium and large tokamaks, with lower-divertor strike points below the midplane and upper-divertor strike points above it. Related boundary geometry is described by [vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary](name:vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary) and controlled relative to reference locations such as [vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point](name:vertical_coordinate_of_plasma_boundary_gap_reference_point).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the strike-point position lies in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_x_point
NAMES.short: Vertical height of the magnetic X-point in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame used to locate the diverted separatrix.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate of the X-point gives the $Z$ position of the magnetic saddle point where separatrix branches meet in a diverted equilibrium. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. This coordinate fixes the up-down placement of the divertor null and is interpreted together with strike-point locations such as the [divertor strike-point vertical coordinate](name:vertical_coordinate_of_strike_point) and [divertor strike-point major radius](name:major_radius_of_strike_point).

For an axisymmetric equilibrium, the X-point is identified as a saddle point of the poloidal magnetic flux $\psi(R,Z)$:

$$
\nabla_{R,Z}\psi(R_X,Z_X)=0
$$

where $R_X$ and $Z_X$ are the major-radius and vertical coordinates of the X-point, and $\nabla_{R,Z}$ is the gradient in the poloidal plane. The reported quantity is $Z_X$.

It is obtained from equilibrium reconstruction using magnetic probes, flux loops, boundary constraints, and, where available, internal profile or polarimetric information. The value is also used in plasma shape control because shifts of the X-point modify connection lengths and the mapping to the divertor target, complementing global geometry markers such as the [geometric-axis vertical coordinate](name:vertical_coordinate_of_geometric_axis) and [magnetic-axis major radius](name:major_radius_of_magnetic_axis).

Representative diverted tokamak equilibria place the X-point from about -2 to 2 m relative to the machine midplane in medium-size devices, while large devices or strongly elongated configurations can reach several meters of vertical displacement. Lower single-null plasmas have negative values when the null is below the midplane, and upper single-null plasmas have positive values when the null is above it.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the X-point lies in the $+Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_magnetic_field
NAMES.short: Projection of the magnetic-field vector onto the vertical Z direction in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical magnetic field is the component of the local [magnetic field] along the vertical coordinate of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height.
