Together with the [radial magnetic field](name:radial_magnetic_field), it forms the poloidal-plane field whose magnitude is represented by the [poloidal magnetic field](name:poloidal_magnetic_field).

The component is defined by projection onto the vertical basis direction:

$$
B_Z(R,\phi,Z) = \mathbf{B}(R,\phi,Z) \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $B_Z$ is the vertical component, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, and $\hat{Z}$ is the upward vertical unit vector. In axisymmetric equilibrium, this component is closely related to the radial gradient of the [poloidal magnetic flux](name:poloidal_magnetic_flux).

It is computed in equilibrium reconstruction from magnetic measurements, force-balance constraints, and flux-surface geometry; local values may also be constrained by magnetic probes, polarimetry, or motional-Stark-effect information. Representative absolute values range from 0.01-1 T in the confined plasma region, with larger values near shaping coils or close to the plasma boundary in strongly shaped discharges.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the magnetic-field vector points toward increasing vertical coordinate $Z$ along $+\hat{Z}$.

NAMES.name: volume_of_flux_surface
NAMES.short: Volume enclosed by a nested equilibrium magnetic flux surface, used as a radial geometric measure for flux-surface averages and integrated plasma quantities.
NAMES.long:
The volume of a flux surface is the geometric measure of the plasma region bounded by a chosen closed magnetic-flux surface. It provides the radial volume coordinate used to convert flux-surface-local quantities into shell or total integrals, and it reduces to [volume of the plasma boundary](name:volume_of_plasma_boundary) at the last closed flux surface.

For an axisymmetric equilibrium, the enclosed volume for a surface labeled by $\psi_s$ is

$$
V(\psi_s) = \int_{\Omega(\psi_s)} d^3x = \int_{\Omega(\psi_s)} R\,dR\,d\phi\,dZ
$$

where $\Omega(\psi_s)$ is the spatial region inside the flux surface, and $(R,\phi,Z)$ is the right-handed cylindrical coordinate system with $R$ the major radius, $\phi$ the toroidal angle, and $Z$ the vertical height.

This quantity is computed from magnetic-equilibrium reconstruction by integrating the volume element over the region bounded by the reconstructed flux contour. Its radial derivative gives the volume of a thin flux shell and is closely related to the [surface area of a flux surface](name:surface_area_of_flux_surface), which enters flux-surface averaging and transport-volume factors.

Typical enclosed volumes range from about 0.01-1 m^3 in compact experiments, 10-100 m^3 in medium-size tokamaks, and several hundred to over 1000 m^3 in reactor-scale plasmas; at the outermost closed surface it is comparable to the [plasma volume](name:volume_of_plasma_boundary).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ordinary unsigned geometric volume is assigned to the region enclosed by the flux surface.

NAMES.name: volume_of_plasma_boundary
NAMES.short: Space enclosed by the last closed flux surface or separatrix, giving the geometric size of the confined plasma region.
NAMES.long:
The volume of the plasma boundary is the region enclosed by the last closed flux surface, or by the separatrix in diverted equilibria. It is the boundary-explicit form of [plasma volume](name:volume_of_plasma_boundary) and complements the meridional [area of the plasma boundary](name:area_of_plasma_boundary) and the enclosing [surface area of the plasma boundary](name:surface_area_of_plasma_boundary).

For an axisymmetric equilibrium, the volume can be written as the toroidal sweep of the poloidal cross-sectional area:

$$
V = 2\pi \int_{A_p} R\, dA
$$

where $V$ is the enclosed volume, $A_p$ is the poloidal cross-section inside the plasma boundary, $R$ is the major radius in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, and $dA$ is an area element in the $(R, Z)$ plane.

This quantity is computed from equilibrium reconstruction after identifying the outermost closed flux contour or separatrix, using magnetic measurements and, where available, kinetic or polarimetric constraints. It is also related to the enclosed [volume of a flux surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface), evaluated at the boundary rather than at an interior flux surface.

Representative values range from about 10-100 m^3 in medium-size tokamaks and several hundred to more than 1000 m^3 in reactor-scale devices, depending mainly on major radius, [minor radius of the plasma boundary](name:minor_radius_of_plasma_boundary), and shaping.

NAMES.name: area_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Physical cross-sectional area enclosed by a poloidal-field coil element conductor or winding pack, used to characterize conductor size for current density and loading estimates.
NAMES.long:
The area of a poloidal-field coil is the physical cross-section enclosed by the conductor or winding-pack boundary, perpendicular to the local current path through the coil element. It determines the engineering current density when combined with [current of poloidal-field coil](name:current_of_poloidal_field_coil), and it is the aggregate geometric measure associated with dimensional quantities such as [width of poloidal-field coil](name:width_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [height of poloidal-field coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil).

For a general coil-element cross-section $S$, the defining geometric measure is

$$
A_{\mathrm{PF}} = \int_S dS
$$

where $A_{\mathrm{PF}}$ is the coil cross-sectional area and $dS$ is the differential surface element over the conductor or winding-pack cross-section. For rectangular sections this reduces to the product of the radial and vertical dimensions in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame; for annular sections it is related to [inner radius of poloidal-field coil](name:inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [outer radius of poloidal-field coil](name:outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil).

The area is determined from engineering geometry, manufacturing drawings, metrology of the coil casing or winding pack, or electromagnetic model geometry. It may also be reconstructed from measured outline dimensions, with [length of poloidal-field coil](name:length_of_poloidal_field_coil) used for oblique or non-rectangular cross-section descriptions when applicable.

Representative element cross-sections range from about 1e-3-1 m^2 for auxiliary and medium-size poloidal-field coils, and can exceed 1 m^2 for large superconducting coil modules or central-solenoid-like structures.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the cross-section is evaluated as the unsigned physical area enclosed by the poloidal-field coil element boundary.

NAMES.name: current_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Electrical circuit current carried by a poloidal-field coil conductor, setting the coil’s contribution to plasma shaping and vertical-position control.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal-field coil current is the net conduction current circulating around an axisymmetric coil circuit in the toroidal direction. It is the actuator quantity that produces external poloidal magnetic field used for plasma position control, shape control, and inductive flux swing. Through the coil geometry, it determines the [poloidal flux contribution from external coils] and contributes to mechanical loads such as [radial](name:radial_force_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [vertical](name:vertical_force_of_poloidal_field_coil) electromagnetic forces.

For an axisymmetric conductor cross-section $S$, the circuit current can be written as the surface integral of toroidal current density:

$$
I_{\rm PF} = \int_S J_\phi\, dS
$$

where $I_{\rm PF}$ is the poloidal-field coil current, $J_\phi$ is the toroidal current density in A m$^{-2}$, and $dS$ is an element of conductor cross-sectional area in m$^2$. The relevant toroidal direction is defined in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $R$ the major radius, $\phi$ the toroidal angle, and $Z$ the vertical coordinate.

The current is measured with calibrated power-supply readbacks, DC current transformers, Rogowski coils, or precision shunts, and is used in magnetic-equilibrium reconstruction together with coil geometry such as the [major radius](name:major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil), [inner radius](name:inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil), and [outer radius](name:outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) of the poloidal-field coil. Fusion devices commonly operate individual poloidal-field and central-solenoid circuits from about $10^3$ to $10^5$ A, with effective ampere-turns reaching mega-ampere-turn scale when multiple turns are present.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the coil current flows in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: height_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Full vertical extent of a rectangular poloidal-field coil element cross-section, measured between its lower and upper edges.
NAMES.long:
This quantity defines the vertical dimension of a rectangular conductor element used in a poloidal-field coil. Together with the [width of the poloidal-field coil](name:width_of_poloidal_field_coil), it specifies the rectangular cross-section whose product gives the [area of the poloidal-field coil](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil). The element position is completed by the [major radius](name:major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [vertical coordinate](name:vertical_coordinate_of_poloidal_field_coil) of the coil element center.

For an axisymmetric rectangular element in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, with $Z$ denoting vertical height, the signed full height may be written as

$$
h = Z_\mathrm{upper} - Z_\mathrm{lower}
$$

where $h$ is the coil-element height, and $Z_\mathrm{upper}$ and $Z_\mathrm{lower}$ are the vertical coordinates of the upper and lower cross-section edges.

The value is obtained from engineering design geometry, mechanical metrology, or survey reconstruction of the coil conductor envelope. Representative poloidal-field coil element heights range from a few centimeters for small correction coils to several tens of centimeters or more for large shaping and vertical-field coils.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the upper edge of the rectangular coil element has a larger $Z$ coordinate than the lower edge in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Distance from the center of an annular poloidal-field coil conductor cross-section to its inner boundary.
NAMES.long:
The inner radius defines the hollow or non-conducting central boundary of an annular poloidal-field coil conductor cross-section. Together with the [outer radius](name:outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil), it fixes the conductor annulus used to compute [cross-sectional area](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil), resistance, cooling-channel clearance, and electromagnetic loading.

For an ideal annular cross-section, the inner radius $r_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the minimum distance from the annulus center $\mathbf{c}$ to the conducting material boundary in the cross-sectional plane:

$$
r_{\mathrm{in}} = \min_{\mathbf{x}\in\partial\Omega_{\mathrm{cond}}} \left|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c}\right|
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is a point on the inner conductor boundary and $\partial\Omega_{\mathrm{cond}}$ is the boundary of the conducting region. The annular area follows from $A=\pi(r_{\mathrm{out}}^2-r_{\mathrm{in}}^2)$, linking this quantity to [area of the poloidal-field coil](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil).

The value is obtained from coil engineering geometry, conductor manufacturing drawings, or dimensional metrology of the winding pack or conductor element. It is used with [width](name:width_of_poloidal_field_coil), [height](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil), and [length](name:length_of_poloidal_field_coil) when comparing annular and rectangular cross-section parameterizations.

Representative inner radii range from millimeters for small hollow conductors to several tenths of a meter for large superconducting coil winding packs, depending on cooling-channel layout and structural support requirements.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured radially outward from the annulus center to the inner conductor boundary.

NAMES.name: length_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Side length of the oblique cross-section used to define the finite conductor geometry of a poloidal field coil element.
NAMES.long:
This quantity gives the geometric side length of an oblique poloidal-field-coil cross-section, such as the slanted edge of a trapezoidal conductor element. It complements the orthogonal cross-section dimensions [height](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [width](name:width_of_poloidal_field_coil), and together these dimensions determine the conductor footprint used for magnetic-field and force calculations.

For an axisymmetric cross-section described in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, the oblique side length between two cross-section vertices can be written as

$$
L = \sqrt{(R_2 - R_1)^2 + (Z_2 - Z_1)^2}
$$

where $L$ is the side length and $(R_1,Z_1)$ and $(R_2,Z_2)$ are the endpoint coordinates in the poloidal cross-section plane.

The value is obtained from engineering design geometry, metrology of as-built coil components, or geometric reconstruction of the coil cross-section used in electromagnetic analysis. It contributes to the [area](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil) of the conductor cross-section and is analogous to the radial dimensions used for annular descriptions such as [inner radius](name:inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [outer radius](name:outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil).

Representative values range from about 0.05-1 m for small shaping or correction coils to 0.5-3 m for large poloidal-field or central-solenoid elements, depending on conductor pack size and insulation thickness.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the directed oblique edge is followed in its declared local cross-section direction.

NAMES.name: major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of the poloidal-field coil centerline in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame, measured from the toroidal symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
The major radius of a poloidal field coil is the radial coordinate of the coil geometric center or centerline in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It fixes the coil position relative to the toroidal symmetry axis and complements the vertical placement given by [vertical coordinate of a poloidal field coil](name:vertical_coordinate_of_poloidal_field_coil). For finite cross-sections, it is the central radial reference from which dimensions such as [width of a poloidal field coil](name:width_of_poloidal_field_coil), [height of a poloidal field coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil), and [outer radius of a poloidal field coil](name:outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) are defined.

For an axisymmetric coil whose center has Cartesian coordinates $(x_c,y_c,z_c)$ in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x},\hat{y},\hat{z})$ basis with $\hat{z}$ vertical, the corresponding major radius is

$$
R_c = \sqrt{x_c^2 + y_c^2}
$$

where $R_c$ is the coil center major radius and $x_c,y_c$ are the horizontal coordinates of the same point.

This quantity is obtained from coil engineering geometry, metrology of the installed conductors, or reconstruction of the magnetic-field-system layout used for electromagnetic force and field calculations. It is closely related to the [radial outline of a poloidal field coil](name:radial_outline_of_poloidal_field_coil), which describes the radial boundary rather than the center reference.

Representative values range from about 0.5-4 m in compact tokamaks and 2-12 m in large tokamak poloidal-field systems, depending on whether the coil is inboard, outboard, upper, or lower relative to the plasma.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured outward from the toroidal symmetry axis along $+\hat{R}$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Radial distance from the center of an annular poloidal-field coil conductor cross-section to its outer conducting boundary.
NAMES.long:
The outer radius defines the external circular boundary of an annular poloidal-field coil conductor cross-section. Together with the [inner radius of the poloidal field coil](name:inner_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil), it fixes the conductor thickness and determines the current-carrying area relevant to coil resistance, inductance, cooling, and electromagnetic loading.

For a circular annular cross-section with local coordinates $u$ and $v$ in the conductor plane, the outer radius $a_{\rm out}$ can be defined from the conductor boundary $\partial\Omega$ as:

$$
a_{\rm out} = \max_{(u,v)\in\partial\Omega}\sqrt{(u-u_c)^2+(v-v_c)^2}
$$

where $(u_c,v_c)$ is the annulus center and $\Omega$ is the conducting region. The cross-sectional [area of the poloidal field coil](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil) follows from the annular geometry and is distinct from rectangular measures such as the [width of the poloidal field coil](name:width_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [height of the poloidal field coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil).

This dimension is obtained from coil engineering design, manufacturing metrology, or survey reconstruction of the conductor pack. Representative values range from a few centimeters for compact copper correction coils to several tens of centimeters or more for large superconducting poloidal-field coil elements.
NAMES.sign: Positive when measured outward from the annulus center to the outer conducting boundary.

NAMES.name: radial_force_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Major-radius component in the cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame of the electromagnetic Lorentz load acting on a poloidal field coil conductor.
NAMES.long:
The radial force of a poloidal field coil is the projection of the net electromagnetic load on the coil conductor onto the major-radius direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is a structural-design quantity because it determines outward or inward loading on coil cases, supports, insulation, and pre-compression systems. It is complementary to the [vertical force of a poloidal field coil](name:vertical_force_of_poloidal_field_coil), which describes the orthogonal $Z$ projection of the same Lorentz loading.

For a conductor volume $V$, the radial component is obtained from the Lorentz force density integrated over the coil:

$$
F_R = \int_V (\mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \hat{R}\, dV
$$

where $F_R$ is the radial force in N, $\mathbf{J}$ is current density in A m$^{-2}$, $\mathbf{B}$ is magnetic flux density in T, $\hat{R}$ is the outward major-radius unit vector, and $dV$ is a conductor volume element in m$^3$. The force scales with the [current of the poloidal field coil](name:current_of_poloidal_field_coil) and with the background magnetic field produced by plasma and neighboring coils.

In practice this load is computed from electromagnetic field calculations using the coil geometry, current waveform, and surrounding conductors; mechanical validation can use strain gages, support load measurements, or displacement monitoring during commissioning pulses. Geometry quantities such as the [radial outline of a poloidal field coil](name:radial_outline_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [width of a poloidal field coil](name:width_of_poloidal_field_coil) set the integration domain and affect the distribution of stress.

Representative values range from $10^4$-$10^6$ N for small auxiliary shaping coils to $10^6$-$10^8$ N for large central-solenoid or equilibrium-field coils in reactor-scale devices, depending on current, radius, and magnetic coupling.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the force points toward increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_outline_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Major-radius coordinate of the boundary points that define a poloidal-field-coil conductor in the right-handed cylindrical (R, phi, Z) frame.
NAMES.long:
The radial outline of a poloidal field coil is the major-radius coordinate $R$ of points on the conductor boundary in the poloidal cross-section. It specifies the coil shape relative to the toroidal symmetry axis and complements the coil center coordinate [major radius of poloidal field coil](name:major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) and the conductor size [width of poloidal field coil](name:width_of_poloidal_field_coil).

For a point expressed in the right-handed Cartesian $(\hat{x}, \hat{y}, \hat{z})$ basis with $\hat{z}=\hat{Z}$, the corresponding major radius in the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame is

$$
R = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are horizontal Cartesian coordinates in meters measured from the toroidal symmetry axis, and $R$ is the distance from that axis.

This coordinate is obtained from coil engineering geometry, surveying, or electromagnetic model geometry used to compute fields and forces. It is interpreted together with the vertical outline coordinate when reconstructing the coil cross-section; related geometric summaries include [outer radius of poloidal field coil](name:outer_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil), [vertical coordinate of poloidal field coil](name:vertical_coordinate_of_poloidal_field_coil), and [area of poloidal field coil](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil).

Typical values range from about 0.5-15 m in present and reactor-scale tokamaks, depending on whether the coil is an inboard shaping coil, an outboard vertical-field coil, or an external solenoid-adjacent winding.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $R$ is measured outward from the toroidal symmetry axis in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_coordinate_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Vertical position of the geometric center of a poloidal field coil element in the right-handed cylindrical R-phi-Z machine frame.
NAMES.long:
The vertical coordinate locates the geometric center of a poloidal field coil element along the $Z$ axis of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. Together with the [major radius of the poloidal field coil](name:major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil), it fixes the coil element center in the poloidal cross-section used for magnetic-field and force calculations. It is distinct from the [height of a poloidal field coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil), which describes the vertical extent of the conductor cross-section rather than its location.

For a coil element center position vector $\mathbf{x}_c$, the coordinate is the projection onto the vertical basis direction:

$$
Z_c = \mathbf{x}_c \cdot \hat{Z}
$$

where $Z_c$ is the vertical coordinate of the coil element center and $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector of the cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

This quantity is determined from engineering geometry, metrology surveys, or magnetic-system design models, and is used when computing coil-generated poloidal flux, Lorentz forces, and free-boundary equilibrium constraints. The [radial outline of the poloidal field coil](name:radial_outline_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [area of the poloidal field coil](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil) provide complementary shape information for finite conductor models.

Typical values range from about -5 to 5 m in medium-size tokamaks and can exceed ±10 m in large devices, depending on the coil set layout relative to the machine midplane. Comparison with the [vertical coordinate of the magnetic axis](name:vertical_coordinate_of_magnetic_axis) helps characterize the vertical placement of the external field system relative to the plasma.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the coil element center is displaced in the +Z direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: vertical_force_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Upward-downward component of the net electromagnetic load on a poloidal-field coil, used to assess structural support requirements.
NAMES.long:
The vertical force on a poloidal-field coil is the component of the net load acting along the $Z$ direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height. It is paired with the [radial force of a poloidal-field coil](name:radial_force_of_poloidal_field_coil) to describe the principal mechanical loads on the coil support structure.

For an electromagnetic load, the coil force follows the volume integral of the Lorentz force density:

$$
F_Z = \int_V (\mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}) \cdot \hat{Z}\, dV
$$

where $F_Z$ is the vertical force, $\mathbf{J}$ is current density, $\mathbf{B}$ is magnetic field, $\hat{Z}$ is the vertical unit vector, and $V$ is the conducting coil volume. The sign and magnitude depend on the [current of the poloidal-field coil](name:current_of_poloidal_field_coil), the magnetic field produced by other coils and plasma currents, and the coil position given by quantities such as [major radius of the poloidal-field coil](name:major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [vertical coordinate of the poloidal-field coil](name:vertical_coordinate_of_poloidal_field_coil).

This force is computed from magnetostatic or transient electromagnetic models and can be checked indirectly using support reactions, strain gages, or load-cell measurements on coil supports. Representative values range from $10^4$-$10^7$ N for medium-size shaping coils and can exceed $10^8$ N for large central-solenoid or high-current pulsed coils during rapid current changes or disruption scenarios.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the net force on the coil points in the $+Z$ vertical direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: width_of_poloidal_field_coil
NAMES.short: Full horizontal extent of a rectangular poloidal-field-coil conductor cross-section measured between its inner and outer radial faces.
NAMES.long:
The width of a poloidal-field coil is the horizontal dimension of a rectangular conductor or winding-pack cross-section in the machine cross-section. It complements the [height of the poloidal field coil](name:height_of_poloidal_field_coil), and together these dimensions determine the rectangular area represented by [area of the poloidal field coil](name:area_of_poloidal_field_coil).

For a rectangular cross-section aligned with the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system, where $R$ is major radius and $Z$ is vertical height, the width is defined by the separation of the two radial faces:

$$
w = R_{\mathrm{outer}} - R_{\mathrm{inner}}
$$

where $w$ is the coil width, $R_{\mathrm{outer}}$ is the major-radius coordinate of the radially outer face, and $R_{\mathrm{inner}}$ is the major-radius coordinate of the radially inner face.

This engineering geometry is obtained from coil design drawings, conductor-stack dimensions, or as-built metrology, and it is used in electromagnetic models that also require the [major radius of the poloidal field coil](name:major_radius_of_poloidal_field_coil) and [vertical coordinate of the poloidal field coil](name:vertical_coordinate_of_poloidal_field_coil). Fusion-device PF coil widths range from about 0.05-0.5 m for compact shaping coils to 0.5-2 m for large central-solenoid or outer PF coil winding packs.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the outer radial face of the rectangular poloidal-field-coil cross-section lies at larger major radius $R$ than the inner radial face in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ system.

NAMES.name: electric_field
NAMES.short: Electromagnetic force per unit charge that drives charged-particle acceleration, cross-field drifts, and parallel current in a plasma.
NAMES.long:
The electric field is the vector field that gives the electrostatic and inductive force per unit charge on electrons and ions. In magnetized plasmas it controls $E \times B$ drift motion, parallel acceleration, Ohmic current drive, and radial force balance, making it closely coupled to [magnetic field], [electron velocity](name:electron_velocity), and [plasma current density].

A common electromagnetic definition is

$$
\mathbf{E} = -\nabla \Phi - \frac{\partial \mathbf{A}}{\partial t}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric-field vector in V/m, $\Phi$ is the electric potential in V, $\mathbf{A}$ is the magnetic vector potential in V s m$^{-1}$, and $t$ is time in s. In conducting plasma, the parallel component is related to current through transport coefficients such as [electrical conductivity], while perpendicular components enter drift and force-balance relations.

It is inferred from loop-voltage and magnetic-equilibrium analysis, charge-exchange force-balance measurements, heavy-ion-beam probes, Langmuir probes in the edge, and kinetic or transport modeling. Representative tokamak values range from 0.1-10 V/m for inductive toroidal fields, several kV/m to tens of kV/m for core radial fields, and 50-300 kV/m in steep edge transport barriers.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a component of $\mathbf{E}$ points along the positive direction of its stated basis: outward for $+R$ and increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ for $+\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: electrical_conductivity
NAMES.short: Anisotropic transport coefficient that relates electric-field components to conductive current components in a magnetized plasma.
NAMES.long:
Electrical conductivity describes the collisional ability of charged particles to carry current in response to an applied electric field. In a magnetized plasma it is strongly anisotropic, with the field-aligned response represented by [parallel_electrical_conductivity](name:parallel_plasma_electrical_conductivity) and directly connected to the conductive part of [plasma_current_density](name:plasma_current_density).

The defining linear transport relation is

$$
\mathbf{j}_{\rm cond} = \boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\mathbf{E}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}_{\rm cond}$ is the conductive current density in A m$^{-2}$, $\mathbf{E}$ is the [electric_field](name:electric_field) in V m$^{-1}$, and $\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ is the electrical-conductivity tensor in ohm$^{-1}$ m$^{-1}$. In collisional regimes the dominant parallel contribution follows Spitzer-like scaling, increasing approximately as [electron_temperature](name:electron_temperature)$^{3/2}$ and depending on charge state and [normalized_electron_collisionality](name:normalized_electron_collisionality); [electron_density](name:electron_density) enters through collision frequencies and current response.

Conductivity is computed from kinetic or transport models, inferred from current diffusion and loop-voltage evolution, or constrained by combining magnetic equilibrium information with electric-field estimates. Representative core tokamak values are about $10^6$-$10^9$ ohm$^{-1}$ m$^{-1}$, while colder edge and scrape-off-layer plasmas can fall to $10^3$-$10^6$ ohm$^{-1}$ m$^{-1}$.

NAMES.name: electron_density
NAMES.short: Local number of electrons per unit volume, including thermal and non-thermal electron populations participating in plasma quasineutrality.
NAMES.long:
Electron density is the local particle concentration of the full electron population, including both [thermal electrons](name:thermal_electron_density) and [fast electrons](name:fast_electron_density) when present. It sets collisionality, plasma frequency, charge balance with [ion density](name:ion_density), and the pressure contribution combined with [electron temperature](name:electron_temperature) in [electron pressure](name:electron_pressure).

For an electron phase-space distribution $f_e(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)$, the density $n_e(\mathbf{x},t)$ is the zeroth velocity moment:

$$
n_e(\mathbf{x},t) = \int f_e(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\,d^3v
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $f_e$ is normalized so that the integral gives $n_e$ in m$^{-3}$.

Electron density is measured by interferometry, reflectometry, Thomson scattering, and Langmuir probes in colder boundary plasmas; it is also inferred in transport modeling from particle balance and quasineutrality. Core tokamak values commonly span $0.1-2 \times 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, while scrape-off-layer values range from $10^{17}$ to $10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ depending on fueling, confinement regime, and divertor conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron phase-space distribution has a nonzero integral over velocity space.

NAMES.name: electron_pressure
NAMES.short: Isotropic part of the electron momentum-flux tensor, combining thermal bulk and non-thermal electron contributions that enter force balance and transport.
NAMES.long:
Electron pressure is the isotropic electron contribution to plasma momentum balance, including both the Maxwellian bulk population and any non-thermal electron component. It provides the electron part of the total kinetic pressure that competes with magnetic pressure in equilibrium and drives transport through pressure gradients. The thermal component is closely related to [thermal electron pressure](name:thermal_electron_pressure), [thermal electron density](name:thermal_electron_density), and [electron temperature](name:electron_temperature), while comparison with [ion pressure](name:ion_pressure) determines the species partition of plasma pressure.

A common decomposition is

$$
p_e = p_{e,\mathrm{th}} + p_{e,\mathrm{fast}} = n_{e,\mathrm{th}} T_{e,\mathrm{J}} + \frac{1}{3}\mathrm{Tr}(\mathbf{P}_{e,\mathrm{fast}})
$$

where $p_e$, $p_{e,\mathrm{th}}$, and $p_{e,\mathrm{fast}}$ are pressures in Pa, $n_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is thermal electron density in m$^{-3}$, $T_{e,\mathrm{J}}$ is thermal electron temperature expressed as energy per particle in joules, and $\mathbf{P}_{e,\mathrm{fast}}$ is the fast-electron pressure tensor in Pa.

The thermal part is inferred from electron density and temperature diagnostics such as interferometry, Thomson scattering, and electron cyclotron emission. Non-thermal contributions are estimated from suprathermal-electron diagnostics such as hard-X-ray bremsstrahlung, electron cyclotron emission, and kinetic modeling constrained by measured distributions.

Typical core values range from about 1e3-3e5 Pa in tokamak plasmas, with edge and scrape-off-layer values often below 1e3 Pa. Non-thermal electron pressure is usually smaller than the thermal part, but it can become significant in strongly RF-heated plasmas or in runaway-electron scenarios.
NAMES.sign: Positive when random and non-thermal electron particle motion produces compressive isotropic stress on a surface element.

NAMES.name: electron_temperature
NAMES.short: Mean random kinetic energy per degree of freedom of the electron population, expressed as an equivalent thermodynamic temperature.
NAMES.long:
Electron temperature describes the thermal spread of the electron velocity distribution after subtracting any mean fluid motion. It is a kinetic-moment quantity that controls collisional transport, electrical conductivity, ionization balance, and the electron contribution to pressure; it is closely paired with [electron density](name:electron_density) and [thermal electron pressure](name:thermal_electron_pressure).

For a near-Maxwellian electron distribution, the temperature in energy units is related to the mean random kinetic energy per electron by

$$
T_e = \frac{2}{3}\,\langle E_{\mathrm{rand},e}\rangle
$$

where $T_e$ is the electron temperature in eV and $\langle E_{\mathrm{rand},e}\rangle$ is the mean kinetic energy associated with random electron motion, also expressed in eV. In a thermal equation of state, this moment combines with [thermal electron density](name:thermal_electron_density) to determine the thermal part of the electron pressure, while [electron pressure](name:electron_pressure) may include additional nonthermal contributions.

Electron temperature is measured with Thomson scattering, electron cyclotron emission, soft-X-ray spectral methods, Langmuir probes in sufficiently cool edge plasma, or inferred from integrated transport and equilibrium-consistent modeling. Comparisons with [ion temperature](name:ion_temperature) diagnose electron-ion energy exchange and distinguish electron-heated from ion-heated regimes.

Representative values range from 1-30 keV in hot tokamak cores, 50-1000 eV near the pedestal and edge, and 1-100 eV in scrape-off-layer and divertor plasmas, depending on heating power, density, and confinement regime.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron random kinetic energy relative to the mean electron flow is greater than zero.

NAMES.name: electron_velocity
NAMES.short: Mean fluid flow velocity of the electron population, defined by the first velocity-space moment of the electron distribution.
NAMES.long:
Electron velocity is the bulk drift of the electron fluid obtained from the first moment of the electron distribution function, not the random thermal motion associated with [electron_temperature](name:electron_temperature). It enters charge, momentum, and current balance together with [ion_velocity], and its components are resolved relative to radial, poloidal, toroidal, and magnetic-field-aligned directions.

The electron fluid velocity $\mathbf{v}_e$ is defined from the electron distribution function $f_e(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)$ by

$$
\mathbf{v}_e(\mathbf{x},t) = \frac{1}{n_e(\mathbf{x},t)} \int \mathbf{v}\, f_e(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\, d^3v
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $n_e$ is the [electron_density](name:electron_density). In a quasineutral plasma, differences between electron and ion flow contribute to [plasma_current_density]; perpendicular components are often governed by drift motion driven by the [electric_field](name:electric_field) and [magnetic_field].

Electron velocity is computed in fluid, kinetic, neoclassical, and turbulence transport models, and it can be inferred indirectly from current-density reconstruction combined with ion-flow measurements or from edge probes in sufficiently cool boundary plasmas. Direct core measurement is difficult because electron thermal speeds greatly exceed bulk flows.

Representative bulk electron speeds in magnetically confined plasmas range from 10^3-10^5 m.s^-1 for cross-field drift and turbulent transport velocities, and from 10^4-10^6 m.s^-1 for parallel current-carrying flow, depending on density and current density.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a component of $\mathbf{v}_e$ points along the positive direction of its stated basis: outward for radial velocity, increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame for toroidal velocity, increasing poloidal angle for poloidal velocity, and along the local magnetic-field direction for parallel velocity.

NAMES.name: fast_electron_density
NAMES.short: Number of suprathermal electrons per unit volume, separated from the bulk thermal population by an energy- or velocity-space criterion.
NAMES.long:
Fast-electron density is the zeroth velocity-space moment of the nonthermal electron distribution over the part of phase space designated as fast. It complements the bulk [thermal electron density](name:thermal_electron_density) and contributes to the total [electron density](name:electron_density) when the suprathermal population is included.

For an electron distribution function $f_e(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})$, where $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is velocity, and $f_e$ has units m$^{-3}$(m s$^{-1}$)$^{-3}$, the fast-electron density is

$$
n_{e,\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{\Omega_\mathrm{fast}} f_e(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $\Omega_\mathrm{fast}$ is the velocity-space region defining suprathermal electrons relative to the bulk distribution.

It is inferred from diagnostics sensitive to energetic electrons, including hard-X-ray bremsstrahlung, electron cyclotron emission, synchrotron radiation, and kinetic modeling constrained by current-drive or runaway-electron measurements. The same population also sets anisotropic pressure components such as [parallel fast electron pressure](name:parallel_fast_electron_pressure), while [fast ion density](name:fast_ion_density) is the ion counterpart for energetic particles.

Representative values span about 10^14-10^18 m^-3 for weak RF- or wave-driven tails, rising to 10^18-10^20 m^-3 in strong runaway-electron or high-power auxiliary-heating phases; the value remains below or comparable to the bulk electron density in most confined plasmas.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the integrated fast-electron distribution function over the defined fast region is positive.

NAMES.name: fast_electron_pressure
NAMES.short: Gyrotropic pressure of suprathermal electrons resolved into directions parallel and perpendicular to the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
Fast-electron pressure describes the momentum flux carried by a suprathermal electron population whose distribution need not be thermally equilibrated with the bulk electrons. In magnetized plasmas it is commonly represented by parallel and perpendicular pressures relative to the local magnetic-field direction, connecting the shared physics behind [parallel fast-electron pressure](name:parallel_fast_electron_pressure) and the total [electron pressure](name:electron_pressure).

For a gyrotropic fast-electron distribution, the pressure tensor is written as

$$
\mathbf{P}_{fe} = p_{\parallel,fe}\,\hat{b}\hat{b} + p_{\perp,fe}\,(\mathbf{I}-\hat{b}\hat{b})
$$

where $\mathbf{P}_{fe}$ is the fast-electron pressure tensor, $p_{\parallel,fe}$ and $p_{\perp,fe}$ are the pressures parallel and perpendicular to the magnetic-field unit vector $\hat{b}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$, and $\mathbf{I}$ is the identity tensor. The scalar contribution to an isotropized pressure is often formed from $(p_{\parallel,fe}+2p_{\perp,fe})/3$ when comparing with [electron pressure](name:electron_pressure).

Fast-electron pressure is inferred from kinetic modeling constrained by hard-X-ray, electron-cyclotron-emission, synchrotron, or bremsstrahlung measurements, and from transport calculations using the fast-electron distribution function. It is most relevant in plasmas with electron cyclotron current drive, lower-hybrid current drive, runaway-electron populations, or strong auxiliary heating. Values can range from negligible compared with thermal pressure to $10^2$-$10^4$ Pa in localized energetic-electron populations, with larger values possible in disruption-generated runaway beams.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the component represents compressive kinetic pressure from fast-electron random motion along its associated magnetic-field-aligned direction.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_density
NAMES.short: Number of suprathermal ions per unit volume in the non-Maxwellian population with energies above the local thermal bulk.
NAMES.long:
Fast-ion density measures the population of energetic ions that is not part of the thermal Maxwellian bulk. The boundary between fast and thermal ions is operational: it is set by the heating, fusion-product, or transport model, and the total ion population relates to [ion density](name:ion_density) while [thermal ion density] describes the complementary bulk population.

A common kinetic definition integrates the fast-ion distribution function over the selected fast region of velocity space:

$$
n_{fi}(\mathbf{x},t) = \sum_Z \int_{\mathcal{V}_{fast}} f_{i,Z}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v},t)\,d^3v
$$

where $n_{fi}$ is the fast-ion density, $f_{i,Z}$ is the distribution function for ion charge state $Z$ at position $\mathbf{x}$ and time $t$, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $\mathcal{V}_{fast}$ is the model-defined suprathermal velocity-space domain. When charge states are resolved, [fast ion state density](name:fast_ion_state_density) gives the corresponding contribution for a charge-state bundle.

Fast-ion density is inferred from fast-ion D-alpha spectroscopy, neutron emission, neutral-particle analysis, gamma-ray spectroscopy, collective Thomson scattering, and kinetic modeling of neutral-beam, ion-cyclotron, or fusion-born alpha populations. Representative core values in beam-heated or radio-frequency-heated tokamak plasmas span about $10^{15}$-$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$, with burning-plasma alpha populations reaching higher fractions while remaining below the bulk [ion density](name:ion_density). Pressure anisotropy associated with the same population is described by [parallel fast ion pressure](name:parallel_fast_ion_pressure).
NAMES.sign: Positive when the integrated fast-ion phase-space distribution function is nonnegative over the selected suprathermal velocity-space domain.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_pressure
NAMES.short: Gyrotropic pressure of energetic ions resolved into components parallel and perpendicular to the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
Fast-ion pressure is the kinetic stress carried by suprathermal ion populations produced by auxiliary heating, fusion reactions, or acceleration processes. Because these ions often have anisotropic velocity distributions, the pressure is represented by field-aligned parallel and perpendicular components rather than by a single isotropic value. It complements [fast-ion density](name:fast_ion_density) and should be distinguished from thermal-ion quantities such as [ion temperature](name:ion_temperature) and [ion density](name:ion_density).

For a gyrotropic fast-ion distribution, the components are defined from velocity-space moments:

$$
p_{\parallel f}=m_i\int (v_\parallel-u_\parallel)^2 f_f\,d^3v,\qquad p_{\perp f}=\frac{m_i}{2}\int v_\perp^2 f_f\,d^3v
$$

where $m_i$ is the ion mass, $f_f$ is the fast-ion distribution function, $v_\parallel$ and $v_\perp$ are particle velocities relative to the magnetic-field direction, and $u_\parallel$ is the parallel fast-ion flow velocity. The isotropic limit satisfies $p_{\parallel f}=p_{\perp f}$.

Fast-ion pressure is inferred from kinetic modeling constrained by diagnostics such as fast-ion D-alpha spectroscopy, neutral-particle analyzers, collective Thomson scattering, neutron emission, gamma-ray spectroscopy, and charged-fusion-product measurements. Related anisotropic energetic-particle quantities include [fast-ion state pressure] and the electron counterpart [fast-electron pressure].

Representative core values range from 10^2-10^5 Pa in neutral-beam-heated, ion-cyclotron-heated, or alpha-particle-producing plasmas; values are much lower near the plasma edge as energetic-ion confinement degrades.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the fast-ion random kinetic stress is compressive, so the parallel and perpendicular pressure components add positive diagonal entries to the gyrotropic pressure tensor.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_state_density
NAMES.short: Local number density of suprathermal ions belonging to a resolved ionization or charge-state population.
NAMES.long:
Fast-ion state density is the phase-space zeroth moment of the suprathermal ion population for one resolved charge state. It separates energetic particles produced by neutral-beam injection, ion-cyclotron heating, fusion reactions, or strong acceleration from the thermal charge-state population described by [thermal ion state density](name:thermal_ion_state_density). Summing over resolved charge states gives the state-resolved contribution to [fast ion density](name:fast_ion_density), while combining thermal and fast populations contributes to [ion density](name:ion_density).

For a charge state $Z$ and fast-particle velocity-space region $\Omega_f$, the density is

$$
n_{f,Z} = \int_{\Omega_f} f_{i,Z}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $n_{f,Z}$ is the fast-ion density for charge state $Z$, $f_{i,Z}$ is the ion distribution function for position $\mathbf{x}$ and velocity $\mathbf{v}$, and $\Omega_f$ is the part of velocity space above the local thermal bulk criterion.

It is inferred from fast-ion diagnostics such as fast-ion D-alpha spectroscopy, neutron emission, gamma-ray spectroscopy, collective Thomson scattering, and neutral-particle analysis, often combined with kinetic orbit and Fokker-Planck modeling. Representative core values range from $10^{16}$-$10^{19}\;\mathrm{m^{-3}}$ in beam- or radio-frequency-heated tokamak plasmas, commonly a fraction of a percent to several percent of the bulk ion density. The related [parallel fast-ion state pressure](name:parallel_fast_ion_state_pressure) is the corresponding second velocity moment along the magnetic field.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the charge-state-resolved fast-ion distribution function is non-negative over the velocity-space region defining the suprathermal population.

NAMES.name: fast_ion_state_pressure
NAMES.short: Directional kinetic pressure of a charge-state-resolved fast-ion population, resolved parallel and perpendicular to the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
This quantity represents the anisotropic kinetic pressure carried by energetic ions within a specified charge-state bundle. It separates momentum-space pressure into components along and across the magnetic field, providing the charge-state-resolved counterpart of [fast ion pressure](name:fast_ion_pressure). It is closely tied to the energetic-particle population described by [fast ion density](name:fast_ion_density) and differs from thermal-ion pressure associated with [ion temperature](name:ion_temperature).

For a gyrotropic fast-ion distribution, the directional pressures are defined from velocity-space moments:

$$
P_\parallel = m_i \int (v_\parallel-u_\parallel)^2 f_i\,d^3v, \qquad P_\perp = \frac{m_i}{2}\int v_\perp^2 f_i\,d^3v
$$

where $P_\parallel$ and $P_\perp$ are the parallel and perpendicular directional pressures, $m_i$ is ion mass, $f_i$ is the fast-ion distribution function, $v_\parallel$ and $v_\perp$ are particle velocities relative to the magnetic field, and $u_\parallel$ is the parallel mean flow.

It is inferred from kinetic modeling constrained by neutral-particle analyzers, fast-ion D-alpha spectroscopy, neutron emission, gamma-ray measurements, collective Thomson scattering, and charge-exchange diagnostics. Core values in auxiliary-heated tokamaks span about 10^2-10^5 Pa, with larger anisotropy during neutral-beam injection or ion-cyclotron heating.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the directional pressure component represents compressive kinetic momentum flux in the specified parallel or perpendicular direction.

NAMES.name: ion_average_charge
NAMES.short: Density-weighted mean ionization charge state of a specified ion species, averaged over its resolved charge-state populations.
NAMES.long:
Ion average charge is the mean charge state of an ion species after weighting each ionization state by its particle density. It differs from the plasma-wide [effective charge], which weights charge states differently to characterize collisionality and impurity content, and it is tied directly to the species [ion_density](name:ion_density).

The density-weighted charge-state average is

$$
\bar{Z}_i = \frac{\sum_{\zeta} \zeta\, n_{i,\zeta}}{\sum_{\zeta} n_{i,\zeta}}
$$

where $\bar{Z}_i$ is the mean charge state of ion species $i$, $\zeta$ is the integer ionization charge state, and $n_{i,\zeta}$ is the density of that charge state. The denominator is the total density of the species and corresponds to the species contribution to [ion_density](name:ion_density).

This quantity is computed from resolved charge-state densities in transport or collisional-radiative modeling and can be constrained by spectroscopic measurements of line emission, recombination continua, and impurity charge-state balance. For fuel ions such as deuterium and tritium it is usually 1 in fully ionized core plasma, while helium is near 2; medium-Z impurities such as carbon or neon can span several charge states, and tungsten may have mean charge states from about 10 to above 50 depending on electron temperature. The plasma-wide consequence of these charge states is summarized by [plasma_effective_ion_charge].
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion charge states represent net positive electric charge relative to neutral atoms.

NAMES.name: ion_charge_state_pressure
NAMES.short: Total kinetic pressure carried by ions in one resolved ionization charge-state population, including thermal bulk and non-thermal contributions.
NAMES.long:
Ion charge-state pressure is the scalar kinetic pressure associated with ions of a specified species and ionization state, before summing over other charge states. It is the charge-state-resolved contribution that can be accumulated into [ion_pressure](name:ion_pressure) or [total_ion_pressure](name:total_ion_pressure), while [thermal_ion_state_pressure](name:thermal_ion_state_pressure) denotes the thermal-only subset when such a separation is made.

For an isotropic scalar pressure, it is one third of the trace of the kinetic pressure tensor for that charge state:

$$
p_{i,z} = \frac{1}{3}\,\mathrm{Tr}\left[m_i \int (\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_{i,z})(\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_{i,z}) f_{i,z}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v\right]
$$

where $p_{i,z}$ is in Pa, $i$ labels the ion species, $z$ is the integer ionization charge state, $m_i$ is ion mass in kg, $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{u}_{i,z}$ are particle and mean-flow velocities in m s$^{-1}$, and $f_{i,z}$ is the charge-state distribution function.

It is inferred from charge-state-resolved spectroscopy, impurity transport analysis, collisional-radiative modeling, and kinetic calculations constrained by [ion_density](name:ion_density), [ion_temperature](name:ion_temperature), and [ion_average_charge](name:ion_average_charge). Representative core contributions span about 10^2-10^5 Pa for abundant main-ion or impurity charge states in heated tokamaks, while weak impurity states or edge populations can contribute below 1 Pa; energetic components are related to [fast_ion_state_pressure].

NAMES.name: ion_density
NAMES.short: Total ion number density for a species, including thermal and nonthermal populations and summing over charge states when they are resolved.
NAMES.long:
Ion density is the local number of ions of a given species per unit volume, including both bulk thermal ions and nonthermal ion populations. When charge states are resolved, this quantity is the sum over those charge states rather than a single-state population. It is the ion counterpart of [electron density](name:electron_density) and separates into components such as [thermal ion density] and [fast ion density](name:fast_ion_density) when those populations are represented independently.

For a kinetic description, the total ion density can be written as the velocity-space and charge-state sum:

$$
n_i(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_Z \int f_{i,Z}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $n_i$ is the ion number density in m$^{-3}$, $Z$ labels charge state, $f_{i,Z}$ is the phase-space distribution function for that charge state, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, and $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity. Quasi-neutrality connects this quantity to electron density through $n_e \simeq \sum_i Z_i n_i$ when impurities and multiple ion species are included.

Ion density is inferred from particle-balance modeling, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, beam-emission measurements, neutral-particle analysis, and consistency with interferometry or Thomson-scattering measurements of the electron channel. Core deuterium or hydrogen ion densities in tokamak plasmas commonly range from $10^{19}$ to $10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, while edge and scrape-off-layer values are lower and energetic-ion densities are often a small fraction of the bulk population.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the counted ion population exceeds the zero-density reference.

NAMES.name: ion_pressure
NAMES.short: Total kinetic pressure carried by the ion population, combining thermal and non-thermal contributions and summing charge states when unresolved.
NAMES.long:
Ion pressure is the isotropic kinetic pressure associated with ions, including both random thermal motion and non-thermal energetic-ion contributions. It is distinct from [thermal ion pressure](name:thermal_ion_pressure), which excludes fast-particle pressure, and from [ion state pressure](name:ion_charge_state_pressure), which resolves a single charge state rather than the summed ion population.

A common decomposition is

$$
p_i = \sum_Z \left(p_{i,Z}^{\rm th} + p_{i,Z}^{\rm nt}\right), \qquad p_{i,Z}^{\rm th}=n_{i,Z} k_B T_{i,Z}
$$

where $p_i$ is the ion pressure, $Z$ labels ion charge state, $p_{i,Z}^{\rm th}$ is the thermal contribution, $p_{i,Z}^{\rm nt}$ is the non-thermal contribution, $n_{i,Z}$ is number density in m$^{-3}$, $T_{i,Z}$ is thermodynamic temperature in K, and $k_B$ is Boltzmann's constant. If [ion temperature](name:ion_temperature) is expressed in electronvolts, $k_B T_{i,Z}$ is replaced by $eT_{i,Z}$, with $e$ the elementary charge.

Ion pressure is inferred by combining ion density, ion temperature, and energetic-particle information from diagnostics such as charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, neutral-particle analysis, neutron measurements, and transport or equilibrium analysis. It contributes with [electron pressure](name:electron_pressure) to the total plasma pressure balance, while [total ion pressure](name:total_ion_pressure) clarifies the fully summed quantity across all ion species.

Core thermal ion pressures in present tokamaks often span 1-100 kPa; high-performance or burning-plasma scenarios can reach 0.1-1 MPa, while edge and scrape-off-layer values can fall to 1-1000 Pa.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion contribution is compressive, corresponding to positive isotropic normal stress in the plasma pressure tensor.

NAMES.name: ion_temperature
NAMES.short: Mean random kinetic energy per degree of freedom of the bulk ion population, averaged over charge states or species when the context combines them.
NAMES.long:
Ion temperature is the kinetic temperature associated with random ion motion after subtracting the mean ion flow. It represents the thermal part of the ion energy distribution and is distinct from directed [ion_velocity], while combining with [ion_density](name:ion_density) to determine thermal pressure.

For an ion species $s$ with distribution function $f_s(\mathbf{v})$, density $n_s$ in m$^{-3}$, mass $m_s$ in kg, and mean flow velocity $\mathbf{u}_s$, the temperature expressed as energy is

$$
T_{i,s} = \frac{m_s}{3 n_s e}\int |\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}_s|^2 f_s(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $e$ is the elementary charge and $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity. When multiple charge states or ion species are represented by one value, the result is an appropriate population average.

Ion temperature is measured most directly by charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy from Doppler broadening of impurity emission lines, and it can also be inferred from neutron spectroscopy or transport analysis. It is a key input to [thermal_ion_pressure](name:thermal_ion_pressure) and helps distinguish thermal-ion behavior from energetic components described by [fast_ion_density](name:fast_ion_density).

Typical values range from 1-20 keV in tokamak cores, 100-1000 eV in pedestal and edge plasmas, and 1-100 eV in cold scrape-off-layer conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion velocity distribution has a positive second central moment relative to its mean flow.

NAMES.name: ion_velocity
NAMES.short: Bulk flow velocity of the ion fluid, representing the first velocity moment of the ion distribution and coupling particle, momentum, and energy transport.
NAMES.long:
Ion velocity is the bulk fluid motion of the ion population obtained from the first moment of the ion velocity distribution. It is distinct from thermal motion described by [ion_temperature](name:ion_temperature) and contributes to momentum transport, centrifugal effects, and convective particle flux together with [ion_density](name:ion_density).

For an ion species or charge-state-averaged ion population, the fluid velocity $\mathbf{u}_i$ is defined by the ion particle flux density $\mathbf{\Gamma}_i$ divided by the ion number density $n_i$:

$$
\mathbf{u}_i = \frac{\mathbf{\Gamma}_i}{n_i}
$$

where $\mathbf{\Gamma}_i$ is the ion particle flux density and $n_i$ is the ion number density. The velocity may be resolved into radial, poloidal, toroidal, or magnetic-field-parallel projections; comparison with [electron_velocity](name:electron_velocity) determines current-carrying relative motion and is related to [plasma_current_density](name:plasma_current_density).

Ion flow is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, Doppler spectroscopy of impurity or main-ion emission, Mach probes in the scrape-off layer, and momentum-balance calculations constrained by equilibrium and transport modeling. Magnetic-field geometry from [magnetic_field](name:magnetic_field) sets the parallel direction and strongly influences neoclassical poloidal and toroidal rotation.

Typical core toroidal and parallel ion velocities are 1e3-1e5 m.s^-1 in neutral-beam-heated tokamaks, while radial convective velocities are commonly 1-100 m.s^-1 except during transient events. Edge and scrape-off-layer flows can approach the ion sound speed, especially along open magnetic-field lines.
NAMES.sign: Positive when a resolved velocity component is aligned with its positive basis direction: outward across flux surfaces for the radial component, along increasing poloidal angle for the poloidal component, along increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame for the toroidal component, and along the local magnetic-field direction for the parallel component.

NAMES.name: normalized_electron_collisionality
NAMES.short: Dimensionless ratio of the electron collision frequency to the trapped-particle bounce frequency, separating neoclassical transport regimes.
NAMES.long:
Normalized electron collisionality, often denoted $\nu_e^*$, measures how many electron pitch-angle-scattering collisions occur during one trapped-particle bounce period. It controls whether electron neoclassical transport lies in the banana, plateau, or Pfirsch-Schlüter regime and is closely tied to collisional transport of [electron_density](name:electron_density), [electron_temperature](name:electron_temperature), and [electron_pressure](name:electron_pressure).

A common definition is

$$
\nu_e^* = \frac{\nu_e}{\omega_b}
$$

where $\nu_e$ is the effective electron collision frequency in s$^{-1}$ and $\omega_b$ is the bounce frequency of trapped electrons in s$^{-1}$. The exact bounce-frequency model depends on magnetic geometry and pitch-angle convention, so comparisons should use the same normalization basis.

This quantity is computed from kinetic profiles, magnetic geometry, and collisional transport formulas rather than measured directly. Values below about 0.1 correspond to weakly collisional banana-regime behavior, values near 0.1-1 mark the plateau transition, and values above 1 indicate increasingly collisional Pfirsch-Schlüter-like behavior, especially toward colder edge plasma.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron collision frequency is evaluated as a positive rate and divided by a positive bounce frequency.

NAMES.name: parallel_electric_field
NAMES.short: Field-aligned electric force per unit charge that accelerates particles along magnetic-field lines and drives parallel current.
NAMES.long:
The parallel electric field is the projection of the [electric field](name:electric_field) onto the local magnetic-field direction. It is the component that performs work on charged particles along field lines, setting Ohmic current drive, runaway-electron acceleration, and field-aligned transport without being converted into an $E \times B$ drift.

The field-aligned projection is defined by

$$
E_\parallel = \mathbf{E} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{b}} = \frac{\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{B}}{|\mathbf{B}|}
$$

where $E_\parallel$ is the parallel electric field in V m$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric-field vector in V m$^{-1}$, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector in T, and $\hat{\mathbf{b}}=\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{B}|$ is the unit vector along the magnetic field. In resistive single-fluid transport it is closely related to [parallel plasma current density](name:parallel_plasma_current_density) through the [electrical conductivity], while kinetic treatments connect it to [parallel electron velocity](name:parallel_electron_velocity) through the electron momentum balance.

It is inferred from magnetic-flux evolution, loop-voltage constraints, current-density reconstruction, and transport calculations based on generalized Ohm's law; direct local measurement is uncommon because the field-aligned component is small and geometry dependent. The [poloidal electric field](name:poloidal_electric_field) is a coordinate projection, whereas this quantity follows the magnetic-field direction and therefore changes with magnetic pitch.

Representative core values are about 0.01-1 V m$^{-1}$ during tokamak current ramp and flat-top phases, with much larger transient values, 1-100 V m$^{-1}$, possible during rapid current quench, reconnection, or strong runaway-electron drive.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electric-field vector points along the local magnetic-field direction.

NAMES.name: parallel_electron_velocity
NAMES.short: Field-aligned projection of the bulk electron fluid velocity, describing electron flow along the local magnetic-field direction.
NAMES.long:
The parallel electron velocity is the field-aligned component of the bulk electron fluid flow. It is the projection of [electron_velocity](name:electron_velocity) onto the local magnetic-field direction and is distinct from geometric projections such as [radial_electron_velocity](name:radial_electron_velocity), [poloidal_electron_velocity](name:poloidal_electron_velocity), and [toroidal_electron_velocity](name:toroidal_electron_velocity).

The defining projection is

$$
v_{e\parallel} = \mathbf{v}_e \cdot \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{v}_e \cdot \frac{\mathbf{B}}{|\mathbf{B}|}
$$

where $v_{e\parallel}$ is the parallel electron velocity, $\mathbf{v}_e$ is the electron fluid velocity vector, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, and $\mathbf{b}$ is the unit vector along the magnetic field.

This quantity is inferred from transport analysis, electron momentum balance, and current-density constraints combined with measurements of electron density, temperature, magnetic geometry, and plasma rotation. It is often compared with [parallel_ion_velocity](name:parallel_ion_velocity) because the difference between electron and ion parallel flows contributes directly to the parallel current carried by the plasma.

Representative core tokamak values are about $10^3$-$10^5$ m s$^{-1}$, while edge and scrape-off-layer flows can reach $10^4$-$10^6$ m s$^{-1}$ near strong parallel pressure gradients or sheath-connected field lines.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron fluid flow is aligned with the local magnetic-field vector $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: parallel_fast_electron_pressure
NAMES.short: Field-aligned kinetic pressure of the non-thermal electron population, formed from the second velocity moment parallel to the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
Parallel fast-electron pressure is the field-aligned component of the pressure tensor for suprathermal electrons, excluding the bulk thermal electron contribution. It distinguishes kinetic stress associated with motion along the local magnetic-field direction from the perpendicular component, [perpendicular_fast_electron_pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_electron_pressure), and together these components form [fast_electron_pressure].

For a gyrotropic fast-electron distribution, the defining kinetic moment is

$$
p_{f e,\parallel} = m_e \int (v_\parallel - u_\parallel)^2 f_{f e}(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $p_{f e,\parallel}$ is the parallel fast-electron pressure, $m_e$ is the electron mass, $v_\parallel$ is particle velocity projected along the local magnetic field, $u_\parallel$ is the fast-electron mean parallel flow, and $f_{f e}$ is the fast-electron velocity distribution such that $\int f_{f e}\,d^3v$ gives [fast_electron_density](name:fast_electron_density).

This quantity is computed from kinetic fast-electron distribution functions or inferred from diagnostics sensitive to suprathermal electrons, such as hard-X-ray emission, electron cyclotron emission, and RF-wave absorption analysis. It is compared with [parallel_fast_ion_pressure](name:parallel_fast_ion_pressure) when assessing anisotropic energetic-particle pressure balance and wave-particle momentum exchange.

Representative values range from less than $10^2$ Pa in weakly heated plasmas to $10^3$-$10^5$ Pa in regions with strong electron cyclotron or lower-hybrid acceleration; the ratio to perpendicular pressure indicates pressure anisotropy and can affect stability and current-drive efficiency.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the field-aligned random kinetic energy density of the fast-electron population is nonzero.

NAMES.name: parallel_fast_ion_pressure
NAMES.short: Pressure-tensor component from suprathermal ions associated with random particle motion along the local magnetic field direction.
NAMES.long:
Parallel fast-ion pressure is the projection of the energetic-ion pressure tensor along the local magnetic-field direction. It isolates the part of the suprathermal ion kinetic stress associated with velocity-space spread parallel to the field, complementing [perpendicular fast-ion pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_ion_pressure) and forming the directional content of [fast-ion pressure](name:fast_ion_pressure).

For fast-ion species or charge-state populations $s$, the kinetic definition is

$$
p_{\mathrm{fi},\parallel} = \sum_s \int m_s \left(v_\parallel - u_{\parallel,s}\right)^2 f_{\mathrm{fi},s}(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $m_s$ is the ion mass, $v_\parallel$ is particle velocity along the magnetic field, $u_{\parallel,s}$ is the mean parallel flow of that fast-ion population, and $f_{\mathrm{fi},s}$ is the fast-ion velocity distribution function. The parent [fast-ion pressure](name:fast_ion_pressure) is obtained from the corresponding pressure-tensor components, while [fast-ion density](name:fast_ion_density) constrains the zeroth moment of the same distribution.

This quantity is inferred by combining energetic-particle diagnostics such as fast-ion D-alpha spectroscopy, neutron emission, neutral-particle analysis, gamma-ray spectroscopy, or collective Thomson scattering with kinetic modeling of neutral-beam, ion-cyclotron, or fusion-born ion populations. It is compared with [thermal ion pressure](name:thermal_ion_pressure) to assess energetic-particle contributions to equilibrium, Alfvénic stability, and anisotropic transport.

Representative core values span 10^2-10^4 Pa in auxiliary-heated tokamak plasmas, with reactor-relevant fusion-alpha populations reaching about 10^4-10^5 Pa in high-performance scenarios. Strong anisotropy, with parallel and perpendicular components differing substantially, is common when fast ions are created by directed neutral-beam injection or resonant wave heating.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the parallel fast-ion kinetic stress is compressive along the local magnetic-field direction.

NAMES.name: parallel_fast_ion_state_pressure
NAMES.short: Kinetic pressure from suprathermal ions in a resolved charge-state bundle associated with random motion along the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
Parallel fast-ion state pressure is the gyrotropic pressure-tensor component carried by energetic ions in a specified charge-state bundle along the local magnetic field. It is the directional component of [fast-ion state pressure], complementing [perpendicular fast-ion state pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_ion_state_pressure) and distinguishing charge-state-resolved energetic-particle pressure from the charge-summed [parallel fast-ion pressure](name:parallel_fast_ion_pressure).

For a charge-state bundle $a$, the kinetic definition is

$$
p_{\parallel,a}^{\mathrm{fast}} = m_a \int \left(v_\parallel - u_{\parallel,a}\right)^2 f_a^{\mathrm{fast}}(\mathbf{v})\, d^3v
$$

where $m_a$ is the ion mass, $v_\parallel$ is particle velocity projected along the local magnetic field, $u_{\parallel,a}$ is the mean parallel flow of that fast-ion state, and $f_a^{\mathrm{fast}}$ is the suprathermal velocity-space distribution. The corresponding [fast-ion state density](name:fast_ion_state_density) sets the zeroth moment of the same distribution, while [thermal ion state pressure](name:thermal_ion_state_pressure) describes the bulk Maxwellian contribution.

This quantity is computed from kinetic fast-ion distribution models or inferred by combining energetic-particle diagnostics such as neutron emission, fast-ion D-alpha spectroscopy, neutral-particle analysis, gamma-ray spectroscopy, and collective scattering with transport modeling. Representative core values range from about 10^2-10^5 Pa in auxiliary-heated tokamaks, with the largest values in neutral-beam-heated or alpha-particle-dominated plasmas and much smaller values where suprathermal ion density is weak.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the pressure component represents compressive random kinetic stress along the local magnetic-field direction.

NAMES.name: parallel_ion_velocity
NAMES.short: Field-aligned projection of the bulk ion flow velocity, distinguishing motion along magnetic field lines from cross-field drifts.
NAMES.long:
Parallel ion velocity is the component of the ion fluid flow along the local magnetic-field direction. It is the field-aligned part of the full [ion velocity], complementary to cross-field components such as [radial ion velocity](name:radial_ion_velocity) and geometric flow components such as [toroidal ion velocity](name:toroidal_ion_velocity).

The defining projection is

$$
v_{i\parallel} = \mathbf{v}_i \cdot \mathbf{b}, \qquad \mathbf{b}=\frac{\mathbf{B}}{|\mathbf{B}|}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_i$ is the ion fluid velocity, $\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic-field vector, $|\mathbf{B}|$ is its magnitude, and $\mathbf{b}$ is the unit vector along the local field. This component enters parallel momentum balance, neoclassical transport, impurity screening, and comparison with the [parallel electron velocity](name:parallel_electron_velocity) that helps determine field-aligned current.

Parallel ion flow is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, Doppler spectroscopy, or transport modeling combined with magnetic-equilibrium geometry, because diagnostics often measure line-of-sight or toroidal/poloidal projections that must be projected onto $\mathbf{b}$. Representative core values range from $10^3$-$10^5$ m s$^{-1}$, with larger values possible in strongly rotating or neutral-beam-heated plasmas.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion flow is along the local magnetic-field vector $\mathbf{B}$.

NAMES.name: parallel_plasma_electrical_conductivity
NAMES.short: Magnetic-field-aligned electrical conductance of the plasma, relating parallel current density to the electric field through collisional electron momentum transport.
NAMES.long:
Parallel plasma electrical conductivity is the magnetic-field-aligned component of the plasma conductivity tensor. It is the coefficient that converts a parallel electric field into [parallel plasma current density](name:parallel_plasma_current_density), and it is the plasma-specific form of [parallel electrical conductivity](name:parallel_plasma_electrical_conductivity). It is the relevant component of [plasma electrical conductivity] for resistive current diffusion along field lines.

The defining local Ohm-law relation is

$$
j_{\parallel} = \sigma_{\parallel} E_{\parallel}
$$

where $j_{\parallel}$ is the current density along the magnetic field in A m$^{-2}$, $E_{\parallel}$ is the electric field projected along the magnetic field in V m$^{-1}$, and $\sigma_{\parallel}$ is the parallel plasma electrical conductivity in ohm$^{-1}$ m$^{-1}$.

In transport analysis, this quantity is computed from collisional or neoclassical conductivity models and constrained by current diffusion, loop-voltage evolution, and magnetic equilibrium information. It depends mainly on [electron temperature](name:electron_temperature), effective charge through electron-ion collisions, and collisionality, with hotter and cleaner plasmas having larger conductivity.

Typical core tokamak values range from about 10^6-10^8 ohm$^{-1}$ m$^{-1}$, while colder edge and scrape-off-layer plasmas can fall to about 10^3-10^5 ohm$^{-1}$ m$^{-1}$. Low conductivity increases [plasma resistance](name:plasma_resistance) and enhances ohmic dissipation for a given [parallel plasma current].

NAMES.name: perpendicular_fast_electron_pressure
NAMES.short: Kinetic pressure carried by suprathermal electrons in velocity components perpendicular to the local magnetic field, excluding the bulk thermal electron contribution.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular fast electron pressure is the gyrotropic pressure-tensor component associated with suprathermal electron motion transverse to the local magnetic field. It distinguishes magnetic-moment or cyclotron-motion energy from field-aligned kinetic energy and is paired with [parallel_fast_electron_pressure](name:parallel_fast_electron_pressure) as the anisotropic components of [fast_electron_pressure]. It is related to [fast_electron_density](name:fast_electron_density) through the velocity-space moment of the nonthermal electron distribution, not through a Maxwellian temperature assumption.

For a gyrotropic fast electron distribution, the perpendicular pressure is the second velocity moment

$$
p_{\perp,fe} = \int \frac{m_e v_\perp^2}{2} f_{fe}(\mathbf{v}) \, d^3v
$$

where $p_{\perp,fe}$ is the perpendicular fast electron pressure, $m_e$ is the electron mass, $v_\perp$ is particle speed perpendicular to the magnetic field, and $f_{fe}(\mathbf{v})$ is the fast electron velocity distribution normalized so that its velocity integral gives the fast electron number density.

This quantity is inferred by combining kinetic distribution modeling with diagnostics sensitive to suprathermal electrons, such as hard X-ray bremsstrahlung, electron cyclotron emission from nonthermal tails, synchrotron emission, and measurements of RF-driven current or wave absorption. Values depend strongly on heating and current-drive scenario; in present tokamak plasmas they can range from negligible levels to tens or hundreds of pascals, and in strongly driven nonthermal populations may become a significant fraction of the bulk electron pressure. The analogous ion quantity [perpendicular_fast_ion_pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_ion_pressure) is governed by the same pressure-tensor decomposition but by ion-orbit and slowing-down physics.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the perpendicular kinetic energy density of the fast electron population is positive.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_fast_ion_pressure
NAMES.short: Nonthermal fast-ion kinetic pressure associated with gyromotion and random motion perpendicular to the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
Perpendicular fast-ion pressure is the part of the energetic-ion pressure tensor carried by particle velocity components orthogonal to the local magnetic field. Together with [parallel fast-ion pressure](name:parallel_fast_ion_pressure), it describes pressure anisotropy within the parent [fast ion pressure](name:fast_ion_pressure) and affects equilibrium force balance, Alfvénic stability, and energetic-particle transport.

For a fast-ion distribution function, the perpendicular pressure is the second velocity-space moment transverse to the magnetic-field direction:

$$
