p_{f\perp} = \sum_i \int \frac{m_i v_\perp^2}{2} f_{f,i}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $p_{f\perp}$ is the perpendicular fast-ion pressure in Pa, $m_i$ is ion mass in kg, $v_\perp$ is particle speed perpendicular to the local magnetic field in m/s, and $f_{f,i}$ is the fast-ion velocity distribution for ion species or charge state $i$. The related [fast ion density](name:fast_ion_density) is the zeroth moment of the same distribution.

This quantity is computed from kinetic fast-ion models or inferred by combining equilibrium constraints with diagnostics sensitive to energetic ions, such as neutron emission, fast-ion D-alpha spectroscopy, neutral particle analysis, gamma-ray measurements, and collective Thomson scattering. It is also compared with [perpendicular fast-electron pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_electron_pressure) when assessing nonthermal pressure anisotropy across species.

Representative values range from about 10^2-10^4 Pa in neutral-beam-heated tokamak cores and can reach several 10^4 Pa in strongly heated or alpha-particle-dominated plasmas; values near the plasma edge are usually far smaller because energetic-ion confinement weakens.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the fast-ion perpendicular stress is compressive in directions orthogonal to the local magnetic field.

NAMES.name: perpendicular_fast_ion_state_pressure
NAMES.short: Kinetic pressure from charge-state-resolved energetic ions associated with random velocity components across the local magnetic field.
NAMES.long:
This quantity is the perpendicular component of the gyrotropic pressure tensor for a fast-ion charge-state bundle. It represents the momentum flux carried by suprathermal ions in the two velocity-space directions transverse to the local magnetic field, complementing [parallel fast ion state pressure](name:parallel_fast_ion_state_pressure) within [fast ion state pressure].

For a fast-ion distribution in charge state $q$, the perpendicular pressure is the second velocity moment averaged over the two perpendicular degrees of freedom:

$$
p_{\perp,f,q} = \frac{m_i}{2}\int v_\perp^2 f_{f,q}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $p_{\perp,f,q}$ is the perpendicular fast-ion state pressure, $m_i$ is the ion mass, $v_\perp$ is the particle speed perpendicular to the local magnetic field, $f_{f,q}$ is the fast-ion distribution for charge state $q$, and $d^3v$ is the velocity-space volume element. Summing this quantity over resolved charge states gives the charge-state-summed [perpendicular fast ion pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_ion_pressure), while comparison with the parallel component measures pressure anisotropy.

It is inferred from energetic-particle distribution modeling constrained by diagnostics such as neutron emission, gamma-ray spectroscopy, fast-ion D-alpha spectroscopy, neutral-particle analysis, collective Thomson scattering, and charge-exchange measurements. Charge-state resolution is obtained from ionization balance and charge-exchange modeling coupled to the fast-ion distribution.

Representative core values range from about 10^2-10^5 Pa in neutral-beam or radio-frequency heated plasmas, with smaller values near the edge and larger values possible in burning-plasma alpha-particle populations. The pressure scales with [fast ion state density](name:fast_ion_state_density) and with the perpendicular energy content of the nonthermal distribution.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the perpendicular second velocity moment represents compressive fast-ion momentum flux across the local magnetic field.

NAMES.name: plasma_electrical_conductivity
NAMES.short: Transport coefficient relating electric field to conductive current flow in a collisional, magnetized plasma.
NAMES.long:
Plasma electrical conductivity is the effective transport coefficient that connects the electric field to conductive current carried mainly by electrons in a magnetized plasma. Because collisions and magnetic-field geometry make the response anisotropic, the [parallel component](name:parallel_plasma_electrical_conductivity) is often the dominant part and is closely related to the more general [electrical conductivity](name:electrical_conductivity).

The local Ohmic response is expressed as

$$
\mathbf{j} = \boldsymbol{\sigma} \cdot \mathbf{E}
$$

where $\mathbf{j}$ is the [plasma current density](name:plasma_current_density) in A m$^{-2}$, $\mathbf{E}$ is the [electric field](name:electric_field) in V m$^{-1}$, and $\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ is the conductivity in ohm$^{-1}$ m$^{-1}$. In collisional theory, the magnitude is controlled primarily by electron-ion collision frequency, so it increases strongly with [electron temperature](name:electron_temperature) and depends on [electron density](name:electron_density), ion charge state, and [normalized electron collisionality](name:normalized_electron_collisionality).

It is inferred from current diffusion analysis, loop-voltage response, equilibrium-constrained current-density reconstruction, or calculated from neoclassical and Spitzer-like transport models. Representative values range from about $10^4$-$10^6$ ohm$^{-1}$ m$^{-1}$ in cool edge plasmas to $10^7$-$10^9$ ohm$^{-1}$ m$^{-1}$ in hot tokamak cores.

NAMES.name: poloidal_electric_field
NAMES.short: Projection of the electromagnetic force per unit charge onto the poloidal direction around magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
The poloidal electric field is the component of the plasma [electric field](name:electric_field) tangent to the poloidal circuit of a magnetic flux surface. It differs from the [radial electric field](name:radial_electric_field), which points across flux surfaces, and from the [toroidal electric field](name:toroidal_electric_field), which is associated with toroidal induction and loop voltage.

For a local flux-coordinate basis $(\psi,\theta,\phi)$, with $\theta$ the poloidal angle and $\hat{e}_\theta$ the unit vector in the increasing-$\theta$ direction, the component is defined by

$$
E_\theta = \mathbf{E} \cdot \hat{e}_\theta
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric-field vector and $E_\theta$ is its poloidal projection. In electrostatic descriptions this component is related to the poloidal variation of the potential, while in transient plasmas inductive contributions from the time-varying vector potential may also contribute.

It is computed from electric-potential reconstructions, electromagnetic transport models, or constrained by measurements sensitive to flows and force balance. Direct measurement is difficult; charge-exchange spectroscopy, Doppler reflectometry, and comparisons with [poloidal electron velocity](name:poloidal_electron_velocity) can help constrain the associated drift physics.

Representative magnitudes range from a few V m$^{-1}$ in slowly evolving core regions to $10^2$-$10^4$ V m$^{-1}$ near edges, transport barriers, or rapid MHD activity. The [parallel electric field](name:parallel_electric_field) is often treated separately because it controls field-aligned acceleration and Ohmic current drive.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electric-field projection points in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in flux coordinates $(\psi,\theta,\phi)$.

NAMES.name: poloidal_electron_velocity
NAMES.short: Projection of the bulk electron fluid flow onto the poloidal direction around nested magnetic flux surfaces.
NAMES.long:
Poloidal electron velocity is the component of the bulk electron fluid velocity tangent to the poloidal circuit of a magnetic flux surface. It distinguishes motion around the short way of the torus from toroidal rotation and radial transport, and is one component of the full [electron velocity](name:electron_velocity). It is interpreted together with [radial electron velocity](name:radial_electron_velocity), [toroidal electron velocity](name:toroidal_electron_velocity), and [parallel electron velocity](name:parallel_electron_velocity) to separate cross-field flow, field-aligned flow, and rotation.

For a flux-coordinate description $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$, where $\rho$ labels flux surfaces, $\theta$ is the poloidal angle, and $\phi$ is the toroidal angle, the component is the projection of the electron fluid velocity onto the poloidal unit direction:

$$
v_{e\theta} = \mathbf{v}_e \cdot \hat{e}_\theta
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_e$ is the electron fluid velocity, $\hat{e}_\theta$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing poloidal angle, and $v_{e\theta}$ is in m s$^{-1}$.

Direct measurement of electron poloidal flow is difficult; it is commonly inferred from momentum balance, neoclassical transport calculations, radial force balance, and consistency with measured [electron density](name:electron_density), [electron temperature](name:electron_temperature), and electric-field information such as [poloidal electric field](name:poloidal_electric_field). In magnetized tokamak plasmas, values are often smaller than toroidal rotation, with core magnitudes from a few hundred to several thousand m s$^{-1}$ and edge or pedestal values reaching several km s$^{-1}$ depending on collisionality and radial electric-field shear.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron fluid velocity has a component in the direction of increasing poloidal angle $\theta$ in the chosen flux-coordinate system $(\rho, \theta, \phi)$.

NAMES.name: radial_electric_field
NAMES.short: Projection of the plasma electric-field vector along the outward radial direction, controlling cross-field drifts and radial force balance.
NAMES.long:
The radial electric field is the component of the plasma [electric field](name:electric_field) across magnetic flux surfaces, directed outward from the magnetic axis toward the plasma boundary. It is central to neoclassical transport, ambipolar particle flux balance, and sheared $E \times B$ rotation that can influence turbulence suppression. It complements directional components such as the [toroidal electric field](name:toroidal_electric_field), [poloidal electric field](name:poloidal_electric_field), and [parallel electric field](name:parallel_electric_field).

For an electrostatic contribution expressed in a flux-surface radial coordinate $r$, the radial field is related to the electrostatic potential $\Phi$ by

$$
E_r = -\frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial r}
$$

where $E_r$ is the radial electric-field component, $\Phi$ is the electrostatic potential, and $r$ increases outward from the magnetic axis. In more general time-varying cases, inductive contributions from the vector potential may also enter the full [electric field](name:electric_field).

It is computed from radial force balance, neoclassical ambipolarity, or transport modeling, and can be constrained experimentally using charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, Doppler reflectometry, heavy-ion beam probes, or measurements of flows and pressure gradients. Related flow responses include [radial electron velocity](name:radial_electron_velocity), while [parallel plasma electrical conductivity](name:parallel_plasma_electrical_conductivity) controls the current response to the field-aligned component rather than the radial one.

Typical core tokamak values are about 1-50 kV/m, with edge pedestal or transport-barrier values reaching 50-300 kV/m over narrow radial layers.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electric-field vector points outward from the magnetic axis toward increasing flux-surface radius.

NAMES.name: radial_electron_velocity
NAMES.short: Electron fluid flow projected along increasing major radius in the right-handed cylindrical R-phi-Z geometry.
NAMES.long:
Radial electron velocity is the component of the bulk [electron_velocity](name:electron_velocity) directed across nested magnetic surfaces in the radial direction of the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It describes inward or outward electron fluid motion and is closely related to cross-field particle transport, distinct from the field-aligned motion described by [parallel_electron_velocity](name:parallel_electron_velocity) and the geometric angular components [poloidal_electron_velocity](name:poloidal_electron_velocity) and [toroidal_electron_velocity](name:toroidal_electron_velocity).

The projection from the electron fluid velocity vector is

$$
v_{e,R} = \mathbf{v}_e \cdot \hat{R}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_e$ is the electron fluid velocity in m s$^{-1}$, $\hat{R}$ is the unit vector toward increasing major radius, and $v_{e,R}$ is the radial component.

This quantity is inferred from transport analysis, particle continuity, and combinations of density evolution with source and sink estimates; direct interpretation may also use drift decompositions involving the [radial_electric_field](name:radial_electric_field). Representative core values are often small compared with toroidal and parallel flows, commonly from about $10^{-2}$-$10^{1}$ m s$^{-1}$ for slow diffusive particle transport, while edge and transient conditions can reach $10^{2}$-$10^{4}$ m s$^{-1}$. Comparing with [radial_ion_velocity](name:radial_ion_velocity) helps diagnose ambipolarity, charge separation tendencies, and species-dependent cross-field transport.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron fluid velocity component points toward increasing major radius $R$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R,\phi,Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: radial_ion_velocity
NAMES.short: Outward flux-surface-normal component of the ion fluid motion, carrying ion particles across nested magnetic surfaces in transport analyzes.
NAMES.long:
Radial ion velocity is the projection of the ion fluid velocity onto the outward direction normal to nested magnetic flux surfaces. It is the cross-field convective motion of an ion population and is the component of [ion_velocity] most directly associated with particle transport, unlike the field-aligned [parallel ion velocity](name:parallel_ion_velocity) or rotational [toroidal ion velocity](name:toroidal_ion_velocity).

The component is defined by the projection

$$
v_{i,r} = \mathbf{v}_i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{e}}_r
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_i$ is the ion fluid velocity vector, $\hat{\mathbf{e}}_r$ is the outward unit vector normal to the chosen flux surface, and $v_{i,r}$ is the radial component. In transport modeling it enters the ion particle flux through the relation $\Gamma_i = n_i v_{i,r}$, where $n_i$ is the [ion density](name:ion_density).

Direct measurement of this component is difficult because cross-field flows are small compared with toroidal and parallel rotation. It is commonly inferred from particle balance, ion continuity analysis, transport modeling, or consistency with measured charge-exchange flow components and equilibrium geometry; comparison with [radial electron velocity](name:radial_electron_velocity) is used in ambipolar transport studies.

Representative core values are much smaller than thermal speeds, often from fractions of 1 m s^-1 to tens of m s^-1 in quiescent core conditions, with larger transient values during strong fueling, pellets, edge relaxation events, or rapid profile evolution.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the ion fluid motion is outward from the magnetic axis toward larger flux-surface radius.

NAMES.name: thermal_electron_density
NAMES.short: Number of Maxwellian bulk electrons per unit volume, excluding suprathermal electrons treated as a fast population.
NAMES.long:
Thermal electron density is the number density associated with the bulk, near-Maxwellian electron population that participates in collisional transport and quasineutral force balance. It is the thermal-population contribution to [electron density](name:electron_density), distinct from the suprathermal contribution described by [fast electron density](name:fast_electron_density).

A kinetic definition is the velocity-space integral of the thermal part of the electron distribution function:

$$
n_{e,\mathrm{th}}(\mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathcal{V}_\mathrm{th}} f_e(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $n_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal electron density, $f_e$ is the electron distribution function, $\mathbf{x}$ is position, $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity, and $\mathcal{V}_\mathrm{th}$ denotes the velocity-space region assigned to the thermal population.

It is inferred from Thomson scattering, interferometry, reflectometry, and transport analysis; when energetic electrons are present, the thermal component is obtained by separating or subtracting the contribution associated with [fast electron density](name:fast_electron_density). Through quasineutrality, it is closely coupled to [thermal ion density], and together with electron temperature it determines the thermal part of [electron pressure](name:electron_pressure).

Typical core values in magnetic-confinement plasmas span $0.1-2 \times 10^{20}\;\mathrm{m^{-3}}$, while edge and scrape-off-layer values are lower and vary strongly with fueling, recycling, and confinement regime.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the velocity-space integral of the thermal electron distribution function is positive.

NAMES.name: thermal_electron_pressure
NAMES.short: Isotropic kinetic pressure carried by bulk electrons through their random thermal motion, excluding directed flow and nonthermal electron populations.
NAMES.long:
Thermal electron pressure is the isotropic part of the electron kinetic stress associated with random motion about the mean electron flow. It describes the bulk Maxwellian electron contribution and is distinct from total [electron pressure](name:electron_pressure) when fast or nonthermal electron populations contribute.

For a Maxwellian electron population, the pressure is related to density and temperature by

$$
p_{e,\mathrm{th}} = n_{e,\mathrm{th}} e T_e
$$

where $p_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal electron pressure in Pa, $n_{e,\mathrm{th}}$ is the [thermal electron density](name:thermal_electron_density) in m$^{-3}$, $T_e$ is the [electron temperature](name:electron_temperature) in eV, and $e$ is the elementary charge used to convert electron-volts to joules. In a multispecies pressure balance, this contribution is compared with [thermal ion pressure](name:thermal_ion_pressure) and ion charge-state pressures such as [state pressure](name:thermal_ion_state_pressure).

It is computed from combined electron density and temperature measurements, with Thomson scattering, interferometry, electron cyclotron emission, and edge Langmuir probes providing common inputs in magnetized fusion plasmas. Representative values span about 1-200 kPa in hot tokamak cores and 0.01-1 kPa in edge and scrape-off-layer conditions.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron distribution has a positive second central velocity moment.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_pressure
NAMES.short: Isotropic kinetic pressure produced by random thermal motion of the bulk ion population, excluding fast or nonthermal ion contributions.
NAMES.long:
Thermal ion pressure is the isotropic part of the ion stress associated with random particle motion about the mean ion flow. It represents the bulk, thermalized ion contribution and excludes energetic-ion pressure, so it is the thermal component of [ion pressure](name:ion_pressure) and complements [thermal electron pressure](name:thermal_electron_pressure).

For a Maxwellian ion population, the defining relation is

$$
p_{i,\mathrm{th}} = \sum_s n_{i,s}\, e\, T_{i,s}
$$

where $p_{i,\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal ion pressure in Pa, $n_{i,s}$ is the number density of ion charge state or species $s$ in m$^{-3}$, $T_{i,s}$ is the corresponding [ion temperature](name:ion_temperature) in eV, and $e$ is the elementary charge converting eV to joules. If a single thermal ion population is represented, the sum reduces to $p_i = n_i e T_i$, with $n_i$ related to [ion density](name:ion_density).

It is computed from ion density and temperature measurements, with ion temperature often inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, neutral particle analysis, or transport modeling constrained by heating and power-balance data. Core values in present tokamaks range from about $10^3$-$10^5$ Pa, while edge and scrape-off-layer values are often much lower; large departures between this quantity and [perpendicular fast ion pressure](name:perpendicular_fast_ion_pressure) indicate a significant energetic-particle contribution.
NAMES.sign: Positive when random thermal ion motion produces a compressive isotropic pressure contribution in the plasma momentum balance.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_state_density
NAMES.short: Number of thermal ions per unit volume within a resolved ionization or charge-state bundle of an ion species.
NAMES.long:
Thermal ion state density is the population density of bulk, near-Maxwellian ions belonging to a specified ionization or charge-state bundle. Summing over resolved states gives the corresponding [thermal ion density], while including fast populations and unresolved states connects to the total [ion density](name:ion_density).

For a thermal ion species $i$ in charge state $Z$, it is the zeroth velocity-space moment of the state-resolved distribution function:

$$
n^{\mathrm{th}}_{i,Z} = \int f^{\mathrm{th}}_{i,Z}(\mathbf{v})\,d^3v
$$

where $f^{\mathrm{th}}_{i,Z}(\mathbf{v})$ is the thermal ion distribution function in velocity space and $\mathbf{v}$ is particle velocity. The same population contributes to [thermal ion state pressure](name:thermal_ion_state_pressure) through the thermal kinetic moment, and it is distinct from [fast ion state density](name:fast_ion_state_density), which describes suprathermal ions.

This quantity is inferred from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, passive line emission with collisional-radiative modeling, impurity transport analysis, and quasineutrality constraints combined with [electron density](name:electron_density). Representative core main-ion densities are $10^{19}$-$10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, while individual impurity charge-state densities can span $10^{14}$-$10^{18}$ m$^{-3}$ depending on concentration, ionization balance, and transport.

NAMES.name: thermal_ion_state_pressure
NAMES.short: Isotropic kinetic pressure produced by random thermal motion of ions within a resolved charge-state population, excluding fast-ion contributions.
NAMES.long:
Thermal ion-state pressure is the isotropic kinetic pressure carried by the thermal part of a resolved ion charge-state population. It is the charge-state-resolved contribution to [thermal ion pressure](name:thermal_ion_pressure) and excludes directional nonthermal pressure represented for energetic populations such as [fast ion-state pressure].

For a charge-state bundle with temperature expressed as an energy per particle, the defining relation is

$$
p_{i,Z}^{\mathrm{th}} = n_{i,Z}^{\mathrm{th}} e T_{i,Z}
$$

where $p_{i,Z}^{\mathrm{th}}$ is the thermal pressure, $n_{i,Z}^{\mathrm{th}}$ is the [thermal ion-state density](name:thermal_ion_state_density) in m$^{-3}$, $T_{i,Z}$ is the charge-state-resolved thermal ion temperature in eV, and $e$ is the elementary charge in coulombs. Summing over charge states gives the corresponding species contribution to [ion pressure](name:ion_pressure) when nonthermal components are absent or treated separately.

This quantity is computed from charge-state-resolved density and ion-temperature estimates. Density fractions are inferred from spectroscopy and collisional-radiative ionization balance, while thermal ion temperature is obtained from charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, Doppler broadening, or transport inference constrained by power balance.

Core values in fusion plasmas commonly span about $10^2$-$10^5$ Pa for abundant ion charge states, with edge and scrape-off-layer values falling to roughly $10^{-1}$-$10^3$ Pa depending on density, ionization state, and temperature. The total [ion-state pressure](name:ion_charge_state_pressure) may exceed this value when fast-ion or anisotropic pressure contributions are included.

NAMES.name: toroidal_electric_field
NAMES.short: Projection of the plasma electric field along the toroidal direction, driving toroidal current and inductive acceleration around the symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
The toroidal electric field is the component of the electromagnetic force per unit charge along the toroidal direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame. It is the component of [electric field](name:electric_field) most directly associated with inductive current drive, Ohmic heating, and acceleration of charged particles around the device symmetry axis.

The component is defined by the projection

$$
E_\phi = \mathbf{E} \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{E}$ is the electric-field vector and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$. In axisymmetric inductive operation, $E_\phi$ is closely related to the loop voltage through the approximate relation $E_\phi \simeq V_{\rm loop}/(2\pi R)$, where $R$ is major radius.

It is inferred from magnetic flux evolution, loop-voltage measurements, and transport or equilibrium analysis, often constrained together with [toroidal plasma current density](name:toroidal_plasma_current_density) and [electrical conductivity]. The orthogonal components [radial electric field](name:radial_electric_field) and [poloidal electric field](name:poloidal_electric_field) describe different force-balance and drift physics, while [parallel electric field](name:parallel_electric_field) captures acceleration along the magnetic field.

Typical values are 0.01-1 V m$^{-1}$ in inductively driven tokamak cores, with several V m$^{-1}$ possible during current ramp-up, disruptions, or current-quench phases.
NAMES.sign: Positive when $E_\phi$ points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_electron_velocity
NAMES.short: Bulk electron-fluid flow projected onto the toroidal direction, capturing electron rotation around the device symmetry axis.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal electron velocity is the azimuthal component of the bulk electron-fluid velocity around the torus. In the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height, it is the toroidal projection of [electron_velocity](name:electron_velocity) and complements [poloidal_electron_velocity](name:poloidal_electron_velocity), [radial_electron_velocity](name:radial_electron_velocity), and [parallel_electron_velocity](name:parallel_electron_velocity).

The defining projection is

$$
v_{e\phi} = \mathbf{v}_e \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{v}_e$ is the bulk electron-fluid velocity and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle. Through the current relation $\mathbf{j} = e n_e (\mathbf{v}_i - \mathbf{v}_e)$, the toroidal electron flow is coupled to [electron_density](name:electron_density), ion rotation such as [toroidal_ion_velocity](name:toroidal_ion_velocity), and the driven response to [toroidal_electric_field](name:toroidal_electric_field).

Direct measurement of electron toroidal flow is uncommon; it is commonly inferred from current-density reconstruction, electron momentum balance, density measurements, and constraints on ion flow. In edge or low-temperature plasmas, probe and spectroscopic methods may provide additional constraints on electron drift velocities.

Representative core values range from about $10^3$-$10^5$ m.s$^{-1}$, with larger magnitudes possible where strong current density, electric field, or steep pressure gradients drive electron motion relative to the ion fluid.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the electron fluid moves in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$ in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame.

NAMES.name: toroidal_ion_velocity
NAMES.short: Projection of bulk ion fluid motion around the device symmetry axis, capturing toroidal plasma rotation and angular momentum transport.
NAMES.long:
Toroidal ion velocity is the component of the bulk ion flow around the toroidal direction in the right-handed cylindrical $(R, \phi, Z)$ frame, where $R$ is major radius, $\phi$ is toroidal angle, and $Z$ is vertical height. It is the toroidal projection of [ion_velocity], distinct from thermal random motion described by [ion_temperature](name:ion_temperature), and it controls toroidal rotation, momentum confinement, and centrifugal effects.

The defining projection is

$$
v_{i\phi} = \mathbf{u}_i \cdot \hat{\phi}
$$

where $\mathbf{u}_i$ is the ion fluid velocity vector and $\hat{\phi}$ is the unit vector in the direction of increasing toroidal angle. This component complements [radial_ion_velocity](name:radial_ion_velocity), which describes cross-surface transport, and [parallel_ion_velocity](name:parallel_ion_velocity), which follows the magnetic-field direction.

Toroidal ion velocity is inferred from Doppler shifts of impurity or main-ion spectral lines, most often using charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, and may also be constrained by momentum-balance analysis. Core tokamak values commonly range from $10^4$ to $3\times10^5$ m.s$^{-1}$, with larger values in strongly beam-heated plasmas and smaller values in weakly driven or edge regions. Comparison with [toroidal_electron_velocity](name:toroidal_electron_velocity) helps separate bulk rotation from current-carrying electron-ion relative motion.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ion flow points in the direction of increasing toroidal angle $\phi$.

NAMES.name: total_ion_pressure
NAMES.short: Thermal kinetic pressure obtained by summing the isotropic pressure contributions of all ion species and resolved charge states.
NAMES.long:
Total ion pressure is the thermal isotropic pressure carried by the complete ion population, aggregated over ion species and resolved charge states. It is the ion part of the plasma thermal pressure and should be distinguished from [ion_pressure](name:ion_pressure) when that quantity includes non-thermal ion contributions.

For Maxwellian ion subpopulations, the defining relation is

$$
p_{i,\mathrm{tot}} = \sum_s \sum_Z n_{sZ} k_B T_{sZ}
$$

where $n_{sZ}$ is the number density of ion species $s$ in charge state $Z$, $T_{sZ}$ is its temperature, and $k_B$ is Boltzmann's constant. A single resolved contribution corresponds to [ion_state_pressure](name:ion_charge_state_pressure) or [ion_charge_state_pressure](name:ion_charge_state_pressure), while charge-state weighting is related to [ion_average_charge](name:ion_average_charge).

It is computed from ion density and temperature measurements, using charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, impurity line spectroscopy, neutral-particle analysis, and quasineutrality constraints combined with [ion_density](name:ion_density) and [ion_temperature](name:ion_temperature). Representative values range from 10^2-10^4 Pa near the edge to 10^4-10^5 Pa in high-performance tokamak cores; reactor-grade plasmas can reach several 10^5 Pa when electron and ion temperatures are both high.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the summed ion momentum flux corresponds to a compressive isotropic stress on a local surface element.

NAMES.name: total_thermal_ion_species_density
NAMES.short: Aggregate number density of Maxwellian bulk ion species contributing to quasineutrality, excluding suprathermal fast-ion populations.
NAMES.long:
This quantity represents the local sum of number densities over all thermal ion species in the bulk plasma. It differs from a single-species [thermal ion density] by aggregating species contributions, and it excludes energetic populations described by [fast ion density](name:fast_ion_density).

The species-summed thermal ion density is

$$
n_{i,\mathrm{th}}^{\mathrm{tot}} = \sum_s n_{s,\mathrm{th}}
$$

where $s$ labels each thermal ion species and $n_{s,\mathrm{th}}$ is that species' thermal number density in m$^{-3}$. In quasineutral plasmas it is constrained together with charge states by the electron balance, so interpretation often uses [electron density](name:electron_density), [ion density](name:ion_density), and [ion average charge](name:ion_average_charge).

It is inferred from a combination of interferometry or Thomson-scattering electron density, charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy, visible spectroscopy of impurities, neutral-beam or gas-fueling particle balance, and transport modeling that separates thermal species from fast-ion components.

Representative core values in present tokamak plasmas are about $0.1-1.5 \times 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, with lower edge and scrape-off-layer values around $10^{17}-10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ depending on fueling, confinement regime, and impurity dilution. The closely related [total thermal ion density] may be used when the thermal ion ensemble is not resolved by species.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_electron_density
NAMES.short: Plasma-volume mean of the electron number density, weighting each spatial element by its contribution to the confined plasma volume.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged electron density is the global mean electron number density over the confined plasma volume. It condenses the spatially varying [electron density](name:electron_density) into a single particle-inventory measure and is interpreted together with [plasma volume](name:volume_of_plasma_boundary) when comparing fueling level and confinement between discharges.

The defining average is

$$
\langle n_e \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_p}\int_{V_p} n_e(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $n_e(\mathbf{x})$ is the local electron density in m$^{-3}$, $dV$ is the volume element in m$^3$, and $V_p$ is the confined plasma volume in m$^3$. The same averaging operation applied to ion populations gives [volume-averaged ion density](name:volume_averaged_ion_density), while [volume of flux surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface) provides the geometric basis for flux-surface-resolved volume integration.

It is computed from density reconstructions constrained by interferometry, Thomson scattering, reflectometry, or microwave diagnostics, combined with an equilibrium boundary defining the averaging volume. Representative tokamak values are about $0.1-2\times10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$ in the confined plasma, with startup and low-density phases below this range and high-performance scenarios approaching operational density limits.
NAMES.sign: Positive when electrons contribute positive particle number density to the confined plasma inventory.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_ion_density
NAMES.short: Plasma-volume mean number concentration of the ion population, used as a global measure of ion inventory and fueling state.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged ion density is the spatial mean of the local ion number density over the confined plasma volume bounded by the last closed flux surface. It compresses the distribution described by [ion density](name:ion_density) into a single inventory-like measure, enabling comparison with [volume-averaged electron density](name:volume_averaged_electron_density) and with thermal-population measures such as [total thermal ion density].

The defining average is

$$
\langle n_i \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V_p}\int_{V_p} n_i(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $n_i(\mathbf{x})$ is the local ion number density at position $\mathbf{x}$, $V_p$ is the enclosed plasma volume, and $dV$ is the volume element. The geometric normalization is set by the same confined volume concept used in [volume of flux surface](name:volume_of_flux_surface).

It is inferred from particle-balance analysis, charge-state and quasineutrality constraints, ionization modeling, and density diagnostics combined with composition measurements. Representative core-fusion values are about $0.1-2 \times 10^{20}$ m$^{-3}$, with lower values during startup or low-density operation and higher values in fueled H-mode plasmas. It is often interpreted together with [volume-averaged ion temperature](name:volume_averaged_ion_temperature) to assess ion thermal content and confinement.
NAMES.sign: Positive when ions are counted as particles contributing positively to the volume integral.

NAMES.name: volume_averaged_ion_temperature
NAMES.short: Ion thermal energy per degree of freedom averaged over the confined plasma volume, giving a global measure of ion heat content.
NAMES.long:
The volume-averaged ion temperature is the spatial average of the local ion thermal temperature over the confined plasma volume, usually bounded by the last closed flux surface. It compresses the local [ion temperature](name:ion_temperature) distribution into a single global transport metric that is directly related to stored ion thermal energy and confinement quality.

For plasma volume $V$ and local ion temperature $T_i(\mathbf{x})$, the volume average is

$$
\langle T_i \rangle_V = \frac{1}{V}\int_V T_i(\mathbf{x})\,dV
$$

where $\mathbf{x}$ denotes position in the plasma volume and $dV$ is the physical volume element. Combined with [volume-averaged ion density](name:volume_averaged_ion_density), this quantity constrains the ion contribution to thermal pressure and energy content; the related local thermodynamic measure is [ion pressure](name:ion_pressure).

It is computed by integrating ion-temperature measurements or reconstructed ion-temperature fields over the confined volume. Charge-exchange recombination spectroscopy provides common local ion-temperature measurements, while profile reconstruction and equilibrium geometry define the volume weighting; neutron spectroscopy can add constraints in high-temperature deuterium-tritium plasmas.

Typical volume-averaged values range from 0.2-5 keV in present medium-size tokamak discharges and can reach 5-20 keV in high-performance reactor-relevant plasmas. The value is lower than the central ion temperature when edge and pedestal regions occupy a substantial fraction of the plasma volume.
NAMES.sign: Positive when the averaged ion thermal energy is above the zero-energy reference used for temperature.
